papers_seen.author: Alvarado
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing neural networks into smaller, faster models by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations from teacher to student. A broad family of distillation techniques has been developed—logit (soft-label) matching, feature and layer-wise mimicry, multi-teacher and confidence-weighted schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware variants—enabling deployment across vision, language, graphs, recommender systems, and federated settings. While distillation often preserves most teacher performance and can even improve student generalization, effectiveness depends on what is transferred, layer alignment, teacher quality, availability and match of data, and complementary compression methods. This synthesis summarizes the operational variants, key empirical findings, domain-specific applications, common failure modes, and practical recommendations distilled from the provided studies.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad family of KD objectives and workflows—soft-target matching, intermediate-representation mimicking, relational or attention-map transfer, multi-teacher and self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware variants—has been developed and applied across vision, language, graph, and recommendation settings. Empirical and theoretical work demonstrates substantial practical gains in latency, memory, and deployability when KD is combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware mapping), but success depends on careful choices about teacher quality, student capacity, data, and objective design; remaining challenges include optimization difficulties, distribution shift, rare-token performance, and bias or privacy leakage.

papers_seen.author: Bray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task‑Aware Tool for Model Compression (with Limits and Practical Remedies)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a practical, versatile framework for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized students. When applied with task‑aware objectives, appropriate data strategies, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, or architecture search), KD routinely yields compact models suitable for latency- and memory-constrained deployment. However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher quality and compatibility with the student, the choice of distilled signals, data availability and augmentation, and mitigation of teacher artifacts. Careful protocol design—pre-training compact architectures, selecting what to distill, using effective augmentation or data synthesis, and combining KD with complementary methods—produces the most reliable results in practice.

papers_seen.author: Welch
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression and Generalization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a niche compression trick into a broadly applicable paradigm that enables deployment of large models across modalities, supports privacy- and resource-constrained federated scenarios, and improves generalization when combined with task- and architecture-specific techniques. Empirical evidence shows that KD alone yields large gains for small students, while hybrid approaches that distill internal representations, use curriculum or meta-learning, augment data, or jointly optimize architecture and distillation produce state-of-the-art trade-offs between size, speed, and task performance. KD is therefore a foundational tool for modern model compression strategies and should be used in concert with complementary methods (e.g., pretraining, low-precision numerics, structural compression, and privacy-aware distillation) to meet real-world deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hughes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically effective family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models to meet deployment constraints (latency, memory, compute, and privacy). KD spans logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, many-to-many layer mappings, online and multi‑teacher protocols, and data‑free or synthetic‑data variants. While KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss, its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, distillation signals, data availability, and safeguards against bias and privacy leakage. Thus KD should be treated as a configurable core of compression pipelines—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and task‑aware engineering—rather than a plug‑and‑play cure-all.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Mckee
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central, flexible approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, retrieval, generative modeling, and federated settings. A broad set of techniques—matching soft logits, imitating intermediate features or attention, adversarial and curriculum-based sample selection, ensemble and multi-teacher guidance, and data- or privacy-aware generation—enable students to retain much of teacher performance while reducing parameters, latency, and memory. Empirical evidence shows distilled students often approach teacher performance, but limitations persist (teacher errors, optimization gaps, domain and data mismatch, low-frequency phenomena, and heterogeneity of devices/architectures). Advances such as feature-based distillation, curriculum strategies, adversarial sample use, many-to-many layer alignment, student-friendly teacher design, and teacher-free/self-distillation extend applicability and mitigate failure modes. Key open problems include principled theory for which teacher signals matter across tasks, robust private and data-free distillation, and automated co-design of student architectures and distillation objectives for heterogeneous deployments.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Findings from the Provided Literature
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact students. KD methods operate at multiple levels (output logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive signals) and through diverse protocols (offline, online, self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free, and privacy-aware variants). Empirical and practical work shows KD often recovers most of a teacher’s performance while enabling large gains in latency, memory, and deployment cost; however, its reliability is context-dependent, hinging on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, data availability and augmentation, and integration with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture design.

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models to reduce latency, memory, and compute while retaining much of teacher performance. A diverse set of distillation targets and training protocols has been developed (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive signals; offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, and data‑free variants). Empirical work across vision, language, speech and multimodal tasks shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and is most effective when integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and when training/data procedures are adapted to task and deployment constraints. Remaining gaps include principled layer alignment across heterogeneous architectures, robust distillation under limited or private data, preservation of long‑tail/low‑frequency behaviors, and theoretical understanding of when particular teacher signals are necessary.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Private Model Compression via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The soaring demand for intelligent mobile applications calls for deploying powerful deep neural networks (DNNs) on mobile devices. However, the outstanding performance of DNNs notoriously relies on increasingly complex models, which in turn is associated with an increase in computational expense far surpassing mobile devices' capacity. What is worse, app service providers need to collect and utilize a large volume of users' data, which contain sensitive information, to build the sophisticated DNN models. Directly deploying these models on public mobile devices presents prohibitive privacy risk. To benefit from the on-device deep learning without the capacity and privacy concerns, we design a private model compression framework RONA. Following the knowledge distillation paradigm, we jointly use hint learning, distillation learning, and self learning to train a compact and fast neural network. The knowledge distilled from the cumbersome model is adaptively bounded and carefully perturbed to enforce differential privacy. We further propose an elegant query sample selection method to reduce the number of queries and control the privacy loss. A series of empirical evaluations as well as the implementation on an Android mobile device show that RONA can not only compress cumbersome models efficiently but also provide a strong privacy guarantee. For example, on SVHN, when a meaningful $(9.83,10^{-6})$-differential privacy is guaranteed, the compact model trained by RONA can obtain 20$\times$ compression ratio and 19$\times$ speed-up with merely 0.97% accuracy loss.

papers_seen.author: Obrien
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broad toolbox for transferring predictive capacity from large, expensive models to smaller, faster, or privacy-preserving models. Methods range from soft-logit supervision to internal representation matching, contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical evidence across vision, NLP, graphs, and federated settings shows KD can recover much of a teacher's performance in resource-constrained deployments, while challenges remain in teacher selection, data availability, bias propagation, and task-specific design.

papers_seen.author: Chambers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a broad family of techniques that transfer information from larger, often multi-source or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across vision, language, speech, multimodal and generative settings, KD has evolved beyond simple logit matching to include representation- and relation-level objectives, adversarial or data-free generation, online and self-distillation protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization and architecture search. These approaches routinely enable large reductions in inference cost and memory while preserving much of teacher performance, but reliable deployment requires task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data. Important open directions remain in principled theory, robust distillation under heterogenous and low-data regimes, and preserving long-tail or low-frequency behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Andrews
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression: Essential, Context‑Sensitive, and Best Used as Part of an Integrated Pipeline
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an essential, broadly applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical and methodological work across vision, language, graph, and recommendation systems shows KD can recover much of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, latency, and memory. However, KD’s success is strongly context-dependent: it requires task-aware choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data and deployment constraints. Responsible, robust compression therefore treats KD as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline that also uses complementary techniques and explicit mitigations for known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Contextual Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and empirically validated approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained students. It operates at multiple levels (soft targets, intermediate representations, attention/relational signals, contrastive and adversarial objectives) and is most effective when tailored to the task, student capacity, data regime, and deployment constraints. Practical deployments combine distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and explicit protocols to mitigate failure modes such as teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and the transfer of biases or private information. Responsible application requires task-aware teacher–student design, data strategies (including data-free or few-shot methods when necessary), and monitoring for degraded behavior on low-frequency or structured outputs.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models (or ensembles) to smaller, more deployable student models. KD variants—ranging from soft-target (logit) matching to intermediate-feature and relational objectives, multi- and self-distillation, adversarial schemes, and data- or privacy-aware variants—have been applied across vision, language, graph, generative, and federated settings. When combined with careful teacher selection, data strategies, layer mapping, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design), KD routinely yields favorable trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and model size, while posing important challenges around distribution shift, teacher–student mismatch, bias transfer, and preserving fine-grained behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Morales
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Conditional Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and practical set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD succeeds by transferring rich forms of information — soft logits, intermediate features, attention patterns, relational or contrastive structure, and even synthesized data — and by being combined with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. However, KD is not an automatic remedy: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, data availability and privacy constraints, and defenses against transferring teacher errors or low-frequency phenomena. Treating KD as a configurable, task-aware component within a broader compression pipeline, and adopting practices such as layer- and task-aware objectives, multi-teacher confidence weighting, adversarial or decision-boundary sample generation, and data-aware synthesis or augmentation, yields the most reliable trade-offs between efficiency and fidelity. Remaining research directions include principled guidance for selecting which signals to transfer, robust privacy-preserving distillation, and automated, deployment-aware distillation pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a broad family of techniques for transferring information from larger or richer models (teachers) into smaller, more efficient models (students). KD methods range from matching teacher output distributions to aligning internal representations and using synthesized or privatized data; they are effective across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal tasks and are commonly integrated with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical evidence shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while improving inference cost, but success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and safeguards against propagating undesirable teacher properties. Current practice treats KD as a configurable component of wider compression pipelines rather than a single algorithm, and several methodological extensions and safeguards have been proposed to address its known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Sensitive Strategy for Model Compression: Efficacy, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably reduces model size and inference cost by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller students. KD encompasses a range of transfer signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structures), training protocols (offline, online, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation), and deployment strategies (data‑constrained, privacy‑aware, federated and heterogeneous devices). While KD is an effective first‑line tool for many compression needs, its success depends on careful choice of what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and integration with complementary compression techniques. Responsible deployment requires explicit safeguards against propagating teacher errors, biased behavior, and degradation on low‑frequency or out‑of‑distribution phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners transfer logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or decision-boundary information and combine KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or data-free generation) to meet latency, memory, privacy, and domain constraints. Empirical work shows distilled students often recover most teacher performance and, in some cases, match or exceed teachers when distillation is paired with careful teacher design, layer mapping, and data or training schedules. Major limitations remain in imperfect belief matching, distribution shift, handling low-frequency phenomena, heterogeneous or privacy-constrained data, and principled teacher selection—areas where methodological and theoretical progress continues to be needed.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Towards Model Agnostic Federated Learning Using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Is it possible to design an universal API for federated learning using which an ad-hoc group of data-holders (agents) collaborate with each other and perform federated learning? Such an API would necessarily need to be model-agnostic i.e. make no assumption about the model architecture being used by the agents, and also cannot rely on having representative public data at hand. Knowledge distillation (KD) is the obvious tool of choice to design such protocols. However, surprisingly, we show that most natural KD-based federated learning protocols have poor performance.   To investigate this, we propose a new theoretical framework, Federated Kernel ridge regression, which can capture both model heterogeneity as well as data heterogeneity. Our analysis shows that the degradation is largely due to a fundamental limitation of knowledge distillation under data heterogeneity. We further validate our framework by analyzing and designing new protocols based on KD. Their performance on real world experiments using neural networks, though still unsatisfactory, closely matches our theoretical predictions.

papers_seen.author: Murray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential but Context‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical set of techniques for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models in deep learning and NLP. KD can preserve much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but its success depends on task-aware choices: what signals to transfer (logits, features, attention, relations), teacher–student alignment, available data (real, synthetic, or none), and complementary compression strategies (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Responsible and robust deployment further requires addressing distribution shift, low‑frequency or structured outputs, privacy and fairness concerns, and principled selection of distillation targets. I argue KD should be treated as a configurable toolkit — often essential for practical compression — rather than a turnkey solution; practitioners should select and combine distillation recipes according to capacity, data, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Garrison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational, Practical, but Not Sufficiently Complete Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, widely applicable approach for compressing large or ensemble models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their accuracy. KD techniques extend beyond logit matching to feature- and layer-level alignment, attention and projection-based mappings, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and data-constrained regimes (few-shot, data-free). KD reliably improves deployment trade-offs (latency, memory, and sometimes robustness or privacy), but it has concrete limits—teacher–student capacity mismatch, data heterogeneity, and task-specific design needs—that make KD most effective when integrated with complementary compression and training practices.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). However, surprisingly, the simple baseline of just pre-training and fine-tuning compact models has been overlooked. In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. To accelerate future research, we will make our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models publicly available.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: A Central, Context‑Aware Tool for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD can transfer predictive behavior and internal representations through many targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive signals) and protocols (offline teacher, multi‑teacher, online, adversarial, and data‑free variants). Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability and nature of distillation data, and protections against transferred biases or privacy leakage. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline—chosen and tuned with task, data regime, and deployment constraints in mind—rather than a standalone cure‑all.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Yet Contextual, Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has repeatedly enabled substantial reductions in model size and inference cost across modalities while retaining much of the performance of larger models. Empirical work shows KD can transfer predictive behavior, inductive biases, and task-specific capabilities from teacher to student, and can be adapted via logit-, feature-, and layer-level objectives, multi-teacher schemes, adversarial procedures, and data- or privacy-aware variants. However, KD is not a universal solution: optimization difficulties, teacher–student mismatch, data heterogeneity, and propagation of teacher errors limit its effectiveness unless combined with careful protocol design and complementary compression techniques. I argue KD should be treated as a first-class tool in compression toolkits, but only when used with task-aware filtering, capacity-aware targets, and architecture- or data-aware refinements to mitigate known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Wallace
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically proven family of methods for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more deployable student models. KD spans outputs-only approaches (soft targets) to rich objectives that match intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure, or contrastive signals. It operates across many data regimes (full-data, limited-data, data-free, synthetic-data), and is frequently combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to achieve deployment constraints on latency, memory, privacy, and device heterogeneity. The effectiveness of KD is strongly context dependent: success requires attention to teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distilled signals and layer mappings, and data strategies (including augmentation, curriculum, and synthetic generation). Common failure modes include propagation of teacher errors or biases, difficulty preserving low-frequency or long-tail behaviors, and optimization barriers that prevent perfect mimicry, motivating targeted remedies such as multi-signal objectives, multi-teacher ensembles, teacher scheduling, meta-learned teachers, and joint optimization with other compression tools.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Cross-Domain Argument for Practical, Responsible, and Multi-Modal Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are indispensable for deploying modern deep models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. Across vision, language, graph, and generative domains, distillation methods can preserve most of a teacher's performance while reducing latency, memory, and communication. Best results come from (a) matching appropriate internal representations (layer mapping, attention, many-to-many mappings), (b) designing teachers or multi-teacher schemes that are student-aware, and (c) combining distillation with complementary techniques (pruning, NAS, adversarial training, federated schemes). However, practitioners must be mindful of failure modes—bias amplification, degraded modeling of rare phenomena, and gaps when no training data are available—and adopt targeted mitigations such as task-adaptive compression, confidence-aware multi-teacher weighting, and data-free or privacy-preserving distillation when necessary.

papers_seen.author: Scott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression: Evidence, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable technique for compressing large models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. KD has been shown to work across modalities and tasks by transferring logits, intermediate representations, attention patterns, or relational structure. It can also be combined with data augmentation, adversarial schemes, online or teacher-free training, and architecture-aware adaptations to meet deployment constraints. KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on choices about which teacher signals to transfer, alignment of inputs and architectures, student capacity, and the availability or synthesis of suitable data. When used as part of a task-aware compression pipeline that addresses these issues, KD delivers substantial practical benefits for latency- and resource-constrained deployments.

papers_seen.author: Jefferson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central and Practical — but Context‑Dependent — Core of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or auxiliary teacher models into compact students. KD can recover much of teacher performance across modalities when paired with task‑aware choices of distilled targets, data strategies, and complementary compression primitives; however, its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and explicit safeguards against transferred artifacts and distributional mismatch. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline rather than as a plug‑and‑play silver bullet.

papers_seen.author: Murray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Insufficient Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, flexible approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical evidence across vision and language shows KD can substantially reduce inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance, but its success depends on careful choices about what information is transferred, how teachers and students are aligned, and how distillation is combined with complementary compression methods. I argue KD should be treated as the central element of an integrated, task-aware compression pipeline rather than a sole solution.

papers_seen.author: Guerrero
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Component of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an empirically validated and flexible approach for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers. KD reliably reduces inference cost and enables deployment across modalities when integrated thoughtfully with complementary compression methods. Its success is context dependent — determined by teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer and loss of rare behaviors — so practitioners should treat KD as a configurable element of a broader compression pipeline rather than a one-shot solution.

papers_seen.author: Guerrero
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. KD supports many transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention, relational constraints), can be adapted to data‑limited and data‑free regimes, and combines productively with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). However, reliable deployment requires task‑aware design: selecting appropriate distillation objectives, aligning teacher and student capacities and architectures, addressing data regimes and privacy constraints, and mitigating failure modes such as bias transfer and degradation on rare or low‑frequency phenomena. Treated as a configurable core of compression pipelines and paired with targeted algorithmic and engineering practices, KD enables practical, deployable model compression across modalities and settings.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied framework for compressing large models, improving generalization, and transferring capabilities across modalities and deployment constraints. Research spans teacher-student paradigms (including multi-teacher and self-distillation), data-free and zero-shot distillation, task-adaptive compression, and applications to specialized tasks (detection, retrieval, translation, multimodal learning, federated settings, and graph problems). Empirical work shows KD can yield large speed and size gains while retaining much of the teacher's performance, but also exposes important limitations tied to optimization, data used for distillation, and potential bias transfer. Recent methods address these limitations via curriculum scheduling, confidence- or reinforcement-based teacher weighting, task-adaptive architecture search, domain- and modality-aware losses, and efficient label-generation or student-focused training regimes.

papers_seen.author: Pollard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for training smaller, faster models by transferring information from larger teacher models. Across vision, language, graphs, and multimodal tasks, KD methods transfer predictive and representational signals (soft logits, internal features, attention maps, relational or contrastive signals) and operate under a range of training protocols (offline teacher→student, online/co-distillation, multi-teacher, self-distillation, and data-free or synthetic-data approaches). Empirical work shows KD often recovers much of teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, distillation signals, and data strategy are chosen carefully. Practical deployment typically treats KD as a core, configurable component of a broader compression pipeline that also includes pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data-side strategies. Open challenges include principled theory of transferable signals, robust distillation under data scarcity and heterogeneity, privacy-aware or data-free methods, and preserving low-frequency or long-tail behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Rivas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers information from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under resource or privacy constraints, and sometimes improve calibration, robustness, or task adaptation. The field has evolved from logits-based soft-target training to a rich toolkit that includes intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free approaches, multi-teacher and online schemes, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity and task constraints, handling limited or mismatched data, and explicitly addressing risks such as transferred biases or privacy leakage. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a single turnkey algorithm.

papers_seen.author: Morris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Sensitive Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable method for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and communication while often retaining much of teacher performance; it admits many transfer targets (logits, features, attention maps, relational signals) and protocols (offline, online, data-free, multi‑teacher). However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and alignment, and careful objective and pipeline design. Best practice treats KD as a core element of an integrated, task-aware compression strategy combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware mapping) and targeted remedies for failure modes such as capacity mismatch, distribution shift, rare-token degradation, and bias transfer.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Ranking Distillation: Learning Compact Ranking Models With High Performance for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel way to train ranking models, such as recommender systems, that are both effective and efficient. Knowledge distillation (KD) was shown to be successful in image recognition to achieve both effectiveness and efficiency. We propose a KD technique for learning to rank problems, called \emph{ranking distillation (RD)}. Specifically, we train a smaller student model to learn to rank documents/items from both the training data and the supervision of a larger teacher model. The student model achieves a similar ranking performance to that of the large teacher model, but its smaller model size makes the online inference more efficient. RD is flexible because it is orthogonal to the choices of ranking models for the teacher and student. We address the challenges of RD for ranking problems. The experiments on public data sets and state-of-the-art recommendation models showed that RD achieves its design purposes: the student model learnt with RD has a model size less than half of the teacher model while achieving a ranking performance similar to the teacher model and much better than the student model learnt without RD.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.author: Kane
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Powerful, but Context‑Aware
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and mature family of techniques that enables compact models to inherit much of the performance and functionality of larger teachers, making it a central tool for deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD has been extended far beyond simple logits matching to include intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols. While KD routinely yields major efficiency gains and often recovers most teacher performance, reliable deployment requires task- and data-aware design choices and complementary compression methods; KD alone is not a universal remedy.

papers_seen.author: Ferguson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones while retaining much of their performance. KD has been extended from soft-label/logit transfer to a rich set of representation- and task-level objectives (feature matching, attention and relation alignment, projector modules, online/multi-teacher schemes, and data-free methods). When applied with task awareness — choosing what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data, privacy, and hardware constraints — KD consistently enables substantial reductions in size and latency with modest accuracy loss. However, KD is not a panacea: its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, data availability, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and low-frequency behaviors. Best practice treats KD as a configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline combined with pruning, quantization, and hardware-aware design.

papers_seen.author: Lawson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context-Aware Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a proven, flexible approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers across vision and NLP. KD works at multiple levels (logits, features, layers) and is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods and task-aware engineering. At the same time, KD has concrete limitations (teacher imperfections, data scarcity, student capacity mismatch) that require deliberate mitigation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Potter
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible set of methods for transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models to enable deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, or privacy. Across vision and natural language tasks, distillation targets range from soft logits to intermediate representations and relational signals; KD is frequently combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with domain- or task-specific procedures to improve efficacy. KD delivers strong empirical gains in many settings but is bounded by teacher quality, availability and match of data, teacher–student capacity gaps, and the risk of transferring teacher biases; effective application therefore requires task-aware choices of signals, data strategies, and often hybrid compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of methods for transferring knowledge from large, high-capacity teacher models to smaller, efficient student models so that students achieve improved accuracy, latency, or resource use while retaining much of teacher behavior. Methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, internal features, relational structure, or contrastive/global representations), how supervision is scheduled (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation), and how distillation is combined with other compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work shows substantial gains across vision, language, graphs, recommendation, and generative models, but limitations remain around data availability, teacher-student mismatch, low-frequency information transfer, privacy constraints, and robustness under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Strong
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesized Review
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior and richer internal information. A broad toolbox of distillation targets and protocols has emerged—soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free sample synthesis, self- and online-distillation, and multi-teacher schemes—and these are routinely combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD has been applied across vision, language, graphs, speech, generative models, and federated settings, yielding large reductions in model size and inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance when design choices are task- and architecture-aware. Remaining challenges include teacher–student mismatch, propagation of teacher errors and biases, data scarcity or privacy constraints, and instability in optimization; practical remedies emphasize task-aware signal selection, learned teacher adaptation, layer mapping strategies, and data-synthesis or privacy-preserving protocols. This review synthesizes empirical patterns, common mechanisms, practical recommendations, and open problems for KD-driven compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a diverse set of methods for transferring behavior and representations from large or ensemble teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained students so they can be deployed under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD techniques range from matching soft output distributions to aligning intermediate features, transferring relational structure, adversarial or data‑free supervision, and teacher/student co‑design; when combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search, KD forms a central part of modern compression pipelines. Empirical work shows distilled students frequently retain much of teacher performance and can improve generalization, but reliable deployment requires task‑aware engineering to address teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity, distribution shift, and the risk of transferring teacher biases.

papers_seen.author: Perkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a flexible, task-aware family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, efficient students while often preserving much of teacher performance. KD encompasses a range of distilled signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structure), training protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free and few-shot), and data strategies (authentic, augmented, synthetic, or generated replay). Empirical work across vision, speech, language, graphs, and multimodal tasks shows that KD produces meaningful efficiency–accuracy trade-offs when teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and signal selection are aligned; however, KD is not automatic and faces limits from capacity mismatch, teacher artifacts, low-frequency or structured outputs, data heterogeneity, and fairness/privacy concerns. Best practice treats KD as a configurable toolbox that is integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with safeguards for robustness, privacy, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Cordova
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core of Practical Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely applicable strategy for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD routinely reduces inference cost and memory while preserving a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but its reliability is context-dependent: teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, architecture alignment, and complementary compression primitives critically shape outcomes. A pragmatic recommendation is to treat KD as the central component of compression pipelines while explicitly adapting objectives, data protocols, and auxiliary methods to the deployment constraints and known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Thompson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Foundational but Context‑Dependent Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly useful and empirically validated approach for transferring behavior from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD reliably reduces inference cost and enables deployment, privacy-aware releases, and domain adaptation when designed with task- and data-awareness. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the availability and match of data, and careful handling of transferred biases and low-frequency phenomena. The strongest practical systems treat KD as a central component within an integrated compression pipeline that includes pruning, quantization, architecture search, and targeted data strategies.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broad family of techniques for compressing large or expensive models into smaller, faster, or more deployable ones by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Methods differ in the form of transferred knowledge (soft logits, hidden features, contrastive distributions, synthetic data, or cross-modal alignments), in how and when distillation is applied (offline, online, layer-wise, task-adaptive, or data-free), and in the problems they target (classification, detection, generation, language tasks, graph learning, or novel-view synthesis). Empirical work demonstrates that appropriate choices about teacher signals, data manipulation, and architectural search can yield compact models that retain much of teacher performance across modalities; theoretical work begins to clarify when soft labels help and when hard labels or mixed supervision are needed. Remaining challenges include optimization gaps between teacher and student, dataset and fairness concerns, and scaling distillation reliably in large distributed settings.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical, and Context‑Aware Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across deep learning and NLP. KD reliably transfers predictive behavior and internal representations using a variety of signals and training protocols, and when combined with complementary compression methods and task-aware choices it enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is context dependent: its success hinges on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of transferred errors, robustness deficits, and fairness or privacy issues. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a stand‑alone cure.

papers_seen.author: Gilbert
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger or more complex teacher models into smaller, faster student models to meet constraints of latency, memory, privacy, or deployment. The field presents a diverse toolbox of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational structure), protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free), and architecture-aware adaptations that are frequently combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, recommendation, and control shows distilled students can recover much teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, and data strategies are addressed; however, KD faces limits from teacher–student mismatch, limited or absent data, propagation of teacher artifacts, and challenges in reliably transferring robustness, low-frequency behaviors, and fairness. Best practice treats KD as a toolbox within an integrated, task-aware compression pipeline, selecting distilled signals and data strategies according to deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Schmitt
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential, Configurable Core for Practical Model Compression with Explicit Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically proven approach for producing compact models from larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. KD reliably transfers predictive behavior and internal structure when tailored to the task, signals, and deployment constraints, but it has clear limits: teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity, propagation of teacher errors or biases, and difficulty preserving low-frequency behaviors. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-aware objectives, careful layer mapping, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet real-world deployment goals.

papers_seen.author: Cruz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger networks. Across vision, language, graphs, speech, and generative modeling, researchers transfer information via softened output distributions, intermediate-feature matching, relational and attention maps, and many-to-many layer alignment. Variants address resource heterogeneity, data unavailability, privacy, robustness, and fairness. Empirical and analytic work shows that distillation combines information transfer with regularization effects, but its success depends on design choices (what to transfer, teacher quality, data or pseudo-data, and alignment losses). State-of-the-art practice mixes logits-based loss with feature- or representation-level objectives, task-aware augmentations, and architecture- or training-aware modifications to obtain favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs in deployment.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted, practical framework for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, efficient students for deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. A diverse toolkit of distillation objectives and protocols—ranging from soft-label (logit) matching to intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-/self-distillation, and data-free protocols—has been developed and applied across vision, language, speech, graphs, and multimodal tasks. KD is most effective when integrated into task-aware pipelines that align teacher and student architectures, choose appropriate transfer signals, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) while explicitly addressing limitations such as distribution shift, teacher-induced biases, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. A broad and practical toolbox has been developed—output-level (soft-target) matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, contrastive and relational objectives, adversarial and data-free methods, online and multi-teacher protocols, and curriculum- or architecture-aware pipelines. Empirical evidence shows distilled students often recover most teacher performance and can improve generalization when objectives, layer mappings, and data choices are well matched to student capacity and task constraints. Success requires careful design around what to transfer, how to align layers and inputs, how to handle limited or private data, and how to mitigate bias, rare-token degradation, and teacher errors; combining KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, and neural architecture search) and using task-aware curricula or projectors typically yields better accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Bowman
papers_seen.title: TRILLsson: Distilled Universal Paralinguistic Speech Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in self-supervision have dramatically improved the quality of speech representations. However, deployment of state-of-the-art embedding models on devices has been restricted due to their limited public availability and large resource footprint. Our work addresses these issues by publicly releasing a collection of paralinguistic speech models that are small and near state-of-the-art performance. Our approach is based on knowledge distillation, and our models are distilled on public data only. We explore different architectures and thoroughly evaluate our models on the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. Our largest distilled model is less than 15% the size of the original model (314MB vs 2.2GB), achieves over 96% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks, and is trained on 6.5% the data. The smallest model is 1% in size (22MB) and achieves over 90% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks. Our models outperform the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 model on 6 of 7 tasks, and our smallest model outperforms the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks despite being 7% the size.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central and versatile toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. A broad family of distillation objectives and protocols has been developed—ranging from soft-logit matching to intermediate-feature, attention, relational, contrastive, adversarial, and data‑free approaches—and KD is most effective when integrated with complementary compression techniques and task-aware design. Success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and explicit handling of distribution shift, low-frequency behaviors, privacy, and architecture heterogeneity.
