papers_seen.author: Andrews
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, efficient students by transferring information from teachers via outputs, internal representations, or relational signals. KD is broadly applicable across modalities and settings and is most effective when combined with task-aware design choices and complementary compression methods. Despite strong empirical successes, important practical and theoretical challenges remain—teacher–student mismatch, data heterogeneity or scarcity, transferred biases, robustness under distribution shift, and privacy constraints—motivating targeted algorithmic and systems-level remedies and further study.

papers_seen.author: Perkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a flexible, task-aware family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, efficient students while often preserving much of teacher performance. KD encompasses a range of distilled signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structure), training protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free and few-shot), and data strategies (authentic, augmented, synthetic, or generated replay). Empirical work across vision, speech, language, graphs, and multimodal tasks shows that KD produces meaningful efficiency–accuracy trade-offs when teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and signal selection are aligned; however, KD is not automatic and faces limits from capacity mismatch, teacher artifacts, low-frequency or structured outputs, data heterogeneity, and fairness/privacy concerns. Best practice treats KD as a configurable toolbox that is integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with safeguards for robustness, privacy, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Potter
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible set of methods for transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models to enable deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, or privacy. Across vision and natural language tasks, distillation targets range from soft logits to intermediate representations and relational signals; KD is frequently combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with domain- or task-specific procedures to improve efficacy. KD delivers strong empirical gains in many settings but is bounded by teacher quality, availability and match of data, teacher–student capacity gaps, and the risk of transferring teacher biases; effective application therefore requires task-aware choices of signals, data strategies, and often hybrid compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Harvey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer knowledge from larger or multi-modal models to smaller or specialized models to reduce inference cost, enable deployment in constrained environments, and improve robustness or fairness. Across computer vision, natural language processing, speech, recommender systems, graph learning, generative modelling, and multimodal tasks, a broad set of mechanisms—soft-label supervision, feature- and attention-level matching, multi-teacher and ensemble methods, online/peer-distillation, and task- or domain-specific adaptations—have been developed. Empirical results demonstrate that distillation can yield compact models that approach teacher performance, accelerate training or inference, improve small-model self-supervised learning, and enable modality transfer, while theoretical and empirical analyses highlight factors that govern success: student capacity, teacher imperfection, data complexity, data augmentation, and bias-variance tradeoffs. Open challenges remain in principled theory, privacy-preserving and fairness-aware distillation, and extending distillation reliably to generative and highly structured prediction tasks.

papers_seen.author: Bruce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Context‑Dependent Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible set of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance when objectives, teacher–student alignment, and data strategies are chosen to match task and deployment requirements. However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, degradation on low‑frequency or out‑of‑distribution phenomena, and heterogeneous-device constraints. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that combines representational, output‑level, and data-side interventions with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression methods aim to transfer behavior and representations from larger, more expensive models into smaller, efficient ones while retaining task performance. Across modalities and tasks, research has developed many complementary mechanisms — soft-label mimicry, intermediate representation matching, teacher-student curriculum designs, self-distillation, multi-teacher and online schemes, data- or generator-based transfer, and domain- or modality-specific adaptations — to balance accuracy, latency, and resource constraints. Empirical work shows that properly designed distillation can recover most teacher performance (and in some settings even surpass it) while enabling deployment on constrained hardware and improving reproducibility and privacy. Success depends on the distillation targets, the teacher-student pairing and training regime, the use of auxiliary data or synthetic examples, and task-specific modifications.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Bush
papers_seen.title: Multi-Label Image Classification via Knowledge Distillation from Weakly-Supervised Detection
papers_seen.abstract: Multi-label image classification is a fundamental but challenging task towards general visual understanding. Existing methods found the region-level cues (e.g., features from RoIs) can facilitate multi-label classification. Nevertheless, such methods usually require laborious object-level annotations (i.e., object labels and bounding boxes) for effective learning of the object-level visual features. In this paper, we propose a novel and efficient deep framework to boost multi-label classification by distilling knowledge from weakly-supervised detection task without bounding box annotations. Specifically, given the image-level annotations, (1) we first develop a weakly-supervised detection (WSD) model, and then (2) construct an end-to-end multi-label image classification framework augmented by a knowledge distillation module that guides the classification model by the WSD model according to the class-level predictions for the whole image and the object-level visual features for object RoIs. The WSD model is the teacher model and the classification model is the student model. After this cross-task knowledge distillation, the performance of the classification model is significantly improved and the efficiency is maintained since the WSD model can be safely discarded in the test phase. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets (MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE) show that our framework achieves superior performances over the state-of-the-art methods on both performance and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Dunn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically grounded approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. By transferring predictive behavior or internal representations, KD enables substantial reductions in latency and memory while often preserving much of teacher performance. Its effectiveness depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data; when combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware training, KD forms an essential, configurable component of modern compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Pham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Insufficient Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and broadly effective family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of the teachers' performance. Empirical results across vision, language, ranking, detection, translation, federated settings, and reinforcement learning show KD reduces parameters and latency, can improve generalization, and enables domain- and privacy-aware workflows. At the same time, KD has important failure modes—dependence on distillation data and teacher–student alignment, capability mismatches, and transfer of teacher errors or biases—that require targeted solutions. Best practice is to treat KD as a central component of an integrated compression pipeline, combined with representation-level matching, data strategies, architecture-aware transformations, and privacy- or domain-specific adaptations.

papers_seen.author: Mcdonald
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and pragmatic approach for producing compact models that retain much of the behavior of larger teachers. KD enables deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and cross-device constraints when applied with task-aware choices about what to transfer, which examples to use, and how to align teacher and student. However, its success is conditional: careful selection of teacher signals, attention to data regimes and fairness, and integration with complementary compression methods are required for reliable real-world use.

papers_seen.author: Sawyer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, faster student models. KD variants include matching soft outputs, aligning intermediate features or attention, relational and contrastive objectives, online and self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware protocols. When combined with task-aware design choices and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture/architecture-search, and data strategies), KD often recovers much of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, outcomes are context-dependent: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and selection, and training design materially shape success. Practical use treats KD as a configurable component within integrated compression pipelines rather than a turnkey algorithm.

papers_seen.author: Vaughn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Demand-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an empirically powerful and practically versatile approach for compressing large models and transferring behavior to smaller students. KD succeeds across modalities by matching logits, intermediate features, attention, or relational structure and is frequently combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Recent work extends KD to settings with no original data, privacy constraints, heterogeneous architectures, and specialized tasks (graphs, non‑autoregressive generation, lifelong learning). However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on teacher–student design, data strategies, and task-aware objectives, and important open problems remain (capacity mismatch, teacher bias transfer, preserving low-frequency behaviors, principled layer mapping, and rigorous theoretical understanding).

papers_seen.author: Baird
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and widely applied family of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger or more expressive teacher models into smaller, faster student models to meet latency, memory, privacy, or deployment constraints. The literature offers a broad taxonomy of distilled signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive structure), training protocols (offline teacher→student, online/self-distillation, multi‑teacher, data‑free or generative), and architecture-aware adaptations that are commonly integrated with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across NLP, vision, visual‑linguistic models, retrieval, and specialized domains shows KD can recover much teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, and data strategies are addressed, but it faces recurring limits from teacher–student mismatch, limited or absent data, propagation of teacher artifacts (biases, failure modes), and challenges in reliably transferring robustness and low‑frequency behaviors. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline rather than a single turnkey solution.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students while attempting to preserve teacher performance. Work in KD spans matching teacher outputs (soft labels), aligning internal representations and features, adversarial or data-free sample synthesis, architecture search and task-adaptive compression, privacy-aware and federated settings, and domain- or task-specific adaptations. Empirical results show KD can yield dramatic reductions in size and compute with modest drops (or even gains) in downstream performance across speech, vision, and NLP tasks, but success depends on what is distilled (outputs versus internal features), optimization and dataset choices, and problem-specific design choices. The literature also identifies limitations and failure modes—optimization difficulties, data heterogeneity, and privacy constraints—that have motivated specialized protocols and theory. This synthesis summarizes the principal approaches, mechanistic explanations, representative empirical outcomes, and practical considerations for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Gallegos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Configurable Core of Hybrid Model‑Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an essential and highly practical class of techniques for producing compact models from larger teachers. Its many variants—soft-label/logit transfer, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, contrastive and relational objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, self-distillation, and data-free generation—make KD applicable across vision, language, reinforcement learning, and multimodal tasks. However, KD is not a universal solution: its reliability depends on careful matching of distilled signals to student capacity, data strategy, and targeted mitigations for bias, rare-case behavior, and distribution shift. papers_seen.author: Vaughn
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical framework for transferring capabilities from large teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. Across architectures and modalities, KD methods reduce inference cost and memory while often preserving much of teacher performance; they are adaptable to settings with limited or no original training data and can be combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and pretraining-aware workflows. Success in practice depends on careful choice of what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data and augmentation strategies, and mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer and degradation on rare phenomena. Important open directions include principled theory for diverse distillation objectives, reliable distillation under data scarcity or privacy constraints, and specialized protocols for structured or generative outputs.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. Effectiveness depends on matching the distillation signals to student capacity and task structure, and on addressing failure modes such as teacher bias and data scarcity. Combining KD with complementary techniques (quantization, architecture transformations, pruning, and task-aware layer mapping) yields the best tradeoffs between compression and downstream accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: BAM! Born-Again Multi-Task Networks for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: It can be challenging to train multi-task neural networks that outperform or even match their single-task counterparts. To help address this, we propose using knowledge distillation where single-task models teach a multi-task model. We enhance this training with teacher annealing, a novel method that gradually transitions the model from distillation to supervised learning, helping the multi-task model surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate our approach by multi-task fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Our method consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Findings from the Provided Literature
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact students. KD methods operate at multiple levels (output logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive signals) and through diverse protocols (offline, online, self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free, and privacy-aware variants). Empirical and practical work shows KD often recovers most of a teacher’s performance while enabling large gains in latency, memory, and deployment cost; however, its reliability is context-dependent, hinging on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, data availability and augmentation, and integration with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture design.

papers_seen.author: Cox
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, graph, multimodal, and federated settings, a diverse set of distillation targets and training protocols have been developed to meet compute, memory, latency, privacy, and domain constraints. When designed in a task- and capacity-aware manner and combined with complementary compression methods, distillation often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance; however, important limitations remain, including teacher–student capacity mismatch, data scarcity or privacy constraints, distribution shift, and trade-offs involving robustness and fairness. This synthesis summarizes prevailing methods, empirical patterns, practical prescriptions, and the main open problems identified in the provided literature.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile set of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, faster student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD techniques encompass output-level supervision (soft logits), representation- and attention-level matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, progressive module replacement, and online or multi-teacher protocols. Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in parameter count and inference cost, but success is context-sensitive: it depends on teacher quality and design, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability and distribution of data (including data-free or synthesized alternatives), and careful loss and layer-mapping choices. Practical pipelines therefore treat KD as a configurable toolbox to be combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and domain-, fairness-, or privacy-aware interventions. Remaining scientific and engineering challenges include principled selection of distillation targets, reliable distillation under limited or mismatched data, mitigation of transferred biases and rare-token degradation, theoretical understanding of when and why different KD objectives help, and automated, hardware-aware co-design for heterogeneous deployment.

papers_seen.author: Thornton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a family of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD methods span soft-target/logit transfer, intermediate-representation and relation-level objectives, multi- and self-distillation, online and data-free protocols, and task-aware layer mapping and projector modules. Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and alignment, and mitigation of transferred biases and robustness deficits.

papers_seen.author: Cortez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, language, and multimodal settings. It can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints, and it interacts naturally with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. However, distillation's success depends on the distillation objective, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and task-specific considerations; when these are not addressed it can propagate teacher errors, struggle with rare outputs, or fail due to optimization issues. Best practice is to treat KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines—combining logits, intermediate feature matching, projector modules, multi-teacher or teacher-adaptive designs, and data-aware schedules—to maximize student utility in real-world deployments.

papers_seen.author: Silva
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become central tools for deploying high-capacity deep learning models in resource-constrained settings. Methods range from transferring soft labels to matching intermediate representations, leveraging ensembles or multiple teachers, synthesizing surrogate data for data-free distillation, and integrating distillation into federated and privacy-sensitive regimes. Empirical gains have been demonstrated across computer vision, generative modeling, graph learning, and natural language processing, while theoretical work and empirical studies highlight nuanced trade-offs related to regularization, sample selection, teacher quality, and heterogeneous/distributed data. Open challenges include robust distillation under data heterogeneity, principled teacher-student design, and compression of generative and transformer models for real-world low-latency deployment.

papers_seen.author: Boyd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential, Multifaceted Toolbox with Clear Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practically essential approach for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD delivers large efficiency gains and can improve generalization or robustness when combined with complementary compression methods, but it is not a single recipe: success depends on what is transferred, teacher–student alignment, data availability and quality, and constraints such as privacy or heterogeneous deployment hardware. Practical KD pipelines therefore treat distillation as a configurable toolkit—selecting objectives, data strategies, and auxiliary interventions (e.g., pruning, quantization, teacher adaptation, or student-aware design) that match the task and constraints—while explicitly addressing known failure modes such as teacher error propagation, low-frequency token degradation, and privacy risks.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt
papers_seen.abstract: Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

papers_seen.author: Sanders
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central, Conditional, and Best-Practice‑Driven for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and practical approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and multimodal settings. KD provides a flexible family of mechanisms (soft-targets, feature and attention matching, multi-teacher and self-distillation, data-free or federated protocols) that, when combined with complementary compression primitives and task-aware design, yield strong empirical trade-offs between efficiency and performance. However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, the choice of distilled signals, data availability or synthesis, and mitigation of transferred biases. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component within an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone recipe.

papers_seen.author: Gilbert
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger or more complex teacher models into smaller, faster student models to meet constraints of latency, memory, privacy, or deployment. The field presents a diverse toolbox of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational structure), protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free), and architecture-aware adaptations that are frequently combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, recommendation, and control shows distilled students can recover much teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, and data strategies are addressed; however, KD faces limits from teacher–student mismatch, limited or absent data, propagation of teacher artifacts, and challenges in reliably transferring robustness, low-frequency behaviors, and fairness. Best practice treats KD as a toolbox within an integrated, task-aware compression pipeline, selecting distilled signals and data strategies according to deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Marshall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Context‑Dependent Path for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for producing compact models suitable for real deployments. KD reliably reduces latency, memory, and compute while often retaining much of teacher performance across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. Its effectiveness, however, depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and deployment constraints; to be maximally effective KD should be treated as a configurable, first‑order tool that is combined with task‑aware design choices and complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, Practical Trade-offs, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models to meet latency, memory, privacy, and deployment constraints. The field encompasses a wide family of distillation targets and protocols (logit matching, feature- and attention-level transfer, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free and federated variants) and is frequently combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across vision, language, recommendation, and other modalities shows that distilled students often recover much of the teacher’s performance, though outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and task-aware choices. Persistent challenges include handling limited or private data, transferring low-frequency/rare behaviors, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and automating teacher–student mappings for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Flexible, but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective and adaptable framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision and NLP. KD supports many transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structure) and training paradigms (offline, online, multi‑teacher, data‑free), enabling substantial reductions in inference cost when integrated with complementary compression techniques. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, available data (or the ability to synthesize it), and deliberate mitigation of failure modes such as transferred bias, distribution shift, and degraded performance on rare outputs. I argue that KD should be treated as a central, configurable component of compression pipelines—powerful when designed and combined with other methods, but requiring task‑aware engineering and explicit safeguards to be reliable in practice.

papers_seen.author: Webster
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Task-Aware Core of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practically essential approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, or specialized models. When designed around task constraints, student capacity, and available data, KD preserves much of a teacher's capabilities while enabling deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy limits. Its greatest value comes from treating distillation as a configurable toolkit—combining soft-targets, representation matching, adversarial or data-free sample synthesis, and multi-teacher or self-distillation—with complementary compression techniques to meet real-world constraints. Success requires careful handling of teacher–student alignment, data scarcity, distribution shift, and bias transfer, but a task-aware, hybrid pipeline makes KD one of the most practical routes to effective model compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Caldwell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Effectiveness, Limitations, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and flexible method for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more interpretable models across vision, language, speech, and recommendation systems. KD works both as a stand-alone compression technique and as a complementary tool that combines well with pruning, quantization, multi-teacher strategies, and privacy-aware or federated settings. While highly effective in practice, KD has limits—especially around data availability, heterogeneity, and theoretical understanding—that recent work addresses with data-free methods, meta-learning teachers, and principled analyses.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks.

papers_seen.author: Mcdonald
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and pragmatic approach for producing compact models that retain much of the behavior of larger teachers. KD enables deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and cross-device constraints when applied with task-aware choices about what to transfer, which examples to use, and how to align teacher and student. However, its success is conditional: careful selection of teacher signals, attention to data regimes and fairness, and integration with complementary compression methods are required for reliable real-world use.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a diverse set of methods for transferring behavior and representations from large or ensemble teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained students so they can be deployed under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD techniques range from matching soft output distributions to aligning intermediate features, transferring relational structure, adversarial or data‑free supervision, and teacher/student co‑design; when combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search, KD forms a central part of modern compression pipelines. Empirical work shows distilled students frequently retain much of teacher performance and can improve generalization, but reliable deployment requires task‑aware engineering to address teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity, distribution shift, and the risk of transferring teacher biases.

papers_seen.author: Walters
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are now core tools for producing smaller, faster models while retaining much of the performance and functionality of larger teachers. The literature has expanded far beyond simple logits matching to include feature- and representation-level transfer, many-to-many layer mapping, contrastive and adversarial objectives, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, multi-teacher and teacher-engineering strategies, and tight integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work demonstrates broad applicability across modalities (vision, NLP, speech, graphs, and generative models) and deployment contexts (edge devices, federated systems, and data-constrained settings). The main practical challenges are (1) choosing what and how to distill for a given task and student architecture, (2) coping with limited or unavailable original training data, (3) avoiding transfer of teacher weaknesses (e.g., biases or low-frequency degradation), and (4) co-designing distillation with other compression primitives and hardware constraints. Progress comes from combining representational objectives, layer-mapping strategies, task-aware teacher selection, and safeguards (privacy or fairness) appropriate to deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Juarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models. Across vision, language, graphs, multimodal tasks and specialized settings (e.g., 3D detection, ranking, medical imaging), KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while often preserving much of teacher performance. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, how teacher and student are aligned, and how data or synthetic alternatives are used; KD is most effective when used as a configurable component combined with complementary compression methods and task-aware training strategies.

papers_seen.author: Mcknight
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, faster models suitable for deployment. KD can transfer logits, intermediate representations, relational or contrastive structure, and can be arranged in offline, online, multi-teacher, or data-free regimes. When chosen and executed with attention to teacher quality, data regime, distilled signals, and student capacity, KD often recovers much of the teacher's performance and enables on-device and privacy-aware deployments. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on context and must be combined with complementary compression and training choices (e.g., architecture search, pruning, quantization, layer mapping, or domain adaptation) to meet production constraints and robustness requirements.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses high-capacity teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad family of distillation objectives—ranging from soft-logit matching to feature-, attention- and layer-wise alignment, relational/contrastive signals, adversarial and data-free sample synthesis, and meta- or multi-teacher schemes—has been developed and applied across vision, language, retrieval, graph, and federated settings. In practice, KD is most effective when combined with task- and architecture-aware design choices and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Remaining challenges include teacher–student mismatch, propagation of teacher errors and biases, limited or private data, and optimization stability; proposed remedies emphasize task-aware filtering of teacher signals, learned teacher adaptation, layer mapping strategies, and data-synthesis or privacy-aware protocols.

papers_seen.author: Mccarty
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely used family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal structure from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. The literature shows a broad set of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational signals), training regimes (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, multi-teacher, and data-free methods), and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical results across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks indicate distilled students can often recover most teacher performance while reducing latency and memory, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the distillation signal and data regime, and safeguards for bias and rare/low-frequency behaviors. Remaining open problems include principled theory connecting distillation choices to guarantees, reliable distillation under limited/private or heterogeneous data, and automated, task-adaptive selection of what and how to transfer.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable, empirically driven set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or composite teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. A diverse toolbox of distillation targets and training protocols has been developed—soft logits, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, self- and online-distillation, data-free and privacy-aware methods—often integrated with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across vision, language, speech, graphs, and multimodal tasks shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance and enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and selection, and training design. Practical deployment treats KD as a configurable component in a broader compression pipeline that must be tailored to task, data regime, and hardware constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Ranking Distillation: Learning Compact Ranking Models With High Performance for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel way to train ranking models, such as recommender systems, that are both effective and efficient. Knowledge distillation (KD) was shown to be successful in image recognition to achieve both effectiveness and efficiency. We propose a KD technique for learning to rank problems, called \emph{ranking distillation (RD)}. Specifically, we train a smaller student model to learn to rank documents/items from both the training data and the supervision of a larger teacher model. The student model achieves a similar ranking performance to that of the large teacher model, but its smaller model size makes the online inference more efficient. RD is flexible because it is orthogonal to the choices of ranking models for the teacher and student. We address the challenges of RD for ranking problems. The experiments on public data sets and state-of-the-art recommendation models showed that RD achieves its design purposes: the student model learnt with RD has a model size less than half of the teacher model while achieving a ranking performance similar to the teacher model and much better than the student model learnt without RD.

papers_seen.author: Gomez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision and NLP, KD spans logits/soft-label matching, feature- and attention-level imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schemes, data‑free and privacy-aware protocols, and self- or teacher-free variants. When combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and designed with attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and task constraints, KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss. Practical deployment requires task-aware choices, careful alignment of teacher and student, and explicit mitigations for distributional mismatch, rare-token behavior, and transferred biases; important open problems remain in principled theory, robust/private data-free distillation, and heterogeneous architecture transfer.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Primary, Configurable Toolkit for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, language, multimodal, and specialized domains. KD supports multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, relational signals), diverse scheduling regimes (offline, online, progressive), and synergistic combination with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). While KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains with modest loss in task performance, its success is context-dependent: teacher quality, student capacity, data availability (or synthetic/data-free strategies), and explicit measures to mitigate bias, robustness, and privacy concerns determine outcomes. Consequently, KD should be treated as a first-order, configurable tool in compression pipelines—selected and tuned according to task, data, and deployment constraints—rather than a one-size-fits-all recipe.

papers_seen.author: Aguirre
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger, more expensive models (teachers) to smaller, cheaper models (students) to reduce inference cost, enable deployment on constrained devices, and support privacy- or resource-constrained settings. Approaches span soft-label distillation, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, data-free and zero-shot methods, multi-teacher and ensemble distillation, self-distillation, task- and modality-specific objectives, and combinations with pruning. Empirical work across vision, speech, 3D detection, recommender systems, and multiple NLP tasks demonstrates that carefully designed distillation strategies can yield compact models that approach teacher performance while significantly reducing latency and memory. The literature also provides growing theoretical insight into when and how distillation helps, and identifies open challenges including imperfect teachers, domain shift, low-frequency token fidelity, modality mismatch, and heterogeneous-device federated settings.

papers_seen.author: Burns
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Configurable Tool for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated family of techniques for transferring behavior from larger teacher models to smaller student models to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD produces large practical gains when it is treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies—and when practitioners attend to teacher–student capacity, data regime, and optimization design. KD is not a panacea: it can propagate teacher errors, struggle with low-frequency phenomena, and fail under data scarcity or severe teacher–student mismatch. Therefore the recommended position is to adopt KD as the default first-line compression strategy, but to explicitly pair it with complementary methods and safeguards tailored to task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Schmidt
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile technique for transferring knowledge from large teacher models to smaller student models to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when combined with task‑aware design, appropriate data strategies, and complementary compression methods; however, its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability, and explicit mitigation of transferred errors, biases, and low‑frequency failures. Treat KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a turnkey solution.

papers_seen.author: Morris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Engine for Practical Model Compression: Benefits, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a practical, widely adopted approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers in deep learning and NLP. KD methods vary by what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals), how transfers are staged (offline, online, multi-teacher, data-free), and which complementary compression techniques are combined (pruning, quantization, architecture search). In practice, KD reliably reduces latency and memory while often preserving much of teacher performance, but it has failure modes—teacher error propagation, difficulty with low-frequency phenomena, capacity and optimization mismatch, and privacy or data-limited regimes—that require task-aware design and integration with other compression strategies. Treated as a configurable component of compression pipelines and paired with targeted remedies, KD is a practical core mechanism for deployable model compression rather than a standalone solution.

papers_seen.author: Byrd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical, flexible toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across modalities and tasks. KD transfers information via logits, intermediate features, attention patterns, and relational or contrastive signals, and it is most effective when integrated with complementary compression methods and task‑aware design choices. However, KD’s success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and selection, and explicit safeguards to avoid transferring undesirable teacher properties. Treating KD as a configurable, first‑line component of an integrated compression pipeline—rather than a plug‑and‑play cure—yields the best outcomes for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Haney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Context‑Aware, and Best Used in Hybrid Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely adopted approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. Empirical and methodological work shows KD supports a variety of transfer signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational maps) and training protocols (offline, online, multi‑teacher, data‑free), and that its benefits are maximized when chosen signals, student capacity, and data strategies are aligned with task and deployment constraints. KD reliably improves student performance but is not always sufficient on its own: the best, robust deployment outcomes arise when KD is integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with safeguards to mitigate transferred biases and data mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective family of methods for producing compact models from larger teachers. When treated as a configurable, task-aware component of an integrated compression pipeline, KD reliably reduces inference cost and memory while often preserving most of a teacher's performance. However, KD is not a standalone cure: its practical success requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle data limitations and privacy, and how to mitigate transferred biases and low-frequency failures. The strongest deployments treat KD as central but combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and safeguards (data strategies, curriculum, evaluation on robustness and fairness).

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Open Problems
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad toolkit of distillation targets and training protocols has been developed — including soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, online and self-distillation, multi-teacher schemes, and data-free or generative-sample approaches — and these techniques are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work across vision, language, retrieval, generative models, and embedded settings shows that careful design of what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which data or synthetic samples to use is crucial: well-designed distillation pipelines can recover much of teacher performance while producing substantial efficiency gains, but challenges remain in data-scarce or privacy-sensitive regimes, heterogeneous teacher–student architectures, distribution shift, and preserving rare or minority behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Mcdaniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Configurable Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD is effective across modalities when treated as a configurable toolbox—choosing what to transfer (logits, features, attention, relations), how to align teacher and student (layer mapping, projectors, curricula), and how to handle data constraints (augmentation, data-free synthesis, federated protocols). KD routinely recovers much of teacher performance and can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search, but it is context-dependent: limitations include teacher–student capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias propagation, and difficulties with rare/long-tail phenomena. Best practice is to use KD as a principled component of an integrated compression pipeline, paired with task-aware design choices and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Beck
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the teacher performance. KD operates through multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, synthetic data) and adapts across modalities (vision, speech, graphs, NLP) and deployment constraints (edge inference, federated settings, privacy-aware releases). While KD frequently yields strong empirical gains, its success depends on careful choices—teacher quality, what to match, layer alignment, projector usage, data selection, and privacy constraints—and benefits from combining complementary methods such as ensembling, task-adaptive architecture search, and federated or privacy-aware protocols.

papers_seen.author: Holt
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Central Utility, Practical Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable technique for transferring capabilities from large teacher models into compact student models so that high-performing systems can run under latency, memory, or privacy constraints. KD supports many transfer targets (soft logits, features, attention, relations) and training regimes (offline, online, multi-teacher, data-free) and is routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to produce deployable models. However, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on task-aware choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and explicit handling of bias, low-frequency behavior, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Component of Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable framework for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of teacher functionality. KD methods have been adapted across modalities and tasks and can enable deployment under strict latency, memory, and privacy constraints. At the same time, KD has concrete failure modes tied to teacher quality, data availability, distribution shift, and architecture mismatch; achieving reliable outcomes requires integrating KD with complementary techniques and designing task-aware protocols that select what to transfer, how to synthesize or select data, and how to weight teacher signals.
