papers_seen.author: Alexander
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. KD has been adapted into many variants and protocols and is commonly combined with complementary compression methods to produce deployable models under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. The technique yields substantial practical gains across modalities and tasks when teacher quality, student capacity, data strategies, and alignment of objectives are addressed; nevertheless, KD has well-documented failure modes and open challenges that require careful engineering and further research.

papers_seen.author: Fields
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Tool — Argument for Integrated, Context‑Aware Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, broadly applicable set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from large teachers. Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, and multimodal tasks shows KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD’s effectiveness is conditional: it depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distilled signals, and the availability or synthesis of suitable training data. For robust, real‑world compression, KD should be treated as a configurable component within an integrated pipeline that combines representation-level transfer, data and curriculum strategies, and architecture‑aware compression (pruning, quantization, or search), together with explicit safeguards for bias, robustness, and low‑frequency behavior.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A synthesis of methods, evidence, and practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a practical, multifaceted toolkit for transferring behavior from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students. The field unifies a set of objectives (soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational/contrastive signals), training protocols (offline, online, self- and mutual-distillation, multi-teacher and teacher-annealed schedules), and data strategies (augmentation, data-free synthesis, adversarial generation) that, when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), enable effective deployment across vision, language, generative modelling, and domain- and privacy-constrained settings. Empirical evidence demonstrates strong gains when distillation is matched to student capacity, teacher quality, and appropriate data/augmentation strategies, but persistent challenges remain in data-scarce, privacy-sensitive, domain-shift, and heterogeneous-architecture regimes.

papers_seen.author: Mccall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Context‑Sensitive, and Best Used in Integrated Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce latency, memory, and compute while preserving much of task performance. Empirical work across vision, language, and multimodal tasks demonstrates that KD can produce deployable models with favorable efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs, but KD alone is not a universal cure: its success depends on what signals are transferred, teacher–student alignment, data availability (including data‑free synthesis), and mitigation of propagated errors or biases. For practical, robust compression, KD should be a central, configurable component of a task‑aware pipeline that incorporates complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), curriculum and sample‑selection strategies, and targeted remedies for distribution shift, low‑frequency phenomena, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Carpenter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. KD reliably reduces latency and memory while often preserving much of teacher performance across vision, language, speech, and generative tasks, but its effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and architectural alignment. For deployment-ready compression, KD should be treated as a cornerstone technique that is combined with task-aware design choices and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to close remaining optimization and generalization gaps.

papers_seen.author: Velasquez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large (teacher) models to smaller (student) models. KD methods vary by what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structure), how teachers and students are paired (single, ensemble, multi-teacher, or self-distillation), and by constraints on data, privacy, and deployment hardware. Across vision, language, speech, graphs, and reinforcement learning, KD produces compact models that often retain much of teacher performance while enabling lower latency, lower memory, and operation under communication- or privacy-constrained settings. However, gains depend on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and architectural alignment; practical pipelines therefore combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware design choices to close optimization and generalization gaps.

papers_seen.author: Morales
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller student models. KD has grown from simple soft-label matching into a rich toolbox that includes intermediate feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher protocols, and data- or privacy-aware variants. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can improve deployment trade-offs (latency, memory, privacy), but its success is conditional on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment and capacity, data availability or synthesis, and mitigation of transferred errors or biases.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses larger teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. A broad toolkit has emerged — soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational/contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free or synthetic-data schemes, and hybrid pipelines combining distillation with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirically, KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and objective design. Important open problems include principled theory linking transfer signals to student generalization, reliable distillation under domain shift and heterogeneous devices, and preserving rare or structured outputs in sequence tasks.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.

papers_seen.author: Chambers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a broad family of techniques that transfer information from larger, often multi-source or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across vision, language, speech, multimodal and generative settings, KD has evolved beyond simple logit matching to include representation- and relation-level objectives, adversarial or data-free generation, online and self-distillation protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization and architecture search. These approaches routinely enable large reductions in inference cost and memory while preserving much of teacher performance, but reliable deployment requires task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data. Important open directions remain in principled theory, robust distillation under heterogenous and low-data regimes, and preserving long-tail or low-frequency behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Perkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a flexible, task-aware family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, efficient students while often preserving much of teacher performance. KD encompasses a range of distilled signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structure), training protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free and few-shot), and data strategies (authentic, augmented, synthetic, or generated replay). Empirical work across vision, speech, language, graphs, and multimodal tasks shows that KD produces meaningful efficiency–accuracy trade-offs when teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and signal selection are aligned; however, KD is not automatic and faces limits from capacity mismatch, teacher artifacts, low-frequency or structured outputs, data heterogeneity, and fairness/privacy concerns. Best practice treats KD as a configurable toolbox that is integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with safeguards for robustness, privacy, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Waller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Practical Core with Clear Limits — Guidance for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely useful set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher's capability. KD spans logits transfer, intermediate feature mimicking, relational and attention-based objectives, self-distillation, ensemble-to-single transfer, and cross-modal variants. Applied thoughtfully — selecting what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which samples or layers to prioritize — KD can produce substantial gains in latency, memory, and sometimes robustness, but it is not a universal remedy: dataset mismatch, optimization difficulty, and propagation of teacher errors are real constraints. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a principled toolbox rather than a single recipe, summarizes practical patterns that succeed across tasks, highlights empirical failure modes, and gives evidence-backed recommendations for practitioners in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Gross
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Path for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical tool that enables deployment of compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teachers to smaller students. KD supports many transfer targets and protocols and can materially reduce model size and inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a universal cure: success depends on task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle limited or private data, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression methods. The most reliable deployments treat KD as the central element of an integrated compression pipeline rather than the sole method.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly useful and empirically validated approach for transferring behavior from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD reliably reduces inference cost and enables deployment, privacy-aware releases, and domain adaptation when designed with task- and data-awareness. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the availability and match of data, and careful handling of transferred biases and low-frequency phenomena. The strongest practical systems treat KD as a central component within an integrated compression pipeline that includes pruning, quantization, architecture search, and targeted data strategies.

papers_seen.author: Mccarthy
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses and transfers knowledge from larger or more complex teacher models into smaller, efficient student models. A broad family of methods—soft-target (logit) transfer, intermediate-feature and attention matching, contrastive and relational objectives, and data-free or teacher-free variants—has been developed and successfully applied across vision, language, graphs, speech, and multimodal problems. Practical success depends on teacher design, data and curriculum choices, alignment of teacher and student representations, and combining KD with complementary compression tools.

papers_seen.author: Snyder
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably transfers behavior from large teacher models into smaller students, enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory and compute while preserving much of task performance. KD techniques span logits/soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level alignment, relational and contrastive signals, online and multi-teacher protocols, and data-free or domain-adaptive variants. Empirical evidence shows KD is a practical first-line strategy for deployment across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks, but it is not a standalone cure: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, objective design, and careful integration with complementary compression tools. For robust, real-world deployment, KD should be treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline combined with targeted engineering to mitigate failure modes such as capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias propagation, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Buchanan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential, Context‑Aware, and Insufficient Alone for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and empirically validated family of techniques that reliably improves the efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs of deep models across modalities. KD enables deployment by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller students, and it supports many training protocols and transfer targets. However, KD is not a standalone solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability or synthesis of suitable data, and careful mitigation of failure modes (distribution shift, low-frequency degradation, and bias propagation). Therefore, for robust real-world deployment KD should be treated as a configurable, task‑aware core of an integrated compression pipeline that combines complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture design), teacher–student co‑design, and data strategies tailored to the application.

papers_seen.author: Villegas
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, configurable family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, deployable student models. Across vision, language, multimodal, and specialized domains, KD reduces latency, memory, and compute while often preserving a large fraction of teacher performance. KD encompasses many targets and protocols (soft logits, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial/data‑free synthesis, multi‑teacher and self‑distillation) and is most effective when combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies appropriate to the task and deployment constraints. Success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability and nature of distillation data, and mitigation of failure modes such as optimization difficulties, bias transfer, and degradation on rare phenomena. Important open directions include principled objectives, robust/private distillation under data scarcity, and specialized protocols for structured or generative outputs.

papers_seen.author: Lyons
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression methods form a broadly applicable toolkit for producing smaller, faster, or more interpretable models from large teacher networks. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners transfer information via softened outputs, intermediate representation matching, attention/relational signals, and synthetic data, and they commonly combine KD with pruning, quantization, and automated architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD often recovers most teacher performance while substantially reducing latency and memory, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and task-specific adaptations.

papers_seen.author: Rodgers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely applied framework for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teachers to compact students. Across vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative tasks, KD variants—ranging from soft-logit matching to intermediate-representation, attention, relational, and contrastive objectives, as well as adversarial, data-free, online, and multi‑teacher protocols—have been adapted to meet deployment constraints (latency, memory, compute, privacy, and domain adaptation). Empirical work shows KD can recover a substantial fraction of teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, signal choice, data strategy, and architecture alignment are addressed; however, KD is not a universal cure and must be integrated with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and safeguards for bias, low‑frequency phenomena, and distribution shift.

We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Garner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Context‑Dependent Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of methods for producing compact models by transferring behavior and internal representations from larger teachers to smaller students. Empirically, KD enables substantial reductions in compute, memory, and latency while often preserving much of teacher performance across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks. However, KD is not automatic: its success depends on deliberate choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and integration with complementary compression and robustness measures. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a core, configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone silver bullet.

papers_seen.author: Hardy
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable set of methods for transferring predictive behavior and representations from larger (teacher) models into smaller (student) models, enabling deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, privacy, or domain mismatch. Across vision, language, multimodal and generative settings, distillation has expanded from logits matching to a diverse toolbox that includes feature- and attention-level imitation, relational objectives, online and self-distillation, data- and privacy-aware protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization and architecture search. Empirical and theoretical work shows distillation often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and stabilizes student training, but success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment and capacity, availability and selection of data, and defenses against transferred biases and degraded modeling of rare phenomena. Practical deployments therefore treat distillation as a configurable component within compression pipelines, pairing distilled signals with task- and deployment-aware engineering.

papers_seen.author: Bell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical, flexible family of techniques for producing compact models from larger teachers. Across vision, language, recommendation, and multimodal systems, variants of KD—soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational/contrastive objectives, ensemble and online schemes, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols—are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can enable latency, memory, and privacy trade-offs, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, data strategy, and explicit mitigation of transferred errors, bias, and low-frequency phenomena. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical findings, practical design considerations, applications, limitations, and promising research directions drawn from the provided studies.

papers_seen.author: Washington
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central but Insufficient — A Task‑Aware, Integrated Approach to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile mechanism for transferring competence from large teacher models to compact student models, enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory, and deployability while retaining much of teacher performance. However, KD alone does not guarantee robust, fair, or hardware‑optimal compression; its effectiveness depends on careful, task‑aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle limited or private data, and how to integrate complementary compression methods. Treating KD as the central element within an engineered pipeline — augmented by teacher selection, data strategies, and pruning/quantization or architecture adaptations — delivers the most reliable outcomes for real deployments.

papers_seen.author: Chambers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Sensitive Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD reliably reduces latency and parameter counts while preserving much of teacher performance when its objectives, data strategy, and teacher–student alignment are chosen with task and deployment constraints in mind. However, KD is not a universal solution: capacity mismatch, teacher errors and biases, limited or private data, and optimization instability limit off‑the‑shelf success. The strongest practical outcomes arise when KD is treated as a configurable core within hybrid compression pipelines that also employ pruning, quantization, architecture search, and task‑aware data procedures.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Highlight Every Step: Knowledge Distillation via Collaborative Teaching
papers_seen.abstract: High storage and computational costs obstruct deep neural networks to be deployed on resource-constrained devices. Knowledge distillation aims to train a compact student network by transferring knowledge from a larger pre-trained teacher model. However, most existing methods on knowledge distillation ignore the valuable information among training process associated with training results. In this paper, we provide a new Collaborative Teaching Knowledge Distillation (CTKD) strategy which employs two special teachers. Specifically, one teacher trained from scratch (i.e., scratch teacher) assists the student step by step using its temporary outputs. It forces the student to approach the optimal path towards the final logits with high accuracy. The other pre-trained teacher (i.e., expert teacher) guides the student to focus on a critical region which is more useful for the task. The combination of the knowledge from two special teachers can significantly improve the performance of the student network in knowledge distillation. The results of experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN and Tiny ImageNet datasets verify that the proposed knowledge distillation method is efficient and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Dodson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential, Task-Aware Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically indispensable approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students across modalities. When designed with task-aware choices about which teacher signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student inputs and capacities, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD reliably yields major efficiency gains with modest performance loss. KD also enables deployment under privacy and communication constraints, and can transfer robustness when done adversarially, but it has well-documented failure modes—teacher bias, domain shift, degradation on low-frequency phenomena, and mismatches between teacher and student—that must be mitigated with targeted strategies such as multi-teacher schedules, sample selection, teacher adaptation, and privacy-aware protocols.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Practical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely applied approach for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, faster, or deployment-specialized students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A large family of distillation objectives and training protocols has been developed—ranging from soft-label (logit) matching to feature- and layer-wise imitation, relational and contrastive signals, adversarial and data-free schemes, and online or multi-teacher setups—and these are frequently combined with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of a teacher’s performance while lowering latency and memory, but practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability or synthesis of data, and careful choice of what and how to transfer. Open problems include robust and private distillation under data scarcity and distribution shift, preserving rare-token or low-frequency behavior, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and automating teacher–student mapping for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge From a Deep Pose Regressor Network
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a novel method to distill knowledge from a deep pose regressor network for efficient Visual Odometry (VO). Standard distillation relies on "dark knowledge" for successful knowledge transfer. As this knowledge is not available in pose regression and the teacher prediction is not always accurate, we propose to emphasize the knowledge transfer only when we trust the teacher. We achieve this by using teacher loss as a confidence score which places variable relative importance on the teacher prediction. We inject this confidence score to the main training task via Attentive Imitation Loss (AIL) and when learning the intermediate representation of the teacher through Attentive Hint Training (AHT) approach. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work which successfully distill the knowledge from a deep pose regression network. Our evaluation on the KITTI and Malaga dataset shows that we can keep the student prediction close to the teacher with up to 92.95% parameter reduction and 2.12x faster in computation time.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, practically driven family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models by transferring information from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into compact student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods encompass matching soft logits, aligning intermediate representations and attention, transferring relational or contrastive structure, and relying on data-aware or data-free training protocols. Empirical work demonstrates that distillation often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distilled signals, and data or data-synthesis strategies. Practical application treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline combined with pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Hunter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses information from large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient student models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. The literature provides a diverse toolkit—soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate feature and attention imitation, contrastive and relational objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or synthetic-data approaches—together with engineering practices that pair KD with pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and data/curriculum strategies. Empirical results show KD often preserves much of the teacher’s performance across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, yet important challenges remain around teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity and privacy, robustness and fairness, and reliable transfer of low-frequency or structured behaviors. Continued progress centers on designing what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to integrate KD into end-to-end compression pipelines for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have matured into a versatile set of techniques for transferring predictive capacity from large, expensive models into smaller, faster, or more private models. Across computer vision, NLP, multimodal systems, federated settings, and generative models, researchers have combined soft-label (logit) distillation, intermediate feature/hint transfer, architecture transformation, quantization, pruning, and automated search to achieve significant reductions in memory, computation, or communication while largely preserving accuracy. Empirical work demonstrates that distillation can enable high-quality low-precision models, speed up inference and training, unify heterogeneous models without shared data, and make distributed learning more communication- and privacy-efficient. The field continues to refine when and what knowledge to transfer (e.g., logits vs. features vs. attention), how to handle multiple or unreliable teachers, how to design student-friendly teachers, and how to integrate distillation with other compression methods such as pruning and search.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression (but Not a Standalone Solution)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically effective tool for producing compact models from larger teachers across vision and NLP. KD reliably reduces inference cost and supports deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but it also has concrete failure modes (capacity mismatch, propagated teacher artifacts, rare-token degradation, and data-availability limits). The best practical strategy treats KD as the default first-line compression mechanism that must be configured to the task and explicitly combined with complementary techniques and safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Hayden
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically grounded framework for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or auxiliary teacher models into compact students. KD methods include soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-representation and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online protocols, data-free or zero-shot schemes, and self-distillation. Empirical work shows KD often recovers much of teacher performance when combined with suitable data strategies, teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD’s effectiveness is context dependent: success requires attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and safeguards against transferred artifacts, distributional mismatch, and social harms. The practical consensus treats KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline rather than a plug-and-play solution.

papers_seen.author: Yu
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression: Central, Context-Sensitive, and Best Used in Hybrid Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD reliably transfers predictive behavior and internal structure across vision and NLP tasks and often recovers much of a teacher's performance, but it is not a universal cure: its reliability depends on what is distilled, how teachers and students are aligned, data availability, and complementary compression choices. Treating KD as a configurable, task-aware component within an integrated compression pipeline yields the most robust and deployable outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Riley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Methods and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing large neural models and transferring knowledge from high-capacity teachers to compact students across vision, language, multimodal, and generative settings. Research has diversified beyond the original logits-based recipes into feature- and layer-level matching, many-to-many layer mappings, self-supervised distillation, data-free and online KD, task- and domain-adaptive compression, and combinations with architecture search and low-precision inference. Empirical and theoretical work highlights trade-offs involving teacher quality, the role of soft targets as regularizers, and practical constraints such as limited data, privacy, and inference latency. This synthesis summarizes key methods, empirical patterns, and open directions drawn from the provided literature.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Context‑Dependent, Foundational Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller student models. KD encompasses many mechanisms (soft logits, intermediate feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, data‑free and multi‑teacher schemes) and is most effective when integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, curriculum, domain adaptation). Its power for deployment in resource‑ or privacy‑constrained settings is well documented; however, KD is not universally sufficient. Success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher‑student compatibility, data availability, and mitigation of failure modes such as optimization mismatch, bias transfer, and degradation on rare phenomena. The pragmatic stance advocated here is to treat KD as a configurable component of a broader compression and deployment pipeline, tuned to task, data regime, and safety constraints.

papers_seen.author: Sims
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Insights, and Applications (Synthesis)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performance teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models by transferring information beyond hard labels. A broad toolkit has emerged — including logits/soft-label transfer, intermediate-feature and attention matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and self-distillation, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search — enabling deployment across vision, speech, language, generative, and multimodal settings. Empirical and theoretical work highlights gains in latency, memory, calibration, and sometimes robustness, while pointing to failure modes driven by teacher quality, capacity mismatch, data scarcity, and distribution shift; best practice treats KD as a core element of a broader, context-aware compression pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Maynard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly effective family of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory footprint, and deployment complexity. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and careful choice of distillation signals. Consequently, KD should be treated as a configurable, task-aware core of integrated compression pipelines that combine representation-level objectives, data strategies, and complementary compression primitives to meet practical deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Revisiting Knowledge Distillation via Label Smoothing Regularization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to distill the knowledge of a cumbersome teacher model into a lightweight student model. Its success is generally attributed to the privileged information on similarities among categories provided by the teacher model, and in this sense, only strong teacher models are deployed to teach weaker students in practice. In this work, we challenge this common belief by following experimental observations: 1) beyond the acknowledgment that the teacher can improve the student, the student can also enhance the teacher significantly by reversing the KD procedure; 2) a poorly-trained teacher with much lower accuracy than the student can still improve the latter significantly. To explain these observations, we provide a theoretical analysis of the relationships between KD and label smoothing regularization. We prove that 1) KD is a type of learned label smoothing regularization and 2) label smoothing regularization provides a virtual teacher model for KD. From these results, we argue that the success of KD is not fully due to the similarity information between categories from teachers, but also to the regularization of soft targets, which is equally or even more important.   Based on these analyses, we further propose a novel Teacher-free Knowledge Distillation (Tf-KD) framework, where a student model learns from itself or manuallydesigned regularization distribution. The Tf-KD achieves comparable performance with normal KD from a superior teacher, which is well applied when a stronger teacher model is unavailable. Meanwhile, Tf-KD is generic and can be directly deployed for training deep neural networks. Without any extra computation cost, Tf-KD achieves up to 0.65\% improvement on ImageNet over well-established baseline models, which is superior to label smoothing regularization.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used approach for transferring predictive behavior from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller, efficient students. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods extend beyond logits-matching to include intermediate-feature and attention-level transfer, data-free and privacy-aware variants, multi-teacher and online protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture design. Empirical work shows KD can yield compact models that retain much teacher performance, but success depends on careful selection of what and how to transfer, data availability, and the match between teacher and student.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably reduces model size and inference cost by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller students. KD encompasses many techniques — from matching soft logits to aligning intermediate features, attention maps, and relational structure — and is effective across vision, language, speech, and graph tasks when designed around task constraints and student capacity. However, KD is not a stand‑alone solution: its practical success depends on data availability, teacher quality, student architecture, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases, robustness deficits, and low-frequency behavior. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline that includes complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, data strategies (including augmentation and data-free synthesis), and robustness or privacy safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied framework for compressing large models, improving generalization, and transferring capabilities across modalities and deployment constraints. Research spans teacher-student paradigms (including multi-teacher and self-distillation), data-free and zero-shot distillation, task-adaptive compression, and applications to specialized tasks (detection, retrieval, translation, multimodal learning, federated settings, and graph problems). Empirical work shows KD can yield large speed and size gains while retaining much of the teacher's performance, but also exposes important limitations tied to optimization, data used for distillation, and potential bias transfer. Recent methods address these limitations via curriculum scheduling, confidence- or reinforcement-based teacher weighting, task-adaptive architecture search, domain- and modality-aware losses, and efficient label-generation or student-focused training regimes.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Ranking Distillation: Learning Compact Ranking Models With High Performance for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel way to train ranking models, such as recommender systems, that are both effective and efficient. Knowledge distillation (KD) was shown to be successful in image recognition to achieve both effectiveness and efficiency. We propose a KD technique for learning to rank problems, called \emph{ranking distillation (RD)}. Specifically, we train a smaller student model to learn to rank documents/items from both the training data and the supervision of a larger teacher model. The student model achieves a similar ranking performance to that of the large teacher model, but its smaller model size makes the online inference more efficient. RD is flexible because it is orthogonal to the choices of ranking models for the teacher and student. We address the challenges of RD for ranking problems. The experiments on public data sets and state-of-the-art recommendation models showed that RD achieves its design purposes: the student model learnt with RD has a model size less than half of the teacher model while achieving a ranking performance similar to the teacher model and much better than the student model learnt without RD.

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Demand-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, broadly applicable framework for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teachers' utility. KD methods span output matching, feature- and layer-level alignment, self- and ensemble-distillation, meta-learned and student-friendly teacher designs, and data- or task-aware adaptations. Empirical work across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks demonstrates KD’s ability to deliver large reductions in model size and compute with modest performance loss, and in many cases to improve robustness or generalization when combined with appropriate procedures. At the same time, KD’s reliability depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data; addressing these constraints through architectural design, curriculum and meta-learning, augmentation and synthetic-data strategies, and multi-teacher or online schemes is central to practical deployment.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Robust and Resource-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation by Generative Pseudo Replay
papers_seen.abstract: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD) allows knowledge transfer from a trained neural network (teacher) to a more compact one (student) in the absence of original training data. Existing works use a validation set to monitor the accuracy of the student over real data and report the highest performance throughout the entire process. However, validation data may not be available at distillation time either, making it infeasible to record the student snapshot that achieved the peak accuracy. Therefore, a practical data-free KD method should be robust and ideally provide monotonically increasing student accuracy during distillation. This is challenging because the student experiences knowledge degradation due to the distribution shift of the synthetic data. A straightforward approach to overcome this issue is to store and rehearse the generated samples periodically, which increases the memory footprint and creates privacy concerns. We propose to model the distribution of the previously observed synthetic samples with a generative network. In particular, we design a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a training objective that is customized to learn the synthetic data representations optimally. The student is rehearsed by the generative pseudo replay technique, with samples produced by the VAE. Hence knowledge degradation can be prevented without storing any samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show that our method optimizes the expected value of the distilled model accuracy while eliminating the large memory overhead incurred by the sample-storing methods.

papers_seen.author: Kelley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Practical, Context-Aware Advocacy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, broadly applicable approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across modalities and tasks. When treated as a flexible, task-aware toolbox—combining logits, feature and relational objectives, multi-teacher or ensemble signals, and data-aware input strategies—KD reliably enables deployments under latency, memory, privacy, and domain-shift constraints. However, KD is context-dependent: its success hinges on teacher quality, signal selection, data availability, and careful alignment of teacher and student. Best results come from integrating KD with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and from adopting targeted practices to mitigate known failure modes such as bias transfer and failures on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Bradshaw
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely adopted family of techniques for transferring behavior and representations from larger or composite teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD spans soft-target/logit matching, intermediate feature and attention imitation, relational or contrastive objectives, self- and multi-teacher schemes, and data-free or generator-based approaches; it is routinely combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and pretraining to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work across vision, speech, graphs, and natural language processing shows KD can substantially reduce model size and latency while preserving much of teacher performance, but its practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and careful choice of transfer targets and training protocols.

papers_seen.author: Douglas
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has grown from a simple teacher→student soft-target idea into a broad, task-aware toolbox for producing compact, faster, and more deployable models in deep learning and NLP. A diverse set of distillation targets and protocols (logits, intermediate representations, attention, relational and contrastive signals; offline, online, multi-teacher, data-free, and federated variants) together with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) enable substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute while often preserving most of teacher performance. Practical success is conditional on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment and capacity, data strategy, and mitigation of failure modes such as transferred errors, distribution shift, rare-output degradation, and privacy constraints. Treating KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline—with task-aware signal selection, layer mappings or projectors, curriculum or sample-selection strategies, and, where needed, adversarial or synthetic-data protocols—yields the most reliable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.
