papers_seen.author: Cherry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and complementary model-compression techniques form a practical toolbox for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Methods vary by what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or channel information, relational structures), whether real training data are available, and whether the goal is efficiency, robustness, privacy, or domain adaptation. Empirical work shows that carefully chosen distillation targets, layer-mapping strategies, teacher selection (including ensembles), and combinations with pruning or architecture-aware compression can recover much of teacher performance and enable deployment under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. Remaining challenges include handling low-frequency phenomena, distributional mismatch in data-free or federated settings, and optimization or alignment difficulties between teacher and student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Carpenter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. KD reliably reduces latency and memory while often preserving much of teacher performance across vision, language, speech, and generative tasks, but its effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and architectural alignment. For deployment-ready compression, KD should be treated as a cornerstone technique that is combined with task-aware design choices and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to close remaining optimization and generalization gaps.

papers_seen.author: Espinoza
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly validated, practical family of techniques for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, graph, and reinforcement-learning settings. A diverse toolkit—soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-teaching, data-free synthesis, and architecture-aware adaptations—enables large reductions in parameter count and inference cost while often preserving most teacher performance. Success in practice depends on choices about which signals to transfer, teacher–student alignment, availability and selection of data (or pseudo-data), and complementary compression steps (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Remaining scientific and engineering challenges include principled theory connecting distilled signals to student generalization, robust transfer across heterogeneous architectures and non-iid data, mitigation of transferred biases and degradation on rare outputs, and reliable privacy-preserving or federated protocols.

papers_seen.author: Green
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and versatile framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD enables substantial reductions in parameter count and latency while often retaining a large fraction of teacher performance. Its strengths derive from a broad family of techniques—soft-target/logit matching, intermediate feature and attention imitation, adversarial or contrastive data synthesis, online co-training, and data-free/zero-shot synthesis—combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. However, KD is not a universal panacea: careful, task-aware choices about which signals to transfer, how to align layers and inputs, how to select or adapt teachers, and how to handle limited or private data are essential to avoid pitfalls like bias transfer, degradation on low-frequency phenomena, and teacher–student mismatch. Treating KD as a configurable toolbox—integrated with pretraining, augmentation, and evaluation practices—yields the best outcomes for practical deployment and research progress.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques for producing compact, deployable neural models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational or contrastive signals) and across diverse protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, and data-free/privacy-aware schemes). When combined with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, KD routinely enables large reductions in latency, memory, and compute while preserving much of teacher performance. Its empirical success is conditional on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability and synthesis strategies, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, distribution shift, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Gaines
papers_seen.title: AdaBERT: Task-Adaptive BERT Compression with Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained language models such as BERT have shown their effectiveness in various natural language processing tasks. However, the huge parameter size makes them difficult to be deployed in real-time applications that require quick inference with limited resources. Existing methods compress BERT into small models while such compression is task-independent, i.e., the same compressed BERT for all different downstream tasks. Motivated by the necessity and benefits of task-oriented BERT compression, we propose a novel compression method, AdaBERT, that leverages differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically compress BERT into task-adaptive small models for specific tasks. We incorporate a task-oriented knowledge distillation loss to provide search hints and an efficiency-aware loss as search constraints, which enables a good trade-off between efficiency and effectiveness for task-adaptive BERT compression. We evaluate AdaBERT on several NLP tasks, and the results demonstrate that those task-adaptive compressed models are 12.7x to 29.3x faster than BERT in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x smaller in terms of parameter size, while comparable performance is maintained.

papers_seen.author: Strong
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesized Review
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior and richer internal information. A broad toolbox of distillation targets and protocols has emerged—soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free sample synthesis, self- and online-distillation, and multi-teacher schemes—and these are routinely combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD has been applied across vision, language, graphs, speech, generative models, and federated settings, yielding large reductions in model size and inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance when design choices are task- and architecture-aware. Remaining challenges include teacher–student mismatch, propagation of teacher errors and biases, data scarcity or privacy constraints, and instability in optimization; practical remedies emphasize task-aware signal selection, learned teacher adaptation, layer mapping strategies, and data-synthesis or privacy-preserving protocols. This review synthesizes empirical patterns, common mechanisms, practical recommendations, and open problems for KD-driven compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core set of techniques for producing compact models from larger teachers to enable deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, or privacy. Methods range from matching teacher logits to aligning internal features, attention maps, and layer correspondences; they are frequently combined with pruning, quantization, low-precision numerics, and architecture search. KD supports many practical settings — including data-limited, data-free, few-shot, federated, and cross-modal scenarios — but its effectiveness depends on choices such as which teacher signals to transfer, student capacity, data availability, and mitigation of transferred biases. Ongoing directions include principled theory for transfer objectives, robust and private distillation, and task-aware designs for structured outputs.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.

papers_seen.author: Barton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential but Non-Automatic Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. KD succeeds across modalities and tasks when practitioners treat it as a configurable set of techniques—logit supervision, intermediate-feature alignment, adversarial or contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, online co-training, and data-free synthesis—combined with complementary compression mechanisms (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful choices about teacher–student alignment, data regimes, and safeguards for robustness and privacy. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its effectiveness depends on explicit design choices and remains constrained by issues such as data scarcity, domain shift, teacher biases, optimization mismatch, and fidelity on low-frequency phenomena. The most reliable outcomes come from integrated pipelines that mix signal types, adapt teachers to students, and evaluate across deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Fair Feature Distillation for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Fairness is becoming an increasingly crucial issue for computer vision, especially in the human-related decision systems. However, achieving algorithmic fairness, which makes a model produce indiscriminative outcomes against protected groups, is still an unresolved problem. In this paper, we devise a systematic approach which reduces algorithmic biases via feature distillation for visual recognition tasks, dubbed as MMD-based Fair Distillation (MFD). While the distillation technique has been widely used in general to improve the prediction accuracy, to the best of our knowledge, there has been no explicit work that also tries to improve fairness via distillation. Furthermore, We give a theoretical justification of our MFD on the effect of knowledge distillation and fairness. Throughout the extensive experiments, we show our MFD significantly mitigates the bias against specific minorities without any loss of the accuracy on both synthetic and real-world face datasets.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of the Provided Literature
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models so they can be deployed under constraints of latency, memory, compute, or privacy. Methods range from matching soft logits to imitating intermediate features, attention maps, and relational structure, and can be combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and specialized data strategies. KD has enabled strong empirical gains across modalities and tasks (classification, generation, translation, graph learning, and recommender systems) but requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle limited or private data, and how to mitigate transfer of undesirable behaviors. Key practical themes include selecting appropriate distillation signals, handling teacher–student capacity and architecture mismatches, designing or synthesizing data when originals are unavailable, and integrating KD with complementary compression methods to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Warren

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their performance. When treated as a configurable toolkit rather than a single recipe—selecting what to transfer (logits, features, relations), how to map teacher and student layers, and whether to synthesize or reweight data—KD reliably enables latency-, memory-, and privacy-aware deployment across vision, language, generative, and structured tasks. However, its success depends on teacher quality, teacher–student alignment, and data availability; therefore best practice combines task-aware distillation objectives with complementary compression techniques and safeguards against transferred errors and biases.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Modalities, and Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques are now essential for deploying high-performing deep learning models under resource, privacy, and latency constraints. A broad set of distillation strategies—ranging from soft-label supervision and feature mimicking to data-free (zero-shot) distillation, adversarially guided feature transfer, self-distillation, and automated architecture search guided by teacher models—enable substantial reductions in model size and computational cost while preserving or even improving performance across vision, language, multimodal, and sequence tasks. Best practice combines input-side methods (data augmentation and mixup), representation-level transfer, and careful teacher-student design choices to match the deployment objectives (efficiency, fairness, interpretability, or privacy).

papers_seen.author: Santana

Its practical value arises when KD is designed around task objectives, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and deployment constraints, and when it is combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, Applications, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical framework for producing smaller, faster, and deployable models from larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and multimodal settings. Research has expanded KD beyond logits-only supervision into a rich set of objectives (feature and representation matching, relational and contrastive signals, adversarial/data-free schemes, and self-distillation), and into diverse data regimes from full-data to data-free, few-shot, federated, and privacy-constrained workflows. KD is frequently combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search, low-precision numerics) and with teacher-aware or student-aware design choices; its empirical success depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, and data strategies. Remaining challenges include handling architecture and distributional mismatch, avoiding propagation of teacher errors and biases (especially on low-frequency phenomena), providing privacy and robustness guarantees, and automating teacher–student co-design for task-specific outputs.

papers_seen.author: Merritt
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and practical family of techniques for transferring information from larger, often ensemble or overparameterized teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. KD methods operate at multiple granularities (soft logits, intermediate features, relational signals, attention maps, and adversarial or generator-based surrogate data) and are widely used across modalities (vision, language, speech, graphs, and multimodal tasks). Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can substantially reduce model size and inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance, but success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, the availability and selection of data (including synthesized or public data in privacy-sensitive settings), and how KD is combined with complementary compression methods. Key open problems include handling teacher–student mismatch, preserving low-frequency or minority phenomena, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and automating teacher and objective design for optimal transfer.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for transferring information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient students. KD variants—ranging from soft-logit matching to representation- and relation-based objectives, layer mapping, online/ensemble schemes, and data-synthesis methods—have been applied across vision, NLP, translation, retrieval, federated learning, and privacy-sensitive releases. When designed with task-awareness (selecting what to distill, aligning teacher and student, and engineering the distillation data and objectives) and combined with complementary compression tools, KD often yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs. However, KD is not a universal remedy: optimization challenges, teacher–student mismatch, data heterogeneity, and potential transfer of teacher errors or biases require careful mitigation. Best practice is to treat KD as a first-class element of a compression toolbox—default to distillation but tailor its form to task and deployment constraints, and combine it with architectural, data, and privacy-aware procedures to achieve robust, deployable models.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Towards Model Agnostic Federated Learning Using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Is it possible to design an universal API for federated learning using which an ad-hoc group of data-holders (agents) collaborate with each other and perform federated learning? Such an API would necessarily need to be model-agnostic i.e. make no assumption about the model architecture being used by the agents, and also cannot rely on having representative public data at hand. Knowledge distillation (KD) is the obvious tool of choice to design such protocols. However, surprisingly, we show that most natural KD-based federated learning protocols have poor performance.   To investigate this, we propose a new theoretical framework, Federated Kernel ridge regression, which can capture both model heterogeneity as well as data heterogeneity. Our analysis shows that the degradation is largely due to a fundamental limitation of knowledge distillation under data heterogeneity. We further validate our framework by analyzing and designing new protocols based on KD. Their performance on real world experiments using neural networks, though still unsatisfactory, closely matches our theoretical predictions.

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Patterns, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or structural information. A broad toolkit of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational and contrastive signals), protocols (offline, online/self-, multi-teacher, data‑free) and engineering practices (layer mapping, projectors, curriculum, data synthesis) has been developed and routinely combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirically, distillation frequently recovers most of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability and augmentation strategies, and explicit mitigation of transferred errors or low-frequency phenomena. Effective deployment requires task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to integrate distillation within end-to-end compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Harrison
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a single teacher-to-student logits-matching recipe into a large, task-aware toolbox for producing compact, efficient models in vision, speech, and natural language processing. Research documents many variants (soft logits, feature and relational matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, data-free and privacy-aware procedures, multi-teacher and online schemes) and shows that KD, when combined with complementary compression methods and task-specific design choices, can deliver substantial reductions in model size and latency while retaining most of a teacher's performance. Effectiveness depends on teacher quality, choice of transfer signals, availability and manipulation of data, student capacity, and deployment constraints; important open problems include theoretical guarantees, optimization gaps, distribution shift, privacy, and preserving rare-token or low-frequency behavior.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Adapt-and-Distill: Developing Small, Fast and Effective Pretrained Language Models for Domains
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained models have achieved great success in many natural language processing tasks. However, when they are applied in specific domains, these models suffer from domain shift and bring challenges in fine-tuning and online serving for latency and capacity constraints. In this paper, we present a general approach to developing small, fast and effective pre-trained models for specific domains. This is achieved by adapting the off-the-shelf general pre-trained models and performing task-agnostic knowledge distillation in target domains. Specifically, we propose domain-specific vocabulary expansion in the adaptation stage and employ corpus level occurrence probability to choose the size of incremental vocabulary automatically. Then we systematically explore different strategies to compress the large pre-trained models for specific domains. We conduct our experiments in the biomedical and computer science domain. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves better performance over the BERT BASE model in domain-specific tasks while 3.3x smaller and 5.1x faster than BERT BASE. The code and pre-trained models are available at https://aka.ms/adalm.

papers_seen.author: Peck
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context‑Dependent Engine for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and flexible family of methods for converting large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical results across vision, language, speech, and recommendation tasks show KD can recover most of a teacher’s performance while delivering substantial reductions in latency, memory, and communication cost. However, KD is not a one-size-fits-all solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime and selection, the choice of transfer signals, and how KD is combined with complementary compression methods. For reliable deployment, practitioners should treat KD as a task‑aware toolbox—selecting what to transfer, aligning teacher and student carefully, addressing data or privacy constraints, and integrating pruning/quantization or architecture-aware design—while explicitly mitigating limitations such as teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and privacy risks.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of large teachers. KD encompasses a range of targets and protocols—output-level supervision, intermediate representation matching, adversarial and data-free synthesis, multi-teacher and self-distillation—and is most effective when combined with architecture-aware design, data strategies, and complementary compression techniques. While KD routinely delivers favorable efficiency–accuracy trade-offs in vision, language, recommender, and multimodal systems, realizing those gains in practice requires attention to teacher–student alignment, data availability and privacy, fairness and low-frequency behavior, and method selection for the deployment constraints at hand.

papers_seen.author: Valdez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and properties of larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal, generative, and privacy-sensitive settings, KD variants transfer logits, intermediate representations, relations, or synthesized data to produce students that meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD often yields favorable trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and model size, but its success depends on data availability, teacher–student compatibility, and careful objective and training choices.

papers_seen.author: Fletcher
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have evolved from a simple teacher-to-student logits-matching recipe into a broad toolbox for producing compact, efficient, and adaptable models in vision, speech, and natural language processing. Research has produced a range of practical methods—logit and feature matching, multi-teacher and self-distillation, data- and privacy-aware variants, and federated or online protocols—and has clarified connections to regularization, ensemble learning, and optimization. Empirical work shows KD can substantially reduce inference cost while preserving much of the teacher's performance, though gains depend on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and adaptation to deployment constraints. This synthesis summarizes core methods, theoretical insights, empirical findings, practical considerations, and open challenges that shape current best practice for KD-driven compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Obrien
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broad toolbox for transferring predictive capacity from large, expensive models to smaller, faster, or privacy-preserving models. Methods range from soft-logit supervision to internal representation matching, contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical evidence across vision, NLP, graphs, and federated settings shows KD can recover much of a teacher's performance in resource-constrained deployments, while challenges remain in teacher selection, data availability, bias propagation, and task-specific design.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge distillation from multi-modal to mono-modal segmentation networks
papers_seen.abstract: The joint use of multiple imaging modalities for medical image segmentation has been widely studied in recent years. The fusion of information from different modalities has demonstrated to improve the segmentation accuracy, with respect to mono-modal segmentations, in several applications. However, acquiring multiple modalities is usually not possible in a clinical setting due to a limited number of physicians and scanners, and to limit costs and scan time. Most of the time, only one modality is acquired. In this paper, we propose KD-Net, a framework to transfer knowledge from a trained multi-modal network (teacher) to a mono-modal one (student). The proposed method is an adaptation of the generalized distillation framework where the student network is trained on a subset (1 modality) of the teacher's inputs (n modalities). We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in brain tumor segmentation with the BraTS 2018 dataset. Using different architectures, we show that the student network effectively learns from the teacher and always outperforms the baseline mono-modal network in terms of segmentation accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Sandoval
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Conditional Strategy for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broadly applicable framework that enables compact, efficient models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teachers to smaller students. KD methods span logits, intermediate-feature and relational matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and cross-modal variants, and complementary integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. While KD often recovers much of a teacher’s performance and provides regularization benefits, its practical success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and selection, and careful choice of what and how to transfer. Effective deployment treats KD as a configurable component within an integrated compression pipeline rather than a one-shot cure, and addresses robustness, privacy, and distribution-shift concerns through protocol design and complementary techniques.

papers_seen.author: Coleman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Principles
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller, deployable student models. Across computer vision, natural language processing, and multimodal tasks, KD supports multiple transfer targets and training regimes, and it is most effective when incorporated into an integrated compression pipeline with complementary primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation) and task-aware design. Empirical work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can sometimes surpass teachers when teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and training protocols are carefully managed. Outstanding challenges include capacity and optimization mismatch, data scarcity and privacy constraints, distribution shift, and preserving low-frequency or rare-case behaviors; practical deployments address these through layered objectives, data synthesis or augmentation, and safeguards for robustness and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques are widely used to produce smaller, faster models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. Work across theory, computer vision, natural language processing, graph learning and systems has explored why distillation works, how to make it practical under constraints (limited or no access to original data, privacy, federated settings), and how to adapt it to specialized settings (pretrained language models, non-autoregressive translation, detectors, GANs, visual-linguistic models). Empirical and theoretical studies identify benefits, failure modes, and design patterns: distillation often simplifies learning targets and stabilizes optimization; matching intermediate representations, attention patterns, or relational structure can improve transfer; mixing soft and hard targets can correct teacher errors; and specialized procedures (e.g., layer mapping, adversarial sample generation, teacher adaptation) are effective for particular tasks. Remaining challenges include handling heterogeneous or private data, preserving low-frequency or rare-token behavior in sequence tasks, and formalizing the optimal teacher-student pairing and data complexity trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Flynn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Synthesis of the Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a flexible, empirically validated family of techniques for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller students. Across modalities and training protocols, distillation operates at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational signals) and is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods and task-aware design. Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, data availability or synthesis, and careful objective and optimization design; important limitations include teacher error propagation, impaired modeling of low-frequency phenomena, and distribution-shift vulnerabilities.

papers_seen.author: Moran
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Path to Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and adaptable strategy for compressing deep models across modalities and tasks. It can preserve much of a teacher's performance while reducing memory, computation, and inference latency; it also enables task-adaptive and privacy-conscious deployments. Remaining challenges—data availability, matching student capacity to teacher signals, and choosing the right transfer targets—can be mitigated by a suite of complementary KD techniques.

papers_seen.author: Simpson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task‑Aware Component of Model Compression: Promise, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and versatile approach for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller students. KD methods vary in their transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals), training paradigms (offline, online, multi‑teacher, meta‑learned teachers, data‑free synthesis), and integration with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across retrieval, vision, speech, and NLP shows distilled students frequently recover a large fraction of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but reliable deployment requires task‑aware design choices, careful teacher–student alignment, suitable data strategies (including synthesis or privacy‑aware protocols), and explicit safeguards against propagated teacher artifacts and distributional mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Cordova
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core of Practical Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely applicable strategy for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD routinely reduces inference cost and memory while preserving a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but its reliability is context-dependent: teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, architecture alignment, and complementary compression primitives critically shape outcomes. A pragmatic recommendation is to treat KD as the central component of compression pipelines while explicitly adapting objectives, data protocols, and auxiliary methods to the deployment constraints and known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Alvarado
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing neural networks into smaller, faster models by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations from teacher to student. A broad family of distillation techniques has been developed—logit (soft-label) matching, feature and layer-wise mimicry, multi-teacher and confidence-weighted schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware variants—enabling deployment across vision, language, graphs, recommender systems, and federated settings. While distillation often preserves most teacher performance and can even improve student generalization, effectiveness depends on what is transferred, layer alignment, teacher quality, availability and match of data, and complementary compression methods. This synthesis summarizes the operational variants, key empirical findings, domain-specific applications, common failure modes, and practical recommendations distilled from the provided studies.

papers_seen.author: Humphrey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Tool for Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broadly applicable approach for compressing and adapting deep models across modalities (text, vision, graphs, speech) and deployment scenarios (edge devices, federated clients, domain shifts). Empirical evidence shows KD can improve student generalization, enable small-footprint models, and facilitate domain- or modality-transfer when combined with representation-level objectives or adversarial/contrastive methods. However, its success depends on optimization, teacher-student design, data availability, and fairness considerations. I argue that KD should be treated as a flexible framework—one that combines logit-level supervision with representation-aware objectives, domain-aware selection of teacher signals, and explicit measures to mitigate undesirable side effects (e.g., lexical errors or bias)—to reliably produce compact, high-quality models for NLP and beyond.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods provide practical routes to deploy high-performing deep models under resource, privacy, and latency constraints. The literature has developed diverse approaches that transfer information via soft logits, intermediate features, attentional maps, channel-wise statistics, and online mutual learning; adaptations address task-specific compression, data-free or few-shot regimes, large-scale distributed training, and teacher-student co-optimization. Empirical and theoretical analyses highlight that distillation combines information transfer with regularization effects, and that selecting what, when, and how to transfer knowledge (e.g., logits vs. features, offline vs. online, task-aware filtering) is crucial to achieve favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across vision and language tasks.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: It is challenging to perform lifelong language learning (LLL) on a stream of different tasks without any performance degradation comparing to the multi-task counterparts. To address this issue, we present Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation (L2KD), a simple but efficient method that can be easily applied to existing LLL architectures in order to mitigate the degradation. Specifically, when the LLL model is trained on a new task, we assign a teacher model to first learn the new task, and pass the knowledge to the LLL model via knowledge distillation. Therefore, the LLL model can better adapt to the new task while keeping the previously learned knowledge. Experiments show that the proposed L2KD consistently improves previous state-of-the-art models, and the degradation comparing to multi-task models in LLL tasks is well mitigated for both sequence generation and text classification tasks.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Methods and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become central tools for deploying high-performance deep models in resource-constrained settings. Across computer vision, generative modeling, 3D rendering, graph learning, and natural language processing, researchers employ a range of distillation paradigms — including teacher-student soft-label transfer, intermediate representation matching, self-distillation, data-free and privacy-preserving distillation, and automated architecture search guided by teacher models — to produce smaller, faster, or more interpretable students while retaining much of the teacher performance. Practical concerns such as limited or unavailable training data, domain shifts, adversarial robustness, and the need for interpretable or low-precision models have driven specific adaptations of KD. Empirical results across tasks show that (1) distillation can greatly reduce model size or runtime with small accuracy loss, (2) internal- and feature-level matching often improves transfer beyond logits-only approaches, and (3) novel protocols (e.g., ensemble teachers, generative pseudo-replay, many-to-many layer alignment) expand KD applicability to privacy-sensitive, multimodal, and generation tasks.

papers_seen.author: Sparks
papers_seen.title: Position: Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Line, Task‑Aware Core of Practical Model Compression (with Explicit Limits and Prescriptions)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the primary, first‑line strategy for compressing large deep and NLP models into deployable students because it is flexible, empirically effective across modalities, and interoperable with complementary compression primitives. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on task‑aware choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data regime, and explicit mitigations for transferred bias, capacity mismatch, and low‑frequency behaviors. Practitioners should adopt KD as a configurable core within integrated pipelines that include task adaptation, selective or curriculum distillation, and complementary methods (pruning, quantization, and architecture search) to meet concrete deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Garner
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically grounded family of methods for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or auxiliary teacher models into compact students. Modern KD methods extend beyond soft-target (logit) matching to include feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online protocols, and data‑free or synthetic‑data approaches. Empirical results across vision, language, speech, recommendation, and graph tasks show KD can recover much of teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, choice of distilled signals, and data strategies are carefully matched; practitioners therefore treat KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and task-aware training. Important limitations remain—teacher bias transfer, capacity mismatch, degraded modeling of rare outputs, distributional shift, privacy concerns, and theoretical gaps—motivating research on adaptive teacher selection, data synthesis, privacy-preserving protocols, and better mappings between distilled signals and student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger systems. Across modalities and tasks—including classification, generation, retrieval, speech, and sequence prediction—distillation has been adapted to transfer ensemble knowledge, reduce computation and storage, improve generalization and fairness, enable private or federated deployment, and inject specialized inductive biases. While effective, distillation requires careful design choices (teacher quality, which examples to transfer, whether to use intermediate-layer alignment, robustness and privacy mechanisms) to avoid failure modes. This work argues that KD should be treated not just as a compression trick but as a unifying framework for controlled transfer of behaviors, and outlines empirical and theoretical findings that guide best practices for its application.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely adopted approach for producing compact models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models. The approach spans simple soft-label transfer to richer objectives that match intermediate representations, attention maps, relational or contrastive structures, and supports many protocols (offline, online/co-distillation, multi-teacher, self-distillation and data-free variants). KD is most effective when integrated into a broader compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, curriculum learning, and data strategies—and when choices about transfer targets, layer alignment, and data are tailored to task and deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD often preserves most of teacher performance and can improve student generalization, but it has concrete failure modes (teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, degradation on rare phenomena, privacy and fairness risks) that require targeted mitigations and evaluation.

papers_seen.author: Brooks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: an Essential, Context‑Aware Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller students. KD methods extend beyond simple logit matching to include representation- and relation-level objectives, multi-teacher and online protocols, and data- or privacy-aware variants. When combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and applied with task-aware design, KD routinely yields favorable efficiency–accuracy trade-offs. However, KD is context-dependent: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of bias, low-frequency/fine-grained behavior, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Schultz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Findings from the Provided Literature
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring information from large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient student models so they can be deployed under constraints of latency, memory, compute, and privacy. The literature treats KD as a flexible, configurable component of compression pipelines rather than a single recipe: methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, channel- or relation-level signals), how transfer is organized (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, data-free/zero-shot), and how KD is combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, adversarial training). Empirical evidence shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but success depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the chosen distillation signals and objectives, and data availability or synthesis strategies. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable, task-aware tool integrated with other compression and robustness practices.

papers_seen.author: Cardenas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models. Across vision, language, and generative settings, KD offers multiple transfer targets and protocols that enable meaningful reductions in latency, memory, and compute while often preserving most of a teacher's performance. However, KD is not a turnkey cure: its practical success requires careful, task‑aware choices about which signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacity and architecture, how to handle limited or private data, and how to pair distillation with complementary compression primitives and safeguards for rare-case behavior and bias. Treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline, KD delivers robust, deployable gains; remaining challenges motivate continued work on principled objectives, data‑efficient and privacy‑aware protocols, and reliable long‑tail preservation.

papers_seen.author: Buchanan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential, Context‑Aware, and Insufficient Alone for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and empirically validated family of techniques that reliably improves the efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs of deep models across modalities. KD enables deployment by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller students, and it supports many training protocols and transfer targets. However, KD is not a standalone solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability or synthesis of suitable data, and careful mitigation of failure modes (distribution shift, low-frequency degradation, and bias propagation). Therefore, for robust real-world deployment KD should be treated as a configurable, task‑aware core of an integrated compression pipeline that combines complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture design), teacher–student co‑design, and data strategies tailored to the application.

papers_seen.author: Powell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context-Sensitive Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and practically effective family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals) and across training protocols (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation and data-free synthesis). Empirical work shows KD frequently recovers much of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in inference cost and memory footprint, but outcomes are highly context-sensitive: they depend on teacher quality and design, student capacity and architecture alignment, availability and distribution of data, and the choice of distillation objectives and layer mappings. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component within hybrid compression pipelines that combine pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and privacy- or domain-aware interventions.

papers_seen.author: Robertson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practical family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more deployable student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods—ranging from soft-logit matching to feature- and attention-level imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and online or self-distillation—are combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet deployment constraints. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often preserves most teacher performance while enabling lower-latency, lower-memory, and privacy-aware deployment, but its success depends critically on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis strategies, and safeguards against transferred biases or degraded performance on rare phenomena; these dependencies motivate configurable, task-aware KD pipelines rather than one-size-fits-all recipes.

papers_seen.author: Orr
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Theory, and Practical Strategies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) encompasses a family of techniques for transferring information from high-capacity teacher models to smaller or otherwise constrained student models so they retain functionality while reducing latency, memory, and computational cost. Over the past decade KD has evolved from logits-based soft-label supervision to a rich toolkit that includes intermediate-feature matching, layer-wise and task-aware mappings, adversarial and contrastive objectives, ensemble and self-distillation, data-free synthesis, and federated or heterogeneous-device protocols. Empirical and theoretical work indicates KD often acts both as knowledge transfer and as a form of regularization; its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and selection, task alignment, and careful design of objectives and model interfaces. Remaining challenges include robust transfer under data scarcity or domain shift, preserving rare-token behavior in sequence tasks, principled layer-to-layer alignment across heterogeneous architectures, and mitigating teacher-induced biases.

papers_seen.author: Lopez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfer behavior and/or internal structure from larger, often ensemble or multi-modal teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels—from soft-label supervision to intermediate-feature, attention, and relational matching—and are widely used to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under memory or latency constraints, and support domain or modality adaptation. The effectiveness of KD depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and selection, and careful design of what and how knowledge is transferred; combining KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and targeted training protocols improves reliability in practice.

papers_seen.author: Shaw
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Insights, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques reduce the size and computational cost of large deep models while retaining much of their performance. Across classification, sequence modeling, generation, and structured prediction, researchers have developed soft-label distillation, intermediate-feature guidance, adversarial and contrastive objectives, projector and embedding modules, and privacy-aware mechanisms to transfer knowledge from large teacher models to smaller students. Empirical and theoretical work highlights trade-offs among bias, variance, teacher quality, and data complexity, and shows that distillation interacts with pre-training, label smoothing, and modality differences. Applications span speech and machine translation to GANs and graph neural networks; complementary methods such as pruning and block-structured compression can further improve deployment on constrained hardware.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Multifaceted Tool for Compression, Robustness, and Responsible NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large models into efficient students while also serving as a lever for regularization, robustness, privacy, fairness, interpretability, and continual/multi-task learning. When applied thoughtfully—combining soft-label distillation with feature- and representation-level matching, layer mapping, attention or projector modules, and task-aware curricula—KD can produce lightweight models that approach or sometimes exceed teacher performance on constrained devices and specialized tasks. However, KD is not automatic: optimization difficulties, data heterogeneity, and mismatches in the information transferred (e.g., for low-frequency tokens or internal features) limit its effectiveness unless complemented by targeted methodological choices. I argue that KD should be treated as a principled toolbox rather than a single recipe: choose distillation targets (outputs, features, internal representations), mapping strategies (many-to-many layer mapping, attention, projectors), and auxiliary safeguards (privacy-preserving noise, fairness interventions, adversarial distillation) to align compression goals with safety and utility requirements.

papers_seen.author: Mendoza
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Effects, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used, flexible framework for producing smaller, faster models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact students. KD encompasses a range of transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive signals) and protocols (offline, online, multi-teacher, data-free, and curriculum-driven). Empirical work demonstrates KD often preserves much of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute, but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, data availability or synthesis, and integration with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone cure-all. Key open directions include principled selection of signals to transfer, robust privacy-preserving distillation, automation of deployment-aware pipelines, and reliable compression of large transformer and generative models.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.author: Bray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task‑Aware Tool for Model Compression (with Limits and Practical Remedies)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a practical, versatile framework for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized students. When applied with task‑aware objectives, appropriate data strategies, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, or architecture search), KD routinely yields compact models suitable for latency- and memory-constrained deployment. However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher quality and compatibility with the student, the choice of distilled signals, data availability and augmentation, and mitigation of teacher artifacts. Careful protocol design—pre-training compact architectures, selecting what to distill, using effective augmentation or data synthesis, and combining KD with complementary methods—produces the most reliable results in practice.

papers_seen.author: Maynard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly effective family of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory footprint, and deployment complexity. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and careful choice of distillation signals. Consequently, KD should be treated as a configurable, task-aware core of integrated compression pipelines that combine representation-level objectives, data strategies, and complementary compression primitives to meet practical deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Christensen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task‑Aware Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable toolkit for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD consistently yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when its signals, data, and optimization are matched to task and student capacity, and when it is integrated with complementary compression techniques. However, KD is not a universal cure: its benefits are context-dependent, and challenges remain around teacher–student optimization gaps, transfer of teacher artifacts (especially for low‑frequency phenomena), privacy and data scarcity, and principled selection of distilled signals. Treating KD as a configurable, task-aware component of a broader compression pipeline yields the most reliable outcomes for deployment.

papers_seen.author: Figueroa
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of their performance. KD encompasses logits-based, feature- and representation-level, multi-teacher, online, self-distillation, and privacy-aware variants, and its effectiveness depends on choosing what to transfer, matching student capacity to teacher signals, and integrating complementary compression and training practices. When combined with architecture-aware design, augmentation or synthetic-data generation, and privacy- or communication-aware protocols, KD enables deployable models across resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive settings.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Is Label Smoothing Truly Incompatible with Knowledge Distillation: An Empirical Study
papers_seen.abstract: This work aims to empirically clarify a recently discovered perspective that label smoothing is incompatible with knowledge distillation. We begin by introducing the motivation behind on how this incompatibility is raised, i.e., label smoothing erases relative information between teacher logits. We provide a novel connection on how label smoothing affects distributions of semantically similar and dissimilar classes. Then we propose a metric to quantitatively measure the degree of erased information in sample's representation. After that, we study its one-sidedness and imperfection of the incompatibility view through massive analyses, visualizations and comprehensive experiments on Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation. Finally, we broadly discuss several circumstances wherein label smoothing will indeed lose its effectiveness. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Self-Knowledge Distillation in Natural Language Processing
papers_seen.abstract: Since deep learning became a key player in natural language processing (NLP), many deep learning models have been showing remarkable performances in a variety of NLP tasks, and in some cases, they are even outperforming humans. Such high performance can be explained by efficient knowledge representation of deep learning models. While many methods have been proposed to learn more efficient representation, knowledge distillation from pretrained deep networks suggest that we can use more information from the soft target probability to train other neural networks. In this paper, we propose a new knowledge distillation method self-knowledge distillation, based on the soft target probabilities of the training model itself, where multimode information is distilled from the word embedding space right below the softmax layer. Due to the time complexity, our method approximates the soft target probabilities. In experiments, we applied the proposed method to two different and fundamental NLP tasks: language model and neural machine translation. The experiment results show that our proposed method improves performance on the tasks.

papers_seen.author: Potter
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible set of methods for transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models to enable deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, or privacy. Across vision and natural language tasks, distillation targets range from soft logits to intermediate representations and relational signals; KD is frequently combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with domain- or task-specific procedures to improve efficacy. KD delivers strong empirical gains in many settings but is bounded by teacher quality, availability and match of data, teacher–student capacity gaps, and the risk of transferring teacher biases; effective application therefore requires task-aware choices of signals, data strategies, and often hybrid compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential, Versatile, and Context-Dependent Toolkit for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical set of techniques for transferring behavior and representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD techniques — spanning soft-label/logit transfer, intermediate-representation matching, adversarial or data-free synthesis, and teacher-aware or multi-teacher strategies — repeatedly enable large reductions in model size and inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on task and data properties, teacher–student alignment, optimization, and deployment constraints, and it works best when combined with complementary compression techniques and task-aware design choices.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression comprise a diverse set of techniques to produce smaller, faster, or more private models by transferring information from larger or auxiliary models. Research spans supervised teacher-student frameworks, self-distillation, multi-teacher and task-adaptive compression, and distillation combined with pruning, architecture search, adversarial training, and data augmentation. Practical work demonstrates benefits across vision, multimodal, graph, and NLP tasks, while theoretical analyses connect distillation to label smoothing, ensemble behavior, and bias–variance tradeoffs. Open challenges include aligning heterogeneous inputs and modalities, preserving robustness and privacy, and handling low-resource or low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.
