papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller, more deployable student models. Over the past decade KD has expanded beyond simple soft-logit matching into a rich toolbox that includes intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, self- and multi-teacher schemes, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and hybrids with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance and enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but its effectiveness depends on careful alignment of objectives, teacher/student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and distributional failures. This review synthesizes methods, empirical patterns, limitations, and practical recommendations for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Hart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the behavior and performance of larger teachers. KD succeeds across modalities and tasks when integrated thoughtfully into compression pipelines and paired with complementary techniques, but its effectiveness is conditional on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student design, data strategy, and safeguards for robustness and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Strategy for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable technique for compressing and adapting large neural models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Across computer vision, generative modeling, cross-modal systems, and NLP, distillation can be combined with complementary methods (pre-training, pruning, quantization, adversarial training, and feature alignment) to meet deployment constraints and domain requirements. Success depends on teacher design, the availability and nature of data used for transfer, careful alignment of representations, and training objectives that address optimization challenges.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Preserving Privacy in Federated Learning with Ensemble Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm where local nodes collaboratively train a central model while the training data remains decentralized. Existing FL methods typically share model parameters or employ co-distillation to address the issue of unbalanced data distribution. However, they suffer from communication bottlenecks. More importantly, they risk privacy leakage. In this work, we develop a privacy preserving and communication efficient method in a FL framework with one-shot offline knowledge distillation using unlabeled, cross-domain public data. We propose a quantized and noisy ensemble of local predictions from completely trained local models for stronger privacy guarantees without sacrificing accuracy. Based on extensive experiments on image classification and text classification tasks, we show that our privacy-preserving method outperforms baseline FL algorithms with superior performance in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Baird
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and widely applied family of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger or more expressive teacher models into smaller, faster student models to meet latency, memory, privacy, or deployment constraints. The literature offers a broad taxonomy of distilled signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive structure), training protocols (offline teacher→student, online/self-distillation, multi‑teacher, data‑free or generative), and architecture-aware adaptations that are commonly integrated with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across NLP, vision, visual‑linguistic models, retrieval, and specialized domains shows KD can recover much teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, and data strategies are addressed, but it faces recurring limits from teacher–student mismatch, limited or absent data, propagation of teacher artifacts (biases, failure modes), and challenges in reliably transferring robustness and low‑frequency behaviors. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline rather than a single turnkey solution.

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression, Adaptation and Privacy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a single recipe for shrinking large models: it is a flexible family of techniques that enables accurate, efficient and deployable models across modalities and tasks. KD can compress huge pretrained language and vision models into lightweight architectures with large speed and memory gains while retaining most of the teacher performance. It also supports variant protocols—online, self-distillation, multi-teacher, representation-level and contrastive forms—that trade off efficiency, robustness, and generalization. Beyond raw compression, KD can enable domain adaptation, privacy-preserving model release, and fairness-aware training when combined with appropriate design choices. However, KD is not a panacea: teacher quality, data heterogeneity, and mismatch between teacher and student inputs/architectures can limit gains and must be addressed by specific strategies such as multi-teacher ensembles, confidence weighting, input alignment, or theoretical safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Warren
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Multifaceted Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their performance. When treated as a configurable toolkit rather than a single recipe—selecting what to transfer (logits, features, relations), how to map teacher and student layers, and whether to synthesize or reweight data—KD reliably enables latency-, memory-, and privacy-aware deployment across vision, language, generative, and structured tasks. However, its success depends on teacher quality, teacher–student alignment, and data availability; therefore best practice combines task-aware distillation objectives with complementary compression techniques and safeguards against transferred errors and biases.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of the Provided Literature
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models so they can be deployed under constraints of latency, memory, compute, or privacy. Methods range from matching soft logits to imitating intermediate features, attention maps, and relational structure, and can be combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and specialized data strategies. KD has enabled strong empirical gains across modalities and tasks (classification, generation, translation, graph learning, and recommender systems) but requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle limited or private data, and how to mitigate transfer of undesirable behaviors. Key practical themes include selecting appropriate distillation signals, handling teacher–student capacity and architecture mismatches, designing or synthesizing data when originals are unavailable, and integrating KD with complementary compression methods to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Mitchell
papers_seen.title: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted family of techniques for transferring information from larger or otherwise stronger teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models to reduce inference cost and enable deployment in constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. The literature documents a wide set of distilled signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive structure), training protocols (offline teacher–student, online/co-distillation, self-distillation, multi-teacher), and data strategies (data-rich, data-free, augmentation and selective-sample curricula). Empirical work across vision, language, graph, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling shows that well-designed KD pipelines — especially those that match internal representations, align layers thoughtfully, and combine KD with pruning/quantization or student-aware teacher design — can retain much of teacher performance while substantially lowering model size and latency. However, KD has failure modes (teacher mismatch, degraded modeling of rare phenomena, privacy and bias transfer, and sensitivity to data availability) that require complementary methods such as data-free synthesis, domain-aware adaptation, privacy-preserving noise, and careful objective design. The field continues to refine when and how to apply KD so that compact models are accurate, robust, and suitable for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques for producing compact, deployable neural models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational or contrastive signals) and across diverse protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, and data-free/privacy-aware schemes). When combined with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, KD routinely enables large reductions in latency, memory, and compute while preserving much of teacher performance. Its empirical success is conditional on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability and synthesis strategies, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, distribution shift, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Efficient Transformer-based Large Scale Language Representations using Hardware-friendly Block Structured Pruning
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained large-scale language models have increasingly demonstrated high accuracy on many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, the limited weight storage and computational speed on hardware platforms have impeded the popularity of pre-trained models, especially in the era of edge computing. In this work, we propose an efficient transformer-based large-scale language representation using hardware-friendly block structure pruning. We incorporate the reweighted group Lasso into block-structured pruning for optimization. Besides the significantly reduced weight storage and computation, the proposed approach achieves high compression rates. Experimental results on different models (BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT) on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark tasks show that we achieve up to 5.0x with zero or minor accuracy degradation on certain task(s). Our proposed method is also orthogonal to existing compact pre-trained language models such as DistilBERT using knowledge distillation, since a further 1.79x average compression rate can be achieved on top of DistilBERT with zero or minor accuracy degradation. It is suitable to deploy the final compressed model on resource-constrained edge devices.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Linkless Link Prediction via Relational Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown exceptional performance in the task of link prediction. Despite their effectiveness, the high latency brought by non-trivial neighborhood data dependency limits GNNs in practical deployments. Conversely, the known efficient MLPs are much less effective than GNNs due to the lack of relational knowledge. In this work, to combine the advantages of GNNs and MLPs, we start with exploring direct knowledge distillation (KD) methods for link prediction, i.e., predicted logit-based matching and node representation-based matching. Upon observing direct KD analogs do not perform well for link prediction, we propose a relational KD framework, Linkless Link Prediction (LLP), to distill knowledge for link prediction with MLPs. Unlike simple KD methods that match independent link logits or node representations, LLP distills relational knowledge that is centered around each (anchor) node to the student MLP. Specifically, we propose rank-based matching and distribution-based matching strategies that complement each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LLP boosts the link prediction performance of MLPs with significant margins, and even outperforms the teacher GNNs on 7 out of 8 benchmarks. LLP also achieves a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference compared to GNNs on the large-scale OGB dataset.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad toolkit—ranging from soft logits to intermediate-feature and adversarial or data-free methods—has been developed and applied across vision, language, speech, and multimodal problems. Practical success depends on matching the distilled signal to student capacity and data regime, combining KD with other compression methods, and explicitly addressing known failure modes such as teacher bias, capacity mismatch, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Aguilar
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger (or specialized) teacher models to smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational/contrastive structure), how mappings between teacher and student are implemented (layer alignment, projectors, many-to-many mappings), and how training is scheduled (fixed teacher, student-friendly teacher learning, meta-learning, or self-distillation). KD is frequently combined with other compression primitives (pruning, quantization, low-precision numerics, progressive module replacement, and architecture search) and with data strategies (augmentation, mixup, data-free synthesis, domain adaptation) to meet deployment, privacy, and domain-shift constraints. While KD often yields strong empirical gains in accuracy, efficiency, and robustness, its success depends on teacher quality, the distilled signals chosen, data availability and complexity, and careful optimization; open problems remain in principled selection of distillation targets, mitigating transferred biases, and integrating KD optimally with other compression tools.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used family of techniques for transferring behavior from larger, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, KD variants—including logits/soft-target matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and adversarial generation, and self-distillation—are combined with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows that carefully designed distillation pipelines typically recover most teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but outcomes depend on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of transfer signals, and the availability or synthesis of data; remaining challenges include robustness, bias transfer, low-frequency/structured-output preservation, privacy-aware distillation, and automating teacher–student co-design.

papers_seen.author: Solis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational, Task‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multifaceted approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD methods span output-level supervision, intermediate-representation matching, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and many-to-many layer mappings, and are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. When applied with task-awareness — i.e., selecting appropriate distilled signals, matching teacher and student capacity, and adapting data and optimization — KD reliably delivers favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across vision, language, speech, detection, and federated settings. Nevertheless, KD has well-documented failure modes (capacity and optimization gaps, bias transfer, degradation on rare phenomena, and privacy concerns), and future progress depends on principled theory, automation of teacher–student matching, and responsible, privacy-aware protocols.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly validated, practical family of methods for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. In practice KD is most effective when integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and when training choices account for teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability, and deployment constraints. KD often preserves most teacher performance and can improve student generalization, but it can also transfer teacher biases or degrade rare-token behavior; therefore it should be treated as a configurable, task-aware component of end-to-end compression pipelines.

Empirically, KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance across vision and language tasks, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of transfer targets, and the availability or synthesis of appropriate distillation data. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a turnkey solution.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large neural models and transferring knowledge across architectures, tasks, and deployment constraints. Work across vision, language, graphs, and generative representations shows diverse KD objectives (soft-target, feature, relational, contrastive, and layer-matching), a range of data regimes (full-data, limited-data, data-free/zero-shot), and many complementary compression mechanisms (pruning, architecture search, block-structured sparsity, and cheap operators). Empirical and theoretical studies clarify when KD helps, how it interacts with data-augmentation and teacher imperfection, and how KD can be adapted for privacy-preserving or federated scenarios. This review summarizes these practical methods, observed trade-offs, and open challenges for robust, efficient, and private model compression.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical, and Context‑Aware Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across deep learning and NLP. KD reliably transfers predictive behavior and internal representations using a variety of signals and training protocols, and when combined with complementary compression methods and task-aware choices it enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is context dependent: its success hinges on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of transferred errors, robustness deficits, and fairness or privacy issues. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a stand‑alone cure.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Few Shot Network Compression via Cross Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Model compression has been widely adopted to obtain light-weighted deep neural networks. Most prevalent methods, however, require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to ensure accuracy, which could be challenged by privacy and security issues. As a compromise between privacy and performance, in this paper we investigate few shot network compression: given few samples per class, how can we effectively compress the network with negligible performance drop? The core challenge of few shot network compression lies in high estimation errors from the original network during inference, since the compressed network can easily over-fits on the few training instances. The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output. To address the problem, we propose cross distillation, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation approach. By interweaving hidden layers of teacher and student network, layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced.The proposed method offers a general framework compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that cross distillation can significantly improve the student network's accuracy when only a few training instances are available.

papers_seen.author: Miles
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically essential framework for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in both vision and natural language settings. A diverse set of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational signals) and training protocols (offline teacher→student, online/self-distillation, multi‑teacher, data‑free or generative) enables substantial reductions in latency and memory while often retaining much of teacher performance. Effective application of KD requires task‑ and data‑aware choices and is most reliable when combined with complementary compression methods and explicit mitigation of known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Distilling Object Detectors with Fine-grained Feature Imitation
papers_seen.abstract: State-of-the-art CNN based recognition models are often computationally prohibitive to deploy on low-end devices. A promising high level approach tackling this limitation is knowledge distillation, which let small student model mimic cumbersome teacher model's output to get improved generalization. However, related methods mainly focus on simple task of classification while do not consider complex tasks like object detection. We show applying the vanilla knowledge distillation to detection model gets minor gain. To address the challenge of distilling knowledge in detection model, we propose a fine-grained feature imitation method exploiting the cross-location discrepancy of feature response. Our intuition is that detectors care more about local near object regions. Thus the discrepancy of feature response on the near object anchor locations reveals important information of how teacher model tends to generalize. We design a novel mechanism to estimate those locations and let student model imitate the teacher on them to get enhanced performance. We first validate the idea on a developed lightweight toy detector which carries simplest notion of current state-of-the-art anchor based detection models on challenging KITTI dataset, our method generates up to 15% boost of mAP for the student model compared to the non-imitated counterpart. We then extensively evaluate the method with Faster R-CNN model under various scenarios with common object detection benchmark of Pascal VOC and COCO, imitation alleviates up to 74% performance drop of student model compared to teacher. Codes released at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

papers_seen.author: Simon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Insufficient Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, recommendation, and multimodal tasks. KD variants transfer outputs, internal representations, attention patterns, or relational structures and are frequently combined with complementary compression techniques (e.g., pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies to meet deployment constraints. While KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and supports domain adaptation, privacy-aware training, and robustness improvements, its practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and alignment, and careful objective and architecture design; therefore KD should be treated as a central element of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone cure-all.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning: Methods, Domains, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger or multi-source models to smaller, faster, or modality-restricted models to reduce memory, compute, and latency while retaining performance. Approaches vary from matching teacher logits to mimicking internal features, and extend to self-distillation, many-to-many layer mapping, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and adaptations for few-shot, federated, and multimodal settings. Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, speech, and generative models shows KD can enable compact models that approach teacher accuracy, improve calibration and fairness, and make deployment on resource-constrained and heterogeneous devices practical. Ongoing challenges include selecting what to transfer (logits, features, relations), aligning heterogeneous architectures, and designing KD protocols robust to limited data, domain shifts, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Le
papers_seen.title: VPN++: Rethinking Video-Pose embeddings for understanding Activities of Daily Living
papers_seen.abstract: Many attempts have been made towards combining RGB and 3D poses for the recognition of Activities of Daily Living (ADL). ADL may look very similar and often necessitate to model fine-grained details to distinguish them. Because the recent 3D ConvNets are too rigid to capture the subtle visual patterns across an action, this research direction is dominated by methods combining RGB and 3D Poses. But the cost of computing 3D poses from RGB stream is high in the absence of appropriate sensors. This limits the usage of aforementioned approaches in real-world applications requiring low latency. Then, how to best take advantage of 3D Poses for recognizing ADL? To this end, we propose an extension of a pose driven attention mechanism: Video-Pose Network (VPN), exploring two distinct directions. One is to transfer the Pose knowledge into RGB through a feature-level distillation and the other towards mimicking pose driven attention through an attention-level distillation. Finally, these two approaches are integrated into a single model, we call VPN++. We show that VPN++ is not only effective but also provides a high speed up and high resilience to noisy Poses. VPN++, with or without 3D Poses, outperforms the representative baselines on 4 public datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.

papers_seen.author: Walls
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have been adapted across modalities (vision, language, graphs, and generative models) to produce smaller, faster, or more robust models while attempting to retain performance of larger teachers. Approaches vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational information, or structural/topological properties), how transfer is scheduled or weighted (confidence-aware, progressive replacement, or multi-teacher aggregation), and how distillation is combined with other compression methods (pruning, architecture search, or compact operator substitution). Empirical work shows strong practical benefits—improved runtime, memory, and sometimes robustness or fairness—while theoretical and analytical work begins to explain when and why distillation helps (e.g., role of soft targets, label smoothing analogies, and behavior with imperfect teachers). Remaining challenges include transferring rare-word or low-frequency information in sequence tasks, preserving relational/global structure in graph and link tasks, adapting to evolving domains, and automating generator compression for GANs. This synthesis summarizes key methods, insights, and open directions from recent literature.

papers_seen.author: Lynn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Aware Component for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically effective family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD routinely yields strong efficiency–accuracy trade-offs across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal settings when its objectives, data strategy, and teacher–student design are selected for the deployment context. However, KD is not a one-size-fits-all cure: its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability (including data-free or few-shot regimes), and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as propagated bias, poor low-frequency behavior, and distribution shift. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-aware distillation, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, and architecture search).

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a broadly useful means to transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller students so that compressed models can be deployed under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD succeeds across modalities and tasks when it is adapted to the problem: what to transfer (logits, features, attention), which data to use or synthesize, how to weight multiple teachers or imperfect supervision, and how to integrate complementary compression techniques. However, KD is neither automatic nor sufficient on its own: careful, task-aware design and combination with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies are required to realize reliable, production-ready compression.

papers_seen.author: Contreras
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal settings. KD yields substantial gains in inference efficiency and can transfer task-relevant structure from teachers to students, but its success depends on careful, task-aware choices of what to transfer, teacher selection, data and optimization strategies, and complementary compression techniques. Responsible deployment requires attention to robustness, fairness, privacy, and teacher–student co-design.

papers_seen.author: Perry
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. A rich taxonomy of distillation signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational maps, contrastive objectives), training protocols (offline, online, self-distillation, data‑free), and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) has been developed. KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks when deployed as part of an integrated, task-aware compression pipeline, but its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability, and explicit mitigations for bias, distribution shift, and low-frequency behaviors. Remaining open directions include principled theory for diverse objectives, reliable data-free and privacy-preserving distillation, and automated teacher–student alignment for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Foley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, First‑Line Tool — Powerful but Not Sufficient for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, flexible family of techniques that routinely enables compact, efficient models to inherit much of the behavior and performance of larger teacher models across vision, language, reinforcement learning, and healthcare applications. However, KD is context-sensitive: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality and alignment, student capacity and architecture, the data or synthetic-data strategy used for transfer, and explicit defenses against propagated biases or rare-case failures. The best practical outcomes treat KD as a configurable, task-aware core within an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-level objectives, data strategies (including data-free or adversarial synthesis when needed), and complementary primitives such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Powell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression and Transfer: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile set of techniques that enable model compression, domain- and task-level transfer, privacy-preserving distillation, and improvements in interpretability and fairness. Empirical and methodological work shows KD can compress large models into efficient students, transfer inductive biases, support multi-task and lifelong learning, and enable data-free or zero-shot distillation when training data are unavailable. At the same time, KD faces concrete limitations due to data heterogeneity, teacher-student capacity mismatch, and the need to select or synthesize appropriate supervision; hybrid solutions that combine feature-level matching, adversarial sample synthesis, curriculum strategies, and architectural compression achieve the best practical results. Based on evidence across domains (vision, language, graphs, retrieval, reinforcement learning), we argue that KD should be used as part of an integrated compression pipeline that is task-aware, data-aware, and often combined with pruning, layer skipping, or module replacement to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Walsh
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Current Methods, Findings, and Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer predictive and representational information from larger or composite models into smaller, faster, or resource-constrained models. A broad set of objectives — from soft-target (logit) matching to feature- and relation-level imitation, contrastive and adversarial schemes, data-free synthesis, and teacher-student co-training — have been developed and adapted to modalities and tasks in NLP, vision, graphs, retrieval, and generative modeling. Empirical work shows that combining carefully chosen distillation objectives with task-aware student design, pretraining of compact architectures, and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) achieves large inference speedups and parameter reductions while preserving most teacher performance. Open challenges include data-heterogeneity and federated limits, teacher error propagation, robustness and privacy preservation, and task-specific design for structured outputs; addressing these requires principled choice of what to transfer, how to select or synthesize data, and how to integrate KD into end-to-end compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Gibson

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, widely applied family of techniques for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. KD methods (logits, features, attention, relational, contrastive, multi‑teacher, online/self and data‑free variants) are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture adaptation to meet deployment constraints, but their success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and alignment, and careful protocol design.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Robust Re-Identification by Multiple Views Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: To achieve robustness in Re-Identification, standard methods leverage tracking information in a Video-To-Video fashion. However, these solutions face a large drop in performance for single image queries (e.g., Image-To-Video setting). Recent works address this severe degradation by transferring temporal information from a Video-based network to an Image-based one. In this work, we devise a training strategy that allows the transfer of a superior knowledge, arising from a set of views depicting the target object. Our proposal - Views Knowledge Distillation (VKD) - pins this visual variety as a supervision signal within a teacher-student framework, where the teacher educates a student who observes fewer views. As a result, the student outperforms not only its teacher but also the current state-of-the-art in Image-To-Video by a wide margin (6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId and 5% on VeRi-776). A thorough analysis - on Person, Vehicle and Animal Re-ID - investigates the properties of VKD from a qualitatively and quantitatively perspective. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

papers_seen.author: Solis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational, Task‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multifaceted approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD methods span output-level supervision, intermediate-representation matching, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and many-to-many layer mappings, and are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. When applied with task-awareness — i.e., selecting appropriate distilled signals, matching teacher and student capacity, and adapting data and optimization — KD reliably delivers favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across vision, language, speech, detection, and federated settings. Nevertheless, KD has well-documented failure modes (capacity and optimization gaps, bias transfer, degradation on rare phenomena, and privacy concerns), and future progress depends on principled theory, automation of teacher–student matching, and responsible, privacy-aware protocols.

Practical success depends on careful selection of distillation targets, alignment of teacher and student architectures, and appropriate data strategies; KD is most effective when integrated with complementary compression primitives and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

However, KD is not a universal solution: capacity mismatch, teacher errors and biases, limited or private data, and optimization instability limit off‑the‑shelf success. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on teacher quality, data strategy, objective design, and architecture alignment. To realize KD's benefits in production and research, practitioners should treat distillation as a configurable component of compression pipelines—combining logits and representation matching, data-aware schedules or synthesis, and complementary compression methods—while applying targeted safeguards for robustness, fairness, and low-frequency behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Warner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted, task‑aware toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), curriculum and data strategies, and explicit teacher–student alignment; however, important limitations remain in distribution shift, low‑frequency phenomena, heterogeneous architectures, privacy and federated settings, and principled teacher selection. This synthesis summarizes prevailing methods, empirical patterns, practical guidance, and open challenges distilled from the supplied literature.

papers_seen.author: Howard
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, faster student models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, or privacy constraints. Practically effective KD requires task- and data-aware choices—what signals to transfer, how to align architectures and layers, how to obtain or synthesize distillation data, and how to combine KD with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search. papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Prescriptions

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: AutoGAN-Distiller: Searching to Compress Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: The compression of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has lately drawn attention, due to the increasing demand for deploying GANs into mobile devices for numerous applications such as image translation, enhancement and editing. However, compared to the substantial efforts to compressing other deep models, the research on compressing GANs (usually the generators) remains at its infancy stage. Existing GAN compression algorithms are limited to handling specific GAN architectures and losses. Inspired by the recent success of AutoML in deep compression, we introduce AutoML to GAN compression and develop an AutoGAN-Distiller (AGD) framework. Starting with a specifically designed efficient search space, AGD performs an end-to-end discovery for new efficient generators, given the target computational resource constraints. The search is guided by the original GAN model via knowledge distillation, therefore fulfilling the compression. AGD is fully automatic, standalone (i.e., needing no trained discriminators), and generically applicable to various GAN models. We evaluate AGD in two representative GAN tasks: image translation and super resolution. Without bells and whistles, AGD yields remarkably lightweight yet more competitive compressed models, that largely outperform existing alternatives. Our codes and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Federated Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Distributed learning frameworks often rely on exchanging model parameters across workers, instead of revealing their raw data. A prime example is federated learning that exchanges the gradients or weights of each neural network model. Under limited communication resources, however, such a method becomes extremely costly particularly for modern deep neural networks having a huge number of model parameters. In this regard, federated distillation (FD) is a compelling distributed learning solution that only exchanges the model outputs whose dimensions are commonly much smaller than the model sizes (e.g., 10 labels in the MNIST dataset). The goal of this chapter is to provide a deep understanding of FD while demonstrating its communication efficiency and applicability to a variety of tasks. To this end, towards demystifying the operational principle of FD, the first part of this chapter provides a novel asymptotic analysis for two foundational algorithms of FD, namely knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD), by exploiting the theory of neural tangent kernel (NTK). Next, the second part elaborates on a baseline implementation of FD for a classification task, and illustrates its performance in terms of accuracy and communication efficiency compared to FL. Lastly, to demonstrate the applicability of FD to various distributed learning tasks and environments, the third part presents two selected applications, namely FD over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and FD for reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Novak

Effective use of KD depends on matching the distillation paradigm to the target problem: use internal/feature-level distillation for representation-heavy NLP tasks, layer- and task-aware filters when capacity mismatch is large, adversarial or boundary-focused sampling to improve generalization, and data-free or federated-aware strategies when data access is restricted. Combining KD with pruning and hardware-aware compression further increases suitability for edge deployment.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger or multi-source models to smaller, faster, or modality-restricted models to reduce memory, compute, and latency while retaining performance. Approaches vary from matching teacher logits to mimicking internal features, and extend to self-distillation, many-to-many layer mapping, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and adaptations for few-shot, federated, and multimodal settings. Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, speech, and generative models shows KD can enable compact models that approach teacher accuracy, improve calibration and fairness, and make deployment on resource-constrained and heterogeneous devices practical. Ongoing challenges include selecting what to transfer (logits, features, relations), aligning heterogeneous architectures, and designing KD protocols robust to limited data, domain shifts, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Vang
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models. KD encompasses a range of transfer targets and training protocols and is commonly combined with complementary compression methods to meet deployment constraints. Practical success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis strategies, and careful choice of distilled signals and training procedures.

papers_seen.author: Koch
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer knowledge from larger or more complex models (teachers, ensembles, or supernets) into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models (students). Across vision, language, and multimodal tasks, distillation strategies include matching logits, mimicking intermediate features, adversarial generation of surrogate data, ensemble compression, and teacher-student co-training. Practical extensions address limited or private data, multi-teacher and domain-shift scenarios, and architecture search for generative models. Empirical results show that carefully chosen distillation objectives, pretraining of compact models, and task-aware feature imitation can preserve much of the teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, and that specialized methods are required for structured outputs (e.g., detection, segmentation, ranking) and domain adaptation.

papers_seen.author: Huff
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a configurable toolkit—selecting appropriate distillation signals, aligning teacher and student capacity, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, or task-adaptive architecture search)—practitioners routinely obtain compact models that retain much of teacher performance. Success requires explicit attention to teacher quality, data availability or synthesis, optimization schedules, and safeguards against transferred biases or degraded rare-token behavior.

papers_seen.author: Pope
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for transferring capabilities of large or ensemble models into smaller, faster, or more deployable models while retaining much of their task performance. Approaches span matching teacher output distributions, aligning intermediate representations, many-to-many layer mappings, attention- and projector-based transfers, data-free and zero-shot schemes, multi-teacher and online protocols, and integrations with quantization, pruning, and architecture search. Empirical work across language, vision, 3D perception, retrieval, and federated settings shows distilled students can approach teacher performance when distillation is combined with suitable data strategies, teacher design, and complementary compression methods. Important open challenges remain in data-scarce or privacy-sensitive regimes, robust transfer across heterogeneous architectures, and principled selection of what and how to transfer.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practically essential family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models by transferring information from larger teacher models. Across vision, language, graphs, recommendation, and federated settings, KD variants transfer soft logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, contrastive signals, synthetic inputs, or ensemble outputs. KD can enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, improve student generalization, support privacy-preserving workflows, and interact fruitfully with pruning and low-precision numerics. However, the benefits depend strongly on data availability, teacher quality, architecture alignment, and training protocols; important failure modes include optimization gaps, preserved or amplified teacher biases, degraded rare-token behavior, and teacher inference cost. The literature provides many practical strategies—feature- and layer-wise matching, multi- and self-distillation, adversarial or data-free sample generation, student-aware teacher design, and hardware-aware co-design—to mitigate these limitations and extend KD to specialized tasks such as federated learning, continual/lifelong learning, graph neural networks, recommendation systems, and cross-modal transfer.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers behavior and internal structure from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory footprint, and communication while often preserving much of task performance. KD is a flexible family of techniques that operate at output, representation, relational, or decision-boundary levels and is commonly combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and alignment, and careful design of objectives and training pipelines.
