papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible framework that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models. KD has evolved into a diverse toolkit—logit and soft-label transfer, feature- and layer-level matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and data-free or privacy-aware procedures—that when combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture replacement) produces compact models suitable for latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained deployment. Effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability or synthesis of data, and alignment of representations; treating KD as a configurable, task-aware element of a broader compression pipeline yields the most reliable real-world results.

papers_seen.author: Stevens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a single trick into a broad, practical family of methods for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or privacy-aware models while retaining much of their performance. The techniques differ by what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or channel statistics), how the transfer is staged (offline teacher-student, online/co-distillation, data-free/zero-shot, few-shot), and which complementary strategies are used (projectors, mixup/data augmentation, pruning, or architecture-aware design). Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often acts both as information transfer and as a regularizer; success depends critically on choices about teacher signals, student capacity, the availability and nature of data, and task-specific design. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation under limited or private data, preventing transfer of teacher errors, adapting to heterogeneous or federated settings, and scaling distillation to very large models and complex structured-output tasks.

papers_seen.author: Morton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Prescriptions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, flexible paradigm for transferring behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller student models so they can be deployed under compute, memory, latency, or privacy constraints. When designed with task-aware objectives, careful teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware search), distillation routinely yields substantial efficiency gains while retaining much of teacher performance. However, distillation is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and the distillation signals chosen; it can propagate teacher artifacts and struggles with optimization gaps, capacity mismatch, and low-frequency behavior. Addressing these limits requires joint teacher–student design, confidence- or curriculum-aware sample selection, data-free or privacy-aware synthesis when data are unavailable, and incorporation into broader compression pipelines tailored to deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Singh
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, Practical Trade-offs, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more deployable student models. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention patterns, relations, or generated samples), in the availability of original training data (data-rich, data-free, federated), and in whether distillation is performed offline, online, or jointly with teacher training. Across vision, language, ranking/retrieval, recommendation, and multimodal tasks, carefully designed distillation objectives combined with complementary compression mechanisms (pruning, quantization, architecture search) routinely yield compact models that approach teacher performance under practical constraints. However, the effectiveness of KD depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data selection and augmentation, and mitigation of risks such as propagated bias, privacy leakage, and poor modeling of rare phenomena. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines, using multi-teacher and confidence-weighting strategies, layer- and feature-matching, student-aware teacher design, and privacy-preserving or data-free synthesis when needed.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: The Case for Task- and Data-Aware Knowledge Distillation: Principles, Pitfalls, and Practical Extensions for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central tool for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Its practical success across vision, language, graph, and generative models depends not only on the generic teacher→student paradigm but on task-aware selection of transferred information, choices about data access (including data-free and privacy-preserving variants), and the use of auxiliary techniques (adversarial training, ensembling, pruning, and architecture search). When these dimensions are addressed explicitly, distillation can produce compact models that approach teacher performance while offering improved robustness, interpretability, or resource-efficiency. However, naive distillation can fail due to optimization difficulties, domain shift, and heterogeneous teacher-student mismatches, so practitioners must adopt targeted strategies that consider the learning objective, available data, and student capacity.

KD encompasses many targets and protocols (soft logits, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial/data‑free synthesis, multi‑teacher and self‑distillation) and is most effective when combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies appropriate to the task and deployment constraints. KD methods span logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and many teacher/student configurations. While KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance, its effectiveness depends on teacher quality and alignment, student capacity, the data used for transfer, and integration with complementary compression methods; successful deployments therefore treat KD as a core component of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline rather than as a standalone solution.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

Across vision, language, graphs, recommendation, and federated settings, KD variants transfer soft logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, contrastive signals, synthetic inputs, or ensemble outputs. KD can enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, improve student generalization, support privacy-preserving workflows, and interact fruitfully with pruning and low-precision numerics. However, the benefits depend strongly on data availability, teacher quality, architecture alignment, and training protocols; important failure modes include optimization gaps, preserved or amplified teacher biases, degraded rare-token behavior, and teacher inference cost. The literature provides many practical strategies—feature- and layer-wise matching, multi- and self-distillation, adversarial or data-free sample generation, student-aware teacher design, and hardware-aware co-design—to mitigate these limitations and extend KD to specialized tasks such as federated learning, continual/lifelong learning, graph neural networks, recommendation systems, and cross-modal transfer.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: AlphaNet: Improved Training of Supernets with Alpha-Divergence
papers_seen.abstract: Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) is an effective technique for automating efficient neural architecture design. Weight-sharing NAS builds a supernet that assembles all the architectures as its sub-networks and jointly trains the supernet with the sub-networks. The success of weight-sharing NAS heavily relies on distilling the knowledge of the supernet to the sub-networks. However, we find that the widely used distillation divergence, i.e., KL divergence, may lead to student sub-networks that over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, leading to inferior performance of the sub-networks. In this work, we propose to improve the supernet training with a more generalized alpha-divergence. By adaptively selecting the alpha-divergence, we simultaneously prevent the over-estimation or under-estimation of the uncertainty of the teacher model. We apply the proposed alpha-divergence based supernets training to both slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS, and demonstrate significant improvements. Specifically, our discovered model family, AlphaNet, outperforms prior-art models on a wide range of FLOPs regimes, including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. We achieve ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% with only 444M FLOPs. Our code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Potency, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile toolkit for compressing and adapting large neural models for deployment, cross-task transfer, federated settings, and multi-modal scenarios. When combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, or module replacement), KD enables substantial reductions in model size and compute with modest accuracy loss. However, gains are not automatic: careful choice of what to distill (outputs, intermediate representations, or selected samples), how to mix hard/soft signals, and how to adapt KD to distributed or data-free regimes strongly affects outcomes. I argue that KD is most effective when it is task-aware, representation-aware, and integrated with other compression methods, and that future work should prioritize principled selection of distilled knowledge, robustness to teacher imperfections, and practical protocols for heterogeneous and privacy-sensitive deployments.

papers_seen.author: Harrison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically driven family of techniques to transfer knowledge from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, faster student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Modern KD encompasses simple soft-target matching as well as richer objectives that imitate intermediate representations, attention patterns, relational structure, and contrastive signals; it is commonly combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Distillation succeeds across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks when aligned to task objectives, teacher–student capacity, and available data, but it has well-documented failure modes (capacity mismatch, teacher bias propagation, domain shift, and scarce/private data) that motivate task-aware design, data strategies, and privacy-preserving or data-free approaches.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: FedZKT: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer towards Resource-Constrained Federated Learning with Heterogeneous On-Device Models
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning enables multiple distributed devices to collaboratively learn a shared prediction model without centralizing their on-device data. Most of the current algorithms require comparable individual efforts for local training with the same structure and size of on-device models, which, however, impedes participation from resource-constrained devices. Given the widespread yet heterogeneous devices nowadays, in this paper, we propose an innovative federated learning framework with heterogeneous on-device models through Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer, named by FedZKT. Specifically, FedZKT allows devices to independently determine the on-device models upon their local resources. To achieve knowledge transfer across these heterogeneous on-device models, a zero-shot distillation approach is designed without any prerequisites for private on-device data, which is contrary to certain prior research based on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. Moreover, this compute-intensive distillation task is assigned to the server to allow the participation of resource-constrained devices, where a generator is adversarially learned with the ensemble of collected on-device models. The distilled central knowledge is then sent back in the form of the corresponding on-device model parameters, which can be easily absorbed on the device side. Extensive experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of FedZKT towards on-device knowledge agnostic, on-device model heterogeneity, and other challenging federated learning scenarios, such as heterogeneous on-device data and straggler effects.

papers_seen.author: Sampson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Tool for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, widely applicable approach that transfers predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, efficient students. KD routinely yields substantial reductions in parameters, latency, and memory while retaining much of teacher performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. However, KD alone does not guarantee robust, fair, or deployment-ready compression: its success depends on choices of distilled signals, data and augmentation strategies, teacher–student alignment, and combination with complementary compression techniques. Treating KD as the core of a task-aware, integrated compression pipeline — rather than a one-shot solution — achieves the best tradeoffs between efficiency and fidelity.

papers_seen.author: Schultz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile framework for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. KD enables deployment on resource-constrained devices, supports domain adaptation and privacy-aware workflows, and integrates naturally with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on teacher quality, data strategy, objective design, and handling of distributional or architectural mismatch. Real-world deployments therefore require KD to be treated as a configurable component within a broader, task-aware compression pipeline that explicitly addresses data availability, robustness, and fairness concerns.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Robust and Resource-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation by Generative Pseudo Replay
papers_seen.abstract: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD) allows knowledge transfer from a trained neural network (teacher) to a more compact one (student) in the absence of original training data. Existing works use a validation set to monitor the accuracy of the student over real data and report the highest performance throughout the entire process. However, validation data may not be available at distillation time either, making it infeasible to record the student snapshot that achieved the peak accuracy. Therefore, a practical data-free KD method should be robust and ideally provide monotonically increasing student accuracy during distillation. This is challenging because the student experiences knowledge degradation due to the distribution shift of the synthetic data. A straightforward approach to overcome this issue is to store and rehearse the generated samples periodically, which increases the memory footprint and creates privacy concerns. We propose to model the distribution of the previously observed synthetic samples with a generative network. In particular, we design a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a training objective that is customized to learn the synthetic data representations optimally. The student is rehearsed by the generative pseudo replay technique, with samples produced by the VAE. Hence knowledge degradation can be prevented without storing any samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show that our method optimizes the expected value of the distilled model accuracy while eliminating the large memory overhead incurred by the sample-storing methods.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques for producing compact, deployable neural models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational or contrastive signals) and across diverse protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, and data-free/privacy-aware schemes). When combined with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, KD routinely enables large reductions in latency, memory, and compute while preserving much of teacher performance. Its empirical success is conditional on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability and synthesis strategies, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, distribution shift, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Cain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a flexible set of methods for transferring information from larger or more expressive teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. KD spans output-level (soft-target) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and protocol variants such as offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free, and privacy-aware workflows. In practice KD is frequently combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and must be tailored to teacher/student capacity, data availability, and deployment constraints; while empirical results across modalities often show students can recover much of teacher performance, important challenges remain in handling capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias and robustness, and formal theoretical guarantees.

papers_seen.author: Chandler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller students by transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or relational structure. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal domains, KD enables substantial reductions in inference cost, memory, and communication while often preserving much of teacher performance; it is most effective when combined with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data augmentation, and hardware-aware design). The literature also highlights several persistent challenges — teacher and capacity mismatch, optimization and data limitations, privacy and distribution shift — and converges on practical strategies such as careful choice of distillation signals, layer alignment, multi-teacher or online protocols, and synthetic-data or data-free approaches to operate under constrained access to original training data.

papers_seen.author: Mendoza
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Effects, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used, flexible framework for producing smaller, faster models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact students. KD encompasses a range of transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive signals) and protocols (offline, online, multi-teacher, data-free, and curriculum-driven). Empirical work demonstrates KD often preserves much of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute, but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, data availability or synthesis, and integration with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone cure-all. Key open directions include principled selection of signals to transfer, robust privacy-preserving distillation, automation of deployment-aware pipelines, and reliable compression of large transformer and generative models.

papers_seen.author: Scott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of approaches for transferring information from large, expensive teacher models into smaller, efficient student models to reduce computation, memory, latency, and communication while attempting to preserve task performance. Over the past decade these techniques have expanded from simple soft-target (logit) supervision to a broad, configurable toolkit that includes intermediate representation matching, attention and relational objectives, online and self-distillation, data‑free and adversarial synthesis, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical evidence shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling practical deployment on constrained hardware, but outcomes depend critically on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the availability and design of data for distillation, and mitigation strategies for transferred errors, distribution shift, and privacy concerns.

papers_seen.author: Boyd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential, Multifaceted Toolbox with Clear Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practically essential approach for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD delivers large efficiency gains and can improve generalization or robustness when combined with complementary compression methods, but it is not a single recipe: success depends on what is transferred, teacher–student alignment, data availability and quality, and constraints such as privacy or heterogeneous deployment hardware. Practical KD pipelines therefore treat distillation as a configurable toolkit—selecting objectives, data strategies, and auxiliary interventions (e.g., pruning, quantization, teacher adaptation, or student-aware design) that match the task and constraints—while explicitly addressing known failure modes such as teacher error propagation, low-frequency token degradation, and privacy risks.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad and practical set of techniques for transferring behaviors and representations from larger or otherwise stronger models (teachers) to smaller or more constrained models (students). KD has been adapted across modalities and tasks—classification, generation, retrieval, speech, graph learning, reinforcement and lifelong learning—yielding work on algorithmic variants (self-distillation, multi-teacher, curriculum, adversarial, relational and loss-function innovations), data- and privacy-aware designs, and hardware-aware/low-precision deployments. Empirical work demonstrates KD can substantially reduce model size and latency while preserving much of the teacher performance, but theoretical and optimization limits remain: students often cannot perfectly match teachers and training/data choices matter greatly. Practical advances address these limits through better supervision signals, input-side design (data augmentation), alternate discrepancy measures, and privacy/communication constraints. The field continues to move toward more efficient, fair, private and domain-robust distilled models suitable for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Lopez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfer behavior and/or internal structure from larger, often ensemble or multi-modal teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels—from soft-label supervision to intermediate-feature, attention, and relational matching—and are widely used to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under memory or latency constraints, and support domain or modality adaptation. The effectiveness of KD depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and selection, and careful design of what and how knowledge is transferred; combining KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and targeted training protocols improves reliability in practice.

papers_seen.author: Harmon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context-Sensitive Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible framework for producing compact, deployable models from larger teacher models. Across modalities and tasks, KD reduces inference cost, memory footprint, and communication while often preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its effectiveness depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher and student design, available data, and integration with complementary compression techniques. Treating KD as a central, configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, data strategies, and safeguards for bias and distributional robustness—yields the most reliable path to deployable, high-performing compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Stephens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD routinely produces compact models that retain a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but its success is strongly context dependent: it requires task‑aware design of transfer signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and explicit mitigations for known failure modes. The practical position argued here is that KD should be treated as the configurable, central element of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, data synthesis/augmentation, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy—rather than as a standalone panacea.

papers_seen.author: Bruce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a proven, flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller students, enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. When properly designed—choosing what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which complementary compression methods to use—KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and supports a range of practical use cases. However, KD is not turnkey: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability of suitable data (or reliable data synthesis), and careful mitigation of failure modes such as transferred biases, degraded low-frequency behavior, and distribution shift. I argue that KD should be treated as a core, configurable component of integrated compression pipelines rather than a standalone solution, and I summarize practical recommendations and open challenges that follow from this position.

papers_seen.author: Chambers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a broad family of techniques that transfer information from larger, often multi-source or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across vision, language, speech, multimodal and generative settings, KD has evolved beyond simple logit matching to include representation- and relation-level objectives, adversarial or data-free generation, online and self-distillation protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization and architecture search. These approaches routinely enable large reductions in inference cost and memory while preserving much of teacher performance, but reliable deployment requires task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data. Important open directions remain in principled theory, robust distillation under heterogenous and low-data regimes, and preserving long-tail or low-frequency behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression comprise a diverse set of techniques to produce smaller, faster, or more private models by transferring information from larger or auxiliary models. Research spans supervised teacher-student frameworks, self-distillation, multi-teacher and task-adaptive compression, and distillation combined with pruning, architecture search, adversarial training, and data augmentation. Practical work demonstrates benefits across vision, multimodal, graph, and NLP tasks, while theoretical analyses connect distillation to label smoothing, ensemble behavior, and bias–variance tradeoffs. Open challenges include aligning heterogeneous inputs and modalities, preserving robustness and privacy, and handling low-resource or low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Murray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential but Context‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical set of techniques for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models in deep learning and NLP. KD can preserve much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but its success depends on task-aware choices: what signals to transfer (logits, features, attention, relations), teacher–student alignment, available data (real, synthetic, or none), and complementary compression strategies (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Responsible and robust deployment further requires addressing distribution shift, low‑frequency or structured outputs, privacy and fairness concerns, and principled selection of distillation targets. I argue KD should be treated as a configurable toolkit — often essential for practical compression — rather than a turnkey solution; practitioners should select and combine distillation recipes according to capacity, data, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt
papers_seen.abstract: Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

papers_seen.author: Schultz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile framework for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. KD enables deployment on resource-constrained devices, supports domain adaptation and privacy-aware workflows, and integrates naturally with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on teacher quality, data strategy, objective design, and handling of distributional or architectural mismatch. Real-world deployments therefore require KD to be treated as a configurable component within a broader, task-aware compression pipeline that explicitly addresses data availability, robustness, and fairness concerns.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: Object DGCNN: 3D Object Detection using Dynamic Graphs
papers_seen.abstract: 3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Cross-modal Knowledge Distillation for Vision-to-Sensor Action Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) based on multi-modal approach has been recently shown to improve the accuracy performance of HAR. However, restricted computational resources associated with wearable devices, i.e., smartwatch, failed to directly support such advanced methods. To tackle this issue, this study introduces an end-to-end Vision-to-Sensor Knowledge Distillation (VSKD) framework. In this VSKD framework, only time-series data, i.e., accelerometer data, is needed from wearable devices during the testing phase. Therefore, this framework will not only reduce the computational demands on edge devices, but also produce a learning model that closely matches the performance of the computational expensive multi-modal approach. In order to retain the local temporal relationship and facilitate visual deep learning models, we first convert time-series data to two-dimensional images by applying the Gramian Angular Field ( GAF) based encoding method. We adopted ResNet18 and multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception as teacher and student network in this study, respectively. A novel loss function, named Distance and Angle-wised Semantic Knowledge loss (DASK), is proposed to mitigate the modality variations between the vision and the sensor domain. Extensive experimental results on UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and competitiveness of the proposed VSKD model which can deployed on wearable sensors.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge by Mimicking Features
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a popular method to train efficient networks ("student") with the help of high-capacity networks ("teacher"). Traditional methods use the teacher's soft logits as extra supervision to train the student network. In this paper, we argue that it is more advantageous to make the student mimic the teacher's features in the penultimate layer. Not only the student can directly learn more effective information from the teacher feature, feature mimicking can also be applied for teachers trained without a softmax layer. Experiments show that it can achieve higher accuracy than traditional KD. To further facilitate feature mimicking, we decompose a feature vector into the magnitude and the direction. We argue that the teacher should give more freedom to the student feature's magnitude, and let the student pay more attention on mimicking the feature direction. To meet this requirement, we propose a loss term based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With the help of this new loss, our method indeed mimics feature directions more accurately, relaxes constraints on feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses of how LSH facilitates feature direction mimicking, and further extend feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Context-Dependent Tools for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression provide a practical, widely applicable route to produce smaller, faster, and often more robust models from larger teachers across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. When combined with representation-matching, contrastive objectives, multi-teacher schemes, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its success depends on teacher quality, the data used for distillation, careful choice of what is transferred, and attention to fairness and domain-shift risks. This paper argues that KD should be treated as an essential yet context-sensitive component of model deployment pipelines, and summarizes best-practice recommendations and promising directions to make distillation reliably effective in applied settings.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a broad set of techniques to compress large or ensemble models into smaller, faster, or more deployable models while preserving performance. Research spans logits-based distillation, feature and representation matching, intermediate-layer alignment, adversarial and self-supervised schemes, curriculum and online protocols, and task-adaptive or privacy-preserving variants. Practical work demonstrates successful applications across NLP (including compressing BERT), vision, graph learning, retrieval, object detection, and large-scale distributed training, with ongoing research focused on teacher design, data augmentation, and robustness under limited or heterogeneous data.

papers_seen.author: Clay
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Insufficient Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, broadly applicable mechanism for transferring behavior from large teacher models into smaller student models and is essential for practical model compression in deep learning and NLP. However, KD alone does not guarantee robust, fair, or hardware‑optimal deployment: it must be designed in a task‑aware way, combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), and paired with data and curriculum strategies to mitigate failure modes such as teacher bias, poor low‑frequency behavior, capacity mismatch, and distribution shift. Treating KD as a configurable core inside an integrated compression pipeline yields the most reliable production outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression methods transfer predictive behavior or internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce memory, compute, and latency while retaining much of task performance. Methods span soft-target (logit) matching, representation- and layer-wise objectives, multi-teacher and ensemble guidance, online and adversarial schemes, and data-free/zero-shot approaches. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often acts both as a mechanism for knowledge transfer and as an implicit regularizer, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and the particular distillation objective. Practical deployments combine KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet resource, privacy, and latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Villa
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses larger or composite models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad family of distillation objectives and workflows—soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive losses, data- or privacy-aware variants, and ensemble or self-distillation—has been adapted across modalities and tasks. When combined with task-aware design, selective data strategies, and complementary compression techniques, distillation produces practical, deployable models but requires careful mitigation of known limits such as capacity mismatch, teacher error transfer, data scarcity, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Pena
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Core, Context‑Sensitive Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated family of techniques for producing compact models from larger teachers. KD methods range from soft-logit matching to intermediate-feature, attention, relational and adversarial objectives, and operate in offline, online, data‑free and federated regimes. While KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, its success is context dependent: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, data strategy, and complementary compression primitives strongly determine outcomes. For reliable deployment, KD should be treated as the core of an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline rather than a standalone cure.

papers_seen.author: Ball
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, and Conditional Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller students, enabling substantial reductions in inference cost, memory footprint, and communication while often preserving—and sometimes improving—task performance. KD methods operate at logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or decision boundaries and are commonly combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data- or privacy-aware procedures. KD delivers strong practical benefits across modalities and tasks but requires careful teacher–student alignment, attention to data and privacy constraints, and complementary techniques to address capacity gaps, domain shift, and rare-token behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Schmidt
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practically effective approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. KD reliably reduces inference cost, memory, and communication while often preserving most of a teacher's performance—but it is context dependent, requiring careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data, privacy, and deployment constraints. Treated as the configurable core of a compression pipeline and combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, and task-aware data strategies), KD enables deployable models for latency- and resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive settings; however, practitioners must explicitly address failure modes such as capacity mismatch, domain shift, low-frequency errors, and propagated biases.

papers_seen.author: Powers
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical, flexible, and widely applicable approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of their performance. Across domains and tasks—language modeling and translation, recommendation, graph learning, vision, continual and domain adaptation, and resource-constrained deployment—KD enables trade-offs between accuracy, latency, memory, privacy, and train-time complexity. Variants such as feature mimicking, self- and teacher-free distillation, ensemble and online distillation, data-free and privacy-aware schemes, and task- or domain-aware adaptations extend KD’s applicability. At the same time, careful choice of training targets, treatment of low-frequency phenomena, and consideration of the teacher-student mismatch are necessary to avoid transferring teacher errors and to realize the full benefits of distillation.

papers_seen.author: Strong
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesized Review
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior and richer internal information. A broad toolbox of distillation targets and protocols has emerged—soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free sample synthesis, self- and online-distillation, and multi-teacher schemes—and these are routinely combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD has been applied across vision, language, graphs, speech, generative models, and federated settings, yielding large reductions in model size and inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance when design choices are task- and architecture-aware. Remaining challenges include teacher–student mismatch, propagation of teacher errors and biases, data scarcity or privacy constraints, and instability in optimization; practical remedies emphasize task-aware signal selection, learned teacher adaptation, layer mapping strategies, and data-synthesis or privacy-preserving protocols. This review synthesizes empirical patterns, common mechanisms, practical recommendations, and open problems for KD-driven compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Small-footprint Highway Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning has significantly advanced state-of-the-art of speech recognition in the past few years. However, compared to conventional Gaussian mixture acoustic models, neural network models are usually much larger, and are therefore not very deployable in embedded devices. Previously, we investigated a compact highway deep neural network (HDNN) for acoustic modelling, which is a type of depth-gated feedforward neural network. We have shown that HDNN-based acoustic models can achieve comparable recognition accuracy with much smaller number of model parameters compared to plain deep neural network (DNN) acoustic models. In this paper, we push the boundary further by leveraging on the knowledge distillation technique that is also known as {\it teacher-student} training, i.e., we train the compact HDNN model with the supervision of a high accuracy cumbersome model. Furthermore, we also investigate sequence training and adaptation in the context of teacher-student training. Our experiments were performed on the AMI meeting speech recognition corpus. With this technique, we significantly improved the recognition accuracy of the HDNN acoustic model with less than 0.8 million parameters, and narrowed the gap between this model and the plain DNN with 30 million parameters.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge From a Deep Pose Regressor Network
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a novel method to distill knowledge from a deep pose regressor network for efficient Visual Odometry (VO). Standard distillation relies on "dark knowledge" for successful knowledge transfer. As this knowledge is not available in pose regression and the teacher prediction is not always accurate, we propose to emphasize the knowledge transfer only when we trust the teacher. We achieve this by using teacher loss as a confidence score which places variable relative importance on the teacher prediction. We inject this confidence score to the main training task via Attentive Imitation Loss (AIL) and when learning the intermediate representation of the teacher through Attentive Hint Training (AHT) approach. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work which successfully distill the knowledge from a deep pose regression network. Our evaluation on the KITTI and Malaga dataset shows that we can keep the student prediction close to the teacher with up to 92.95% parameter reduction and 2.12x faster in computation time.

papers_seen.author: Coleman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Central, but Contextual Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, production-ready approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students. When combined with complementary compression primitives, careful choice of distillation targets and protocols, and task- or data-aware design, KD routinely produces compact models that retain a large fraction of teacher performance. However, KD is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability or synthesis strategy, and attention to robustness, low-frequency phenomena, and distribution shift. Best practice treats KD as a flexible toolkit that must be adapted to deployment constraints and complemented with privacy-, fairness-, and robustness-aware methods.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Preserving Privacy in Federated Learning with Ensemble Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm where local nodes collaboratively train a central model while the training data remains decentralized. Existing FL methods typically share model parameters or employ co-distillation to address the issue of unbalanced data distribution. However, they suffer from communication bottlenecks. More importantly, they risk privacy leakage. In this work, we develop a privacy preserving and communication efficient method in a FL framework with one-shot offline knowledge distillation using unlabeled, cross-domain public data. We propose a quantized and noisy ensemble of local predictions from completely trained local models for stronger privacy guarantees without sacrificing accuracy. Based on extensive experiments on image classification and text classification tasks, we show that our privacy-preserving method outperforms baseline FL algorithms with superior performance in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Rubio
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central set of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students in deep learning and NLP. KD transfers information from teacher to student via soft logits, intermediate representations, attentional or channel signals, and relational objectives; it is often combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies to meet latency, memory, privacy, and domain-adaptation constraints. While KD frequently preserves much of a teacher’s performance and can improve robustness or generalization in some settings, its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and alignment, and responsible handling of bias, privacy, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Hodges
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Ubiquitous, but Demand-Aware
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely applicable approach for compressing high-capacity models into efficient students across modalities and tasks. Empirical results across vision, language, multimodal, graph, and generative settings show KD can recover much of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and device-heterogeneity constraints. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on how knowledge is represented and transferred (logits, features, attention, contrastive objectives), the alignment between teacher and student inputs, the data used for distillation, and attention to robustness, fairness, and privacy. Carefully chosen distillation algorithms and extensions (self-supervised distillation, meta-learned teachers, multi-teacher weighting, online and distributed schemes, and privacy-preserving perturbations) can mitigate common failure modes and broaden KD’s applicability in production and research settings.
