papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and broadly useful approach for compressing large deep and language models into smaller, deployable students. KD methods span soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data‑free schemes, and variants such as multi‑teacher, online, and self‑distillation. KD routinely yields strong tradeoffs between efficiency and performance when it is designed with attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and task constraints, and when it is integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). However, KD is not a universal recipe: practical success requires task‑aware choices, careful layer or feature alignment, and explicit remedies for distribution shift, low‑frequency phenomena, and transferred biases. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a core, configurable component within compression pipelines and offers evidence‑based best practices and caveats for its effective use.

papers_seen.author: Mendoza
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Effects, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used, flexible framework for producing smaller, faster models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact students. KD encompasses a range of transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive signals) and protocols (offline, online, multi-teacher, data-free, and curriculum-driven). Empirical work demonstrates KD often preserves much of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute, but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, data availability or synthesis, and integration with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone cure-all. Key open directions include principled selection of signals to transfer, robust privacy-preserving distillation, automation of deployment-aware pipelines, and reliable compression of large transformer and generative models.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, efficient student models to meet latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. Over the past decade, KD methods have evolved from simple soft-target (logit) matching to a rich toolkit that includes intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi‑teacher and online regimes, and data‑free or adversarial synthesis. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can preserve much of a teacher’s performance and in many cases improve generalization, but practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of signals to transfer, and the availability and match of distillation data; reliable deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-aware objectives, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design.

papers_seen.author: Walter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from A Stronger Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Unlike existing knowledge distillation methods focus on the baseline settings, where the teacher models and training strategies are not that strong and competing as state-of-the-art approaches, this paper presents a method dubbed DIST to distill better from a stronger teacher. We empirically find that the discrepancy of predictions between the student and a stronger teacher may tend to be fairly severer. As a result, the exact match of predictions in KL divergence would disturb the training and make existing methods perform poorly. In this paper, we show that simply preserving the relations between the predictions of teacher and student would suffice, and propose a correlation-based loss to capture the intrinsic inter-class relations from the teacher explicitly. Besides, considering that different instances have different semantic similarities to each class, we also extend this relational match to the intra-class level. Our method is simple yet practical, and extensive experiments demonstrate that it adapts well to various architectures, model sizes and training strategies, and can achieve state-of-the-art performance consistently on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation tasks. Code is available at: https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD .

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: King
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, efficient student models to reduce latency, memory, and deployment cost while often preserving much of the original performance. A broad toolkit has been developed—logit/soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and channel-wise objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and privacy-aware variants, and integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search—that is applied across vision, language, graphs, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD is effective in many settings but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful objective and alignment choices; practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable component of a larger compression pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Lawson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses larger teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations so that compact models meet latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. A diverse toolkit has emerged — soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational/contrastive objectives, self- and online-distillation, multi-teacher schemes, and data strategies including data-free synthesis and targeted augmentation — which is commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. Empirical work shows distilled students frequently recover a large fraction of teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, and distillation data are aligned, but KD has documented limitations (teacher–student mismatch, degradation on low-frequency behaviors, bias and privacy transfer, and sensitivity under data scarcity or distribution shift). Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline, selecting distilled signals, data protocols, and complementary compression techniques according to task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Webster
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Task-Aware Core of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practically essential approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, or specialized models. When designed around task constraints, student capacity, and available data, KD preserves much of a teacher's capabilities while enabling deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy limits. Its greatest value comes from treating distillation as a configurable toolkit—combining soft-targets, representation matching, adversarial or data-free sample synthesis, and multi-teacher or self-distillation—with complementary compression techniques to meet real-world constraints. Success requires careful handling of teacher–student alignment, data scarcity, distribution shift, and bias transfer, but a task-aware, hybrid pipeline makes KD one of the most practical routes to effective model compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Welch
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher performance. When treated as a task‑aware toolkit and embedded within an integrated compression pipeline (including pruning, quantization, and architecture design), KD routinely yields favorable accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs across modalities. Realizing KD’s benefits in practice requires careful choices about what to transfer (logits, features, attention, or relational signals), teacher–student alignment, data strategies (augmentation, data‑free synthesis, or adversarial sample use), and explicit mitigations for known failure modes such as capacity mismatch, bias transfer, and degraded treatment of rare phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Configurable Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable paradigm for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when its objectives, data strategies, and student architectures are chosen with task and deployment constraints in mind. However, KD is not a universal cure: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful mitigation of transferred biases and robustness gaps. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline that includes pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and data- or privacy-aware synthesis.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a foundational technique for compressing large models into efficient, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD is effective across modalities (graphs, vision, speech, and NLP), supports privacy- and communication-constrained settings, can work without original training data, and admits algorithmic and theoretical refinements that improve robustness, interpretability, and efficiency. Combining representation-level objectives, adversarial or data-free sample generation, and task-aware layer mapping yields practical recipes for real-world compression and adaptation.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Distilled Semantics for Comprehensive Scene Understanding from Videos
papers_seen.abstract: Whole understanding of the surroundings is paramount to autonomous systems. Recent works have shown that deep neural networks can learn geometry (depth) and motion (optical flow) from a monocular video without any explicit supervision from ground truth annotations, particularly hard to source for these two tasks. In this paper, we take an additional step toward holistic scene understanding with monocular cameras by learning depth and motion alongside with semantics, with supervision for the latter provided by a pre-trained network distilling proxy ground truth images. We address the three tasks jointly by a) a novel training protocol based on knowledge distillation and self-supervision and b) a compact network architecture which enables efficient scene understanding on both power hungry GPUs and low-power embedded platforms. We thoroughly assess the performance of our framework and show that it yields state-of-the-art results for monocular depth estimation, optical flow and motion segmentation.

papers_seen.author: Douglas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context-Sensitive Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile framework for transferring behavior and representations from large teacher models to smaller student models. When applied with appropriate objectives, layer mappings, data strategies, and safeguards, KD enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and communication while preserving much of teacher performance across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks. However, KD’s success is context-dependent: it interacts with teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, distribution shift, and fairness concerns. Treating KD as a configurable core of a compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, curriculum strategies, and privacy-aware protocols—yields the most reliable deployment outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Stephens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely applied strategy for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teachers into compact students. Across modalities, KD enables substantial reductions in inference cost and memory while often preserving much of teacher performance. Success depends on the choice of distilled signals, teacher and student design, data availability, and integration with complementary compression techniques; awareness of practical failure modes such as capacity mismatch, optimization difficulty, distribution shift, and transferred biases is essential. This synthesis summarizes what is known about KD methods, practical integrations with other compression approaches, representative applications, common limitations, and recommended design principles for robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Bray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task‑Aware Tool for Model Compression (with Limits and Practical Remedies)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a practical, versatile framework for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized students. When applied with task‑aware objectives, appropriate data strategies, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, or architecture search), KD routinely yields compact models suitable for latency- and memory-constrained deployment. However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher quality and compatibility with the student, the choice of distilled signals, data availability and augmentation, and mitigation of teacher artifacts. Careful protocol design—pre-training compact architectures, selecting what to distill, using effective augmentation or data synthesis, and combining KD with complementary methods—produces the most reliable results in practice.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Yet Contextual, Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has repeatedly enabled substantial reductions in model size and inference cost across modalities while retaining much of the performance of larger models. Empirical work shows KD can transfer predictive behavior, inductive biases, and task-specific capabilities from teacher to student, and can be adapted via logit-, feature-, and layer-level objectives, multi-teacher schemes, adversarial procedures, and data- or privacy-aware variants. However, KD is not a universal solution: optimization difficulties, teacher–student mismatch, data heterogeneity, and propagation of teacher errors limit its effectiveness unless combined with careful protocol design and complementary compression techniques. I argue KD should be treated as a first-class tool in compression toolkits, but only when used with task-aware filtering, capacity-aware targets, and architecture- or data-aware refinements to mitigate known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Robust Re-Identification by Multiple Views Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: To achieve robustness in Re-Identification, standard methods leverage tracking information in a Video-To-Video fashion. However, these solutions face a large drop in performance for single image queries (e.g., Image-To-Video setting). Recent works address this severe degradation by transferring temporal information from a Video-based network to an Image-based one. In this work, we devise a training strategy that allows the transfer of a superior knowledge, arising from a set of views depicting the target object. Our proposal - Views Knowledge Distillation (VKD) - pins this visual variety as a supervision signal within a teacher-student framework, where the teacher educates a student who observes fewer views. As a result, the student outperforms not only its teacher but also the current state-of-the-art in Image-To-Video by a wide margin (6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId and 5% on VeRi-776). A thorough analysis - on Person, Vehicle and Animal Re-ID - investigates the properties of VKD from a qualitatively and quantitatively perspective. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

papers_seen.author: Key
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) encompasses a family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger, often ensemble, teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods operate at the logit level, at intermediate representation and attention levels, and via relational or contrastive objectives; they are routinely combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with data strategies ranging from augmentation to data-free synthesis. Empirically, well-designed distillation pipelines can produce compact models that recover a large fraction of teacher performance, enabling deployment under latency, memory, privacy and device constraints. Success depends on choices about what and how to transfer, the quality and alignment of teacher and student, and the availability or synthesis of suitable data; important open problems remain around distribution shift, bias/fairness transfer, low-frequency behavior, and principled theoretical understanding.

papers_seen.author: Welch
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher performance. When treated as a task‑aware toolkit and embedded within an integrated compression pipeline (including pruning, quantization, and architecture design), KD routinely yields favorable accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs across modalities. Realizing KD’s benefits in practice requires careful choices about what to transfer (logits, features, attention, or relational signals), teacher–student alignment, data strategies (augmentation, data‑free synthesis, or adversarial sample use), and explicit mitigations for known failure modes such as capacity mismatch, bias transfer, and degraded treatment of rare phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Shields
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer information from high-capacity teacher models into smaller, faster students to enable deployment under constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and compute. A diverse set of distillation targets and training paradigms—soft-label (logit) matching, intermediate feature and attention-map imitation, layer-wise mapping, adversarial and data-free generation of surrogate examples, online and multi-teacher schemes, self-distillation, and integration with architecture search or pruning—have been developed and adapted to vision, language, multimodal, and generative tasks. Empirical work shows KD often recovers most of the teacher's accuracy (and in some settings improves generalization or robustness) when combined with task-aware choices of signals to transfer, data augmentation, and teacher-student design; remaining gaps and failure modes are linked to teacher quality, data availability and distribution shift, heterogeneous architectures, and fairness or robustness concerns.

papers_seen.author: Bailey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely used family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. The literature develops multi-level transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structure), multi‑teacher and online variants, data-aware and data‑free protocols, and integrations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD routinely recovers much of teacher performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks when teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and mapping between teacher and student are carefully managed; however, success is context-dependent and limited by optimization gaps, data scarcity, capacity mismatch, and the risk of transferring teacher artifacts or biases. Practical pipelines therefore treat KD as a configurable component of broader compression workflows tailored to deployment constraints such as latency, memory, privacy, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Wells
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller, more deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal tasks, KD techniques—ranging from soft-logit matching to feature- and relation-level objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free or privacy-preserving protocols, and online/co-distillation schemes—enable substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute with modest accuracy loss when applied with task-aware design. Effective use of KD typically combines careful selection of what to transfer, attention to teacher–student capacity and data regimes, and integration with complementary compression mechanisms such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Remaining challenges include teacher imperfection and bias transfer, data scarcity and domain shift, capacity and optimization mismatch, and reliably distilling structured or generative outputs.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically supported set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD operates at multiple levels—soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structures—and is effective across modalities (vision, language, speech, and translation) when adapted to task constraints. KD achieves substantial reductions in latency and model size while preserving much of teacher performance, but it is not a turnkey solution: its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and explicit measures to mitigate transferred biases and low-frequency or out-of-distribution failures. Consequently, KD should be treated as a configurable, central component of an integrated compression and deployment pipeline rather than as a standalone recipe.

papers_seen.author: Reese
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Context-Sensitive Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across modalities and tasks. KD reliably reduces inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance when applied with task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data constraints. However, KD is not automatic: its benefits depend on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and complementary compression methods; it also requires safeguards to avoid propagating teacher errors or biases. When treated as a configurable component of compression pipelines and paired with targeted techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data strategies, and selection of transfer signals), KD is the most practical first-line strategy for many deployment scenarios in deep learning and NLP.

Practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable component of broader compression pipelines—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and targeted data strategies—and adopt safeguards for robustness, fairness, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses or transfers capabilities of large models into smaller ones via indirect supervision. Remaining challenges include distillation under data scarcity or privacy constraints, robust transfer of inductive biases, and principled layer-to-layer alignment for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Model Compression with Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation for Web Question Answering System
papers_seen.abstract: Deep pre-training and fine-tuning models (such as BERT and OpenAI GPT) have demonstrated excellent results in question answering areas. However, due to the sheer amount of model parameters, the inference speed of these models is very slow. How to apply these complex models to real business scenarios becomes a challenging but practical problem. Previous model compression methods usually suffer from information loss during the model compression procedure, leading to inferior models compared with the original one. To tackle this challenge, we propose a Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (TMKD for short) method for web Question Answering system. We first develop a general Q\&A distillation task for student model pre-training, and further fine-tune this pre-trained student model with multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream tasks (like Web Q\&A task, MNLI, SNLI, RTE tasks from GLUE), which effectively reduces the overfitting bias in individual teacher models, and transfers more general knowledge to the student model. The experiment results show that our method can significantly outperform the baseline methods and even achieve comparable results with the original teacher models, along with substantial speedup of model inference.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Embracing the Dark Knowledge: Domain Generalization Using Regularized Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Though convolutional neural networks are widely used in different tasks, lack of generalization capability in the absence of sufficient and representative data is one of the challenges that hinder their practical application. In this paper, we propose a simple, effective, and plug-and-play training strategy named Knowledge Distillation for Domain Generalization (KDDG) which is built upon a knowledge distillation framework with the gradient filter as a novel regularization term. We find that both the ``richer dark knowledge" from the teacher network, as well as the gradient filter we proposed, can reduce the difficulty of learning the mapping which further improves the generalization ability of the model. We also conduct experiments extensively to show that our framework can significantly improve the generalization capability of deep neural networks in different tasks including image classification, segmentation, reinforcement learning by comparing our method with existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques. Last but not the least, we propose to adopt two metrics to analyze our proposed method in order to better understand how our proposed method benefits the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a single trick into a broad, practical family of methods for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or privacy-aware models while retaining much of their performance. The techniques differ by what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or channel statistics), how the transfer is staged (offline teacher-student, online/co-distillation, data-free/zero-shot, few-shot), and which complementary strategies are used (projectors, mixup/data augmentation, pruning, or architecture-aware design). Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often acts both as information transfer and as a regularizer; success depends critically on choices about teacher signals, student capacity, the availability and nature of data, and task-specific design. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation under limited or private data, preventing transfer of teacher errors, adapting to heterogeneous or federated settings, and scaling distillation to very large models and complex structured-output tasks.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: ALP-KD: Attention-Based Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is considered as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, namely a teacher and a student, are coupled together during training. The teacher network is supposed to be a trustworthy predictor and the student tries to mimic its predictions. Usually, a student with a lighter architecture is selected so we can achieve compression and yet deliver high-quality results. In such a setting, distillation only happens for final predictions whereas the student could also benefit from teacher's supervision for internal components.   Motivated by this, we studied the problem of distillation for intermediate layers. Since there might not be a one-to-one alignment between student and teacher layers, existing techniques skip some teacher layers and only distill from a subset of them. This shortcoming directly impacts quality, so we instead propose a combinatorial technique which relies on attention. Our model fuses teacher-side information and takes each layer's significance into consideration, then performs distillation between combined teacher layers and those of the student. Using our technique, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer counterparts and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that our combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: Object DGCNN: 3D Object Detection using Dynamic Graphs
papers_seen.abstract: 3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a broad family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more efficient student models to meet latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals) and within diverse protocols (offline teacher→student, online/self-distillation, multi‑teacher, and data‑free/zero‑shot approaches). Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance and can sometimes improve student generalization when objectives, data, and teacher–student design are well matched; however, success is context dependent and sensitive to teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability and distribution shift, and risks of transferring teacher errors or bias. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that combines carefully chosen distillation signals, layer-mapping and curriculum strategies, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, and architecture search) while adopting targeted safeguards for low‑frequency behaviors, privacy, and fairness.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large models into smaller, faster models by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Approaches vary from matching output soft-labels to imitating internal representations, attention maps, or relational structure. Distillation has been applied across modalities and tasks — NLP, vision, detection, generation, ranking, CTR prediction, graph learning, reinforcement learning and federated settings — and can be combined with architecture search and task- or domain-adaptation to produce compact models that preserve much of the teacher’s performance while reducing latency, memory and compute. Practical constraints such as unavailable training data, mismatched inputs or architectures, privacy requirements, and distribution shift motivate specialized techniques including data-free distillation, student-friendly teacher training, adversarial sample generation, many-to-many layer mapping, and generative replay. Empirical results show substantial size and speed gains with modest degradation in performance in many settings, but trade-offs remain and several directions for more robust, automated and privacy-aware distillation remain active.

papers_seen.author: Kennedy
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential but Insufficient — A Practical Position for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central, practically proven strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and deployable students across vision and language tasks. While distilled students often recover much of teacher performance, distillation alone is not a complete solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and careful selection of what to transfer. In practice, distillation should be treated as a configurable core of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline that integrates complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation), explicit fairness and robustness interventions, and data strategies ranging from augmentation to data-free synthesis.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of large teachers. KD encompasses a range of targets and protocols—output-level supervision, intermediate representation matching, adversarial and data-free synthesis, multi-teacher and self-distillation—and is most effective when combined with architecture-aware design, data strategies, and complementary compression techniques. While KD routinely delivers favorable efficiency–accuracy trade-offs in vision, language, recommender, and multimodal systems, realizing those gains in practice requires attention to teacher–student alignment, data availability and privacy, fairness and low-frequency behavior, and method selection for the deployment constraints at hand.

papers_seen.author: Farmer
papers_seen.title: Towards Efficient 3D Object Detection with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite substantial progress in 3D object detection, advanced 3D detectors often suffer from heavy computation overheads. To this end, we explore the potential of knowledge distillation (KD) for developing efficient 3D object detectors, focusing on popular pillar- and voxel-based detectors.In the absence of well-developed teacher-student pairs, we first study how to obtain student models with good trade offs between accuracy and efficiency from the perspectives of model compression and input resolution reduction. Then, we build a benchmark to assess existing KD methods developed in the 2D domain for 3D object detection upon six well-constructed teacher-student pairs. Further, we propose an improved KD pipeline incorporating an enhanced logit KD method that performs KD on only a few pivotal positions determined by teacher classification response, and a teacher-guided student model initialization to facilitate transferring teacher model's feature extraction ability to students through weight inheritance. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on the Waymo dataset. Our best performing model achieves $65.75\%$ LEVEL 2 mAPH, surpassing its teacher model and requiring only $44\%$ of teacher flops. Our most efficient model runs 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100, which is $2.2\times$ faster than PointPillar with even higher accuracy. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/SparseKD}.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically supported approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. A broad set of methods—logit-level transfer, feature- and relation-level matching, adversarial and data-free protocols, and task-aware adaptations—enables KD to serve as a first-order component of practical compression pipelines. However, its success is conditional on teacher–student design, data regime, what is distilled, and integration with complementary compression techniques.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for converting high-capacity teacher models into smaller, more deployable student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods—ranging from soft-target matching to feature-, attention-, and relation-level alignment, as well as online, ensemble, and data-free variants—have enabled substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while often preserving most of the teacher's performance. Practical application requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to generate or select data, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression tools.

papers_seen.author: Adkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Approaches, Applications, and Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: This synthesis summarizes methods, extensions, and applications of knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques in deep learning and NLP. It covers teacher-student paradigms (offline and online), multi-teacher and ensemble strategies, layer- and feature-based distillation, data-free and privacy-aware distillation, task-aware and architecture-aware adaptations, theoretical perspectives, and applications beyond classification (e.g., generation, detection, graph learning, and machine reading). The review highlights recurrent practical challenges—capacity mismatch, optimization difficulty, redundant teacher information, data and privacy constraints—and points to promising directions such as task-aware filtering, many-to-many layer mappings, and adversarial/data-free sample generation to enable distillation under limited resources or access.

papers_seen.author: Mcguire
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Dependent Component of Compression Portfolios
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably reduces the deployment cost of large deep models while preserving much of their predictive and representational power. Rather than being a single recipe, KD is best treated as a flexible, task- and capacity-aware instrument that should be combined with complementary compression tools (e.g., pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with careful choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to mitigate teacher-induced failure modes for robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Duncan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Analyses, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing and adapting large neural models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models while retaining much of their performance. A diverse set of KD approaches operate at the level of final outputs (logits), intermediate features, layer relations, or via adversarial and data-generation mechanisms. KD has been adapted across modalities and tasks — from NLP transformer compression to GAN and speech-model compression, cross-modal transfer, federated settings, and domain-specific applications — and interacts strongly with concerns about robustness, fairness, and transfer of inductive biases. Empirical and theoretical work has clarified when and why various KD variants help, and highlights open challenges in data heterogeneity, teacher-student mismatch, and automatic discovery of compact architectures.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Benefits, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, more efficient students to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. Across vision, language, and multimodal tasks, KD has evolved from simple logits-matching into a configurable toolkit that includes feature- and attention-level matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and privacy-aware variants, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains while retaining much of teacher performance when applied with task-aware objectives, careful teacher–student alignment, and appropriate data strategies; however, important failure modes remain (teacher quality, student capacity, limited data, distribution shift, and propagation of biases), motivating integrated pipelines and targeted mitigation strategies for real deployments.

papers_seen.author: Salas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of the Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used family of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce latency, memory, and compute while preserving much of task performance. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal domains, KD methods range from soft-target (logit) matching to richer objectives that mimic internal representations, attention, relational structure, or contrastive signals. KD is frequently combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and adapted to practical constraints via data-free, few-shot, online, or federated protocols. Success depends on careful, task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited data, privacy, distribution shift, and undesirable teacher behaviors. The literature emphasizes KD as a configurable component of broader compression pipelines rather than a turnkey algorithm.

papers_seen.author: Huff
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a configurable toolkit—selecting appropriate distillation signals, aligning teacher and student capacity, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, or task-adaptive architecture search)—practitioners routinely obtain compact models that retain much of teacher performance. Success requires explicit attention to teacher quality, data availability or synthesis, optimization schedules, and safeguards against transferred biases or degraded rare-token behavior.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Channel Distillation: Channel-Wise Attention for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is to transfer the knowledge from the data learned by the teacher network to the student network, so that the student has the advantage of less parameters and less calculations, and the accuracy is close to the teacher. In this paper, we propose a new distillation method, which contains two transfer distillation strategies and a loss decay strategy. The first transfer strategy is based on channel-wise attention, called Channel Distillation (CD). CD transfers the channel information from the teacher to the student. The second is Guided Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Unlike Knowledge Distillation (KD), which allows the student to mimic each sample's prediction distribution of the teacher, GKD only enables the student to mimic the correct output of the teacher. The last part is Early Decay Teacher (EDT). During the training process, we gradually decay the weight of the distillation loss. The purpose is to enable the student to gradually control the optimization rather than the teacher. Our proposed method is evaluated on ImageNet and CIFAR100. On ImageNet, we achieve 27.68% of top-1 error with ResNet18, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, we achieve surprising result that the student outperforms the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Cross-Domain Argument for Practical, Responsible, and Multi-Modal Deployment
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are indispensable for deploying modern deep models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. Across vision, language, graph, and generative domains, distillation methods can preserve most of a teacher's performance while reducing latency, memory, and communication. Best results come from (a) matching appropriate internal representations (layer mapping, attention, many-to-many mappings), (b) designing teachers or multi-teacher schemes that are student-aware, and (c) combining distillation with complementary techniques (pruning, NAS, adversarial training, federated schemes). However, practitioners must be mindful of failure modes—bias amplification, degraded modeling of rare phenomena, and gaps when no training data are available—and adopt targeted mitigations such as task-adaptive compression, confidence-aware multi-teacher weighting, and data-free or privacy-preserving distillation when necessary.

papers_seen.author: Hamilton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. When applied with attention to the task, available data, and student capacity, KD can deliver substantial reductions in size and latency while preserving most of the teacher's performance. Success depends on selecting what to transfer (logits, features, relations), how to align teacher and student (layer mapping, projectors, annealing), and how to handle limited or private data (data-free synthesis, adversarial generators, teacher-free regularizers). Although KD is broadly effective, it is not a panacea: failures arise from teacher-student mismatch, domain shift, optimization issues, and transferred biases, motivating targeted protocols and continued research into privacy-aware, robust, and automated distillation methods.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Bell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical, flexible family of techniques for producing compact models from larger teachers. Across vision, language, recommendation, and multimodal systems, variants of KD—soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational/contrastive objectives, ensemble and online schemes, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols—are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can enable latency, memory, and privacy trade-offs, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, data strategy, and explicit mitigation of transferred errors, bias, and low-frequency phenomena. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical findings, practical design considerations, applications, limitations, and promising research directions drawn from the provided studies.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Pragmatic, Multifaceted Framework for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. When treated as a multifaceted framework—covering logits, intermediate representations, feature maps, sample selection, and data-side interventions—KD enables deployments under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. Effectiveness depends on matching the distillation signals to student capacity and task structure, and on addressing failure modes such as teacher bias and data scarcity. Combining KD with complementary techniques (quantization, architecture transformations, pruning, and task-aware layer mapping) yields the best tradeoffs between compression and downstream accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Webb
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Central Tool, Context-Aware Integration
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for compressing large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students suitable for deployment. KD variants—matching logits, imitating intermediate representations or attention, using multi-teacher or self-distillation regimes, and supporting data-free or privacy-aware setups—have demonstrated broad applicability across vision, speech, language, retrieval, and multimodal tasks. However, KD is not a universal cure: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, availability and fidelity of distillation data, and task-specific needs. Best outcomes arise when KD is treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that includes complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), careful layer and feature alignment, and data- or task-aware strategies to mitigate known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Graph-less Neural Networks: Teaching Old MLPs New Tricks via Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are popular for graph machine learning and have shown great results on wide node classification tasks. Yet, they are less popular for practical deployments in the industry owing to their scalability challenges incurred by data dependency. Namely, GNN inference depends on neighbor nodes multiple hops away from the target, and fetching them burdens latency-constrained applications. Existing inference acceleration methods like pruning and quantization can speed up GNNs by reducing Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, but the improvements are limited given the data dependency is not resolved. Conversely, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have no graph dependency and infer much faster than GNNs, even though they are less accurate than GNNs for node classification in general. Motivated by these complementary strengths and weaknesses, we bring GNNs and MLPs together via knowledge distillation (KD). Our work shows that the performance of MLPs can be improved by large margins with GNN KD. We call the distilled MLPs Graph-less Neural Networks (GLNNs) as they have no inference graph dependency. We show that GLNNs with competitive accuracy infer faster than GNNs by 146X-273X and faster than other acceleration methods by 14X-27X. Under a production setting involving both transductive and inductive predictions across 7 datasets, GLNN accuracies improve over stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and match GNNs on 6/7 datasets. Comprehensive analysis shows when and why GLNNs can achieve competitive accuracies to GNNs and suggests GLNN as a handy choice for latency-constrained applications.

papers_seen.author: Ortiz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential but Non-Automatic Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, widely applicable approach for compressing large or ensemble models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. Empirical work across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks shows that KD can yield substantial reductions in parameter count and latency with modest accuracy loss, but success depends on careful choices about what to transfer (logits, features, relations, attention), how to align heterogeneous architectures, and how to handle limited or mismatched data. Rather than a single recipe, KD is best treated as a principled toolbox: combine output-level and representation-level objectives, design student-aware teachers or progressive module replacement, and integrate KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and privacy/robustness safeguards to meet practical deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Rosales
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Insufficient Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized models by transferring information from larger or alternative teachers into compact students. KD variants—ranging from logits and feature matching to relational, contrastive, and data-free protocols—have been demonstrated across vision, speech, and NLP to deliver favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. At the same time, KD’s success depends on teacher quality, signal choice, data regime, and careful training design, and it is most reliable when integrated with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware engineering. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a central, configurable element of any compression pipeline, but not as a standalone solution: use KD deliberately, combine it with other methods, and adopt practices that mitigate its failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Orr
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Theory, and Practical Strategies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) encompasses a family of techniques for transferring information from high-capacity teacher models to smaller or otherwise constrained student models so they retain functionality while reducing latency, memory, and computational cost. Over the past decade KD has evolved from logits-based soft-label supervision to a rich toolkit that includes intermediate-feature matching, layer-wise and task-aware mappings, adversarial and contrastive objectives, ensemble and self-distillation, data-free synthesis, and federated or heterogeneous-device protocols. Empirical and theoretical work indicates KD often acts both as knowledge transfer and as a form of regularization; its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and selection, task alignment, and careful design of objectives and model interfaces. Remaining challenges include robust transfer under data scarcity or domain shift, preserving rare-token behavior in sequence tasks, principled layer-to-layer alignment across heterogeneous architectures, and mitigating teacher-induced biases.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or specialized models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. A broad toolkit has emerged — matching soft logits, imitating intermediate features and attention, relational and contrastive objectives, ensemble and multi-teacher schemes, adversarial or data-free sample synthesis, and layer-mapping strategies — and these methods are combined routinely with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Distillation is effective across modalities (vision, language, multimodal) and tasks (classification, generation, detection, retrieval, ranking), but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, availability and nature of distillation data, and task-specific design choices. Practical deployments therefore emphasize task-aware selection of distilled signals, pretraining of compact models, and targeted mitigation of failure modes such as transferred biases and degradation on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.author: Byrd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Indispensable but Task‑Aware
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable family of methods for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD variants have been successfully adapted across modalities and tasks, and when designed with awareness of task constraints, data availability, and student capacity, distillation yields substantial practical gains. However, KD has concrete limits—capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias propagation, and failures on rare phenomena—that make it most effective when integrated into broader, task‑aware compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Rivas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a rich, task-sensitive toolbox for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models to compact students. Practitioners move beyond simple logit matching to transfer internal representations, attention patterns, relational structure, and decision-boundary information, and they combine distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or data-free generation). Empirical results across vision, language, generative models, and structured prediction show distilled students often recover much of teacher performance and can enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but distillation also has failure modes—teacher bias transfer, sensitivity to data availability, capacity mismatch, and degraded modeling of low-frequency phenomena—that require targeted mitigations and continued theoretical and empirical work.
