                    Topic: Knowledge distillation or model compression in deep learning or NLP

                    Articles:
                    [{'author': 'Willis', 'year': 2024, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, multimodal, and structured tasks. The literature frames KD as a configurable toolkit of targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive signals), protocols (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, data-free), and engineering integrations (projectors, curriculum scheduling, data augmentation, architecture search, pruning, quantization). KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can improve robustness or generalization when applied with task-aware design, but its success is context-dependent: it hinges on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and explicit handling of teacher biases, low-frequency phenomena, and distribution shift. Practical systems therefore treat KD as a central component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone, universal recipe.'}, {'author': 'Allen', 'year': 2021, 'title': 'Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically motivated family of techniques for transferring behavior from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels of abstraction (output logits, intermediate features, attention and relational maps), can be adapted to scarce- or privacy-constrained data regimes, and are commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet deployment constraints. Empirically, KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance across vision and language tasks, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of transfer targets, and the availability or synthesis of appropriate distillation data. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a turnkey solution.'}, {'author': 'Hoffman', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Federated Knowledge Distillation', 'abstract': 'Distributed learning frameworks often rely on exchanging model parameters across workers, instead of revealing their raw data. A prime example is federated learning that exchanges the gradients or weights of each neural network model. Under limited communication resources, however, such a method becomes extremely costly particularly for modern deep neural networks having a huge number of model parameters. In this regard, federated distillation (FD) is a compelling distributed learning solution that only exchanges the model outputs whose dimensions are commonly much smaller than the model sizes (e.g., 10 labels in the MNIST dataset). The goal of this chapter is to provide a deep understanding of FD while demonstrating its communication efficiency and applicability to a variety of tasks. To this end, towards demystifying the operational principle of FD, the first part of this chapter provides a novel asymptotic analysis for two foundational algorithms of FD, namely knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD), by exploiting the theory of neural tangent kernel (NTK). Next, the second part elaborates on a baseline implementation of FD for a classification task, and illustrates its performance in terms of accuracy and communication efficiency compared to FL. Lastly, to demonstrate the applicability of FD to various distributed learning tasks and environments, the third part presents two selected applications, namely FD over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and FD for reinforcement learning.'}, {'author': 'Cunningham', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Practical Guidance', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used family of techniques for transferring behavior from larger, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, KD variants—including logits/soft-target matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and adversarial generation, and self-distillation—are combined with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows that carefully designed distillation pipelines typically recover most teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but outcomes depend on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of transfer signals, and the availability or synthesis of data; remaining challenges include robustness, bias transfer, low-frequency/structured-output preservation, privacy-aware distillation, and automating teacher–student co-design.'}, {'author': 'Nelson', 'year': 2023, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Evidence, Methods, and Open Problems', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practically validated set of techniques for transferring information from high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient students so they can be deployed under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. A broad toolkit—ranging from soft-target (logit) matching to intermediate-feature and attention imitation, multi- and self-distillation, data-free or privacy-aware synthesis, and curriculum or adversarial sample selection—enables students to retain much of teacher performance across vision, language, multimodal, retrieval, and federated settings. Despite strong empirical successes, important engineering and scientific challenges remain around teacher–student alignment, data availability and synthesis, preservation of low-frequency behaviors, robustness and fairness, and principled automated design for heterogeneous deployment environments.'}, {'author': 'Shaw', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation transfers information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and latency while often retaining substantial parts of teacher performance. A broad family of distillation targets and training protocols has been developed (logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive signals; offline, online, self-, multi-teacher, and data-free variants). Practical success depends on aligning the distillation signal to task and student capacity and on combining distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Key challenges include teacher–student capacity and architecture mismatch, limited or unavailable data, propagation of teacher biases or errors, distribution shift, and difficulties preserving low-frequency or structured behaviors. Continued progress requires principled choices about what, when, and how to transfer knowledge, better theory linking distillation choices to student generalization, and engineering pipelines that pair KD with task-aware data and model design.'}, {'author': 'Walls', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have been adapted across modalities (vision, language, graphs, and generative models) to produce smaller, faster, or more robust models while attempting to retain performance of larger teachers. Approaches vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational information, or structural/topological properties), how transfer is scheduled or weighted (confidence-aware, progressive replacement, or multi-teacher aggregation), and how distillation is combined with other compression methods (pruning, architecture search, or compact operator substitution). Empirical work shows strong practical benefits—improved runtime, memory, and sometimes robustness or fairness—while theoretical and analytical work begins to explain when and why distillation helps (e.g., role of soft targets, label smoothing analogies, and behavior with imperfect teachers). Remaining challenges include transferring rare-word or low-frequency information in sequence tasks, preserving relational/global structure in graph and link tasks, adapting to evolving domains, and automating generator compression for GANs. This synthesis summarizes key methods, insights, and open directions from recent literature.'}, {'author': 'Freeman', 'year': 2024, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation: Central, Context‑Sensitive, and Best Used as Part of an Integrated Compression Pipeline', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely effective toolkit for producing compact models from larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and graph domains. Empirical evidence shows KD can reduce model size and latency while retaining much of teacher performance, but success depends on what signals are transferred, teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability, and the training protocol. I argue KD should be treated as a central but context‑sensitive component of compression pipelines and combined with representation, data, and architecture strategies to reliably meet deployment goals.'}, {'author': 'Perez', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors', 'abstract': 'To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \\url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.'}, {'author': 'Brown', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers across vision, language, graph, recommendation, and generative settings. KD encompasses a range of techniques—soft-target matching, intermediate feature and attention alignment, contrastive and adversarial objectives, layer- and channel-wise mappings, and data- or task-aware variants—and is frequently combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can enable deployable, lower-latency models, improve robustness and interpretability in some settings, and serve as a substrate for domain adaptation and privacy-aware workflows; its success depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, data availability (including data-free or few-shot regimes), and practical engineering choices.'}, {'author': 'Moore', 'year': 2017, 'title': 'Show, Attend and Distill:Knowledge Distillation via Attention-based Feature Matching', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation extracts general knowledge from a pre-trained teacher network and provides guidance to a target student network. Most studies manually tie intermediate features of the teacher and student, and transfer knowledge through pre-defined links. However, manual selection often constructs ineffective links that limit the improvement from the distillation. There has been an attempt to address the problem, but it is still challenging to identify effective links under practical scenarios. In this paper, we introduce an effective and efficient feature distillation method utilizing all the feature levels of the teacher without manually selecting the links. Specifically, our method utilizes an attention-based meta-network that learns relative similarities between features, and applies identified similarities to control distillation intensities of all possible pairs. As a result, our method determines competent links more efficiently than the previous approach and provides better performance on model compression and transfer learning tasks. Further qualitative analyses and ablative studies describe how our method contributes to better distillation. The implementation code is available at github.com/clovaai/attention-feature-distillation.'}, {'author': 'Dean', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a central and practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and sometimes more interpretable students across vision, language, multimodal, and domain-specific tasks. KD’s flexibility—transferring soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational/contrastive signals—lets practitioners tailor compression to hardware, privacy, or accuracy constraints. Empirical evidence shows that when distillation is designed task- and capacity-aware and combined with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, or progressive module replacement), students can recover much of teacher performance and gain robustness or interpretability in particular settings. At the same time, KD is not automatic: teacher quality, data availability or synthesis, teacher–student mismatch, and the risk of transferring teacher errors or biases require careful protocols (sample selection, layer mapping, objective weighting, and privacy- or robustness-aware extensions). I argue KD should be treated as a first-class, configurable component of compression pipelines—powerful and broadly applicable, but demand-aware and paired with best practices to realize its potential reliably.'}, {'author': 'Williams', 'year': 2020, 'title': 'Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is now a central, broadly applicable approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and functional behavior of larger teachers. The literature describes a rich taxonomy of KD objectives and protocols — from matching soft logits to aligning intermediate features, attention maps, and relational or contrastive structures — together with specialized strategies for online, multi-teacher, data-free, federated, and privacy-sensitive settings. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often improves student generalization and acts as a regularizer, but success depends on task-aware choices: which signals to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures, how to handle limited or private data, and how to mitigate transfer of teacher errors or low-frequency behaviors. Practical pipelines therefore treat KD as a configurable component combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), curriculum and augmentation strategies, and targeted safeguards for robustness and fairness.'}, {'author': 'Kim', 'year': 2018, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression, Adaptation and Privacy', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a single recipe for shrinking large models: it is a flexible family of techniques that enables accurate, efficient and deployable models across modalities and tasks. KD can compress huge pretrained language and vision models into lightweight architectures with large speed and memory gains while retaining most of the teacher performance. It also supports variant protocols—online, self-distillation, multi-teacher, representation-level and contrastive forms—that trade off efficiency, robustness, and generalization. Beyond raw compression, KD can enable domain adaptation, privacy-preserving model release, and fairness-aware training when combined with appropriate design choices. However, KD is not a panacea: teacher quality, data heterogeneity, and mismatch between teacher and student inputs/architectures can limit gains and must be addressed by specific strategies such as multi-teacher ensembles, confidence weighting, input alignment, or theoretical safeguards.'}, {'author': 'Hawkins', 'year': 2020, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically supported set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD operates at multiple levels—soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structures—and is effective across modalities (vision, language, speech, and translation) when adapted to task constraints. KD achieves substantial reductions in latency and model size while preserving much of teacher performance, but it is not a turnkey solution: its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and explicit measures to mitigate transferred biases and low-frequency or out-of-distribution failures. Consequently, KD should be treated as a configurable, central component of an integrated compression and deployment pipeline rather than as a standalone recipe.'}, {'author': 'Parker', 'year': 2020, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broad family of techniques for compressing large or expensive models into smaller, faster, or more deployable ones by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Methods differ in the form of transferred knowledge (soft logits, hidden features, contrastive distributions, synthetic data, or cross-modal alignments), in how and when distillation is applied (offline, online, layer-wise, task-adaptive, or data-free), and in the problems they target (classification, detection, generation, language tasks, graph learning, or novel-view synthesis). Empirical work demonstrates that appropriate choices about teacher signals, data manipulation, and architectural search can yield compact models that retain much of teacher performance across modalities; theoretical work begins to clarify when soft labels help and when hard labels or mixed supervision are needed. Remaining challenges include optimization gaps between teacher and student, dataset and fairness concerns, and scaling distillation reliably in large distributed settings.'}, {'author': 'Snyder', 'year': 2020, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation: A Core, Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and widely applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring information beyond hard labels. KD is most effective when treated as a central element of a broader compression portfolio that includes architecture-aware design, pre-training, pruning/quantization, and privacy- or data-aware protocols. Practical deployment benefits from careful choices about what to transfer (logits, features, relations), how to align teacher and student, and when to apply auxiliary methods; remaining challenges include robustness under distributional shift, teacher imperfections, low-frequency token fidelity, and privacy-sensitive or heterogeneous-device settings.'}, {'author': 'Bruce', 'year': 2025, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a proven, flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller students, enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. When properly designed—choosing what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which complementary compression methods to use—KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and supports a range of practical use cases. However, KD is not turnkey: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability of suitable data (or reliable data synthesis), and careful mitigation of failure modes such as transferred biases, degraded low-frequency behavior, and distribution shift. I argue that KD should be treated as a core, configurable component of integrated compression pipelines rather than a standalone solution, and I summarize practical recommendations and open challenges that follow from this position.'}, {'author': 'Mueller', 'year': 2024, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Work', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing and accelerating deep models by transferring knowledge from larger (teacher) models to smaller (student) models. Beyond straightforward parameter reduction, KD is used to improve student generalization, robustness, interpretability, domain adaptation, continual learning, and to enable deployment in latency- or resource-constrained settings. The literature shows a wide variety of KD objectives (logit/soft-label matching, feature imitation, relational losses), training protocols (multi-teacher, curriculum, adversarial or zero-shot data generation, teacher-free/self-distillation), and application-specific adaptations (detection, retrieval, GANs, speech, lipreading, 3D vision, recommender systems, and NLP). Empirical results demonstrate that carefully designed distillation pipelines can recover much of teacher performance and in some cases surpass teachers on efficiency-accuracy trade-offs, but raise challenges including heterogeneous teacher-student alignment, data availability, preserving low-frequency or fine-grained behaviors, and transferring robustness and domain-general knowledge.'}, {'author': 'Cervantes', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression: Essential, Powerful, but Context‑Dependent', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models. Empirical evidence across vision, language, multimodal, and specialized domains shows KD can recover much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and communication costs. Successful distillation depends on deliberate choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, data availability and preparation, and integration with complementary compression methods. Treated as a toolbox—combining soft-targets with representation matching, progressive schedules, curriculum selection, and pruning/quantization—KD is a first‑order approach for real‑world compression when practitioners explicitly address its known limitations.'}, {'author': 'Cruz', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective family of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models into smaller student models. KD routinely yields large efficiency gains (reduced memory, compute, and latency) while preserving much of teacher performance when applied with task‑aware objectives, appropriate teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression methods. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on what signals are transferred, teacher quality, student capacity, data availability (including privacy or data‑free regimes), and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer and degraded handling of rare phenomena. Treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline and combined with targeted algorithmic and engineering practices, KD enables practical, deployable compression across modalities and settings.'}, {'author': 'Hubbard', 'year': 2019, 'title': 'Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic and widely adopted framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across modalities and tasks, a diverse set of transfer targets and training protocols has emerged — from matching soft logits to imitating intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structures, and even using synthesized or privacy-aware pseudo-data. Best results typically come from combining multiple distilled signals, aligning teacher and student architectures (or adding projector layers), and integrating KD with complementary compression primitives and data strategies. Despite broad empirical success, persistent challenges include handling distribution shift and low-frequency behavior, aligning heterogeneous architectures, safeguarding privacy and fairness, and automating principled teacher selection. This synthesis condenses prevailing methods, empirical patterns, practical guidance, and open research directions documented in the supplied literature.'}, {'author': 'Kidd', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'The Centrality and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation is a versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones while preserving much of their performance. Beyond reducing parameter counts and inference latency, distillation enables transferring inductive biases, protecting privacy in federated settings, enabling few- and zero-shot compression, and supporting task-adaptive and automated compression workflows. However, distillation is not a panacea: dataset heterogeneity, teacher–student mismatch, and redundant teacher representations can limit gains. Best practice combines representation-level and layer-aware techniques, multi-teacher or teacher-free strategies where appropriate, and task-aware selection of distilled information to maximize compressed-model utility.'}, {'author': 'Bowman', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'TRILLsson: Distilled Universal Paralinguistic Speech Representations', 'abstract': 'Recent advances in self-supervision have dramatically improved the quality of speech representations. However, deployment of state-of-the-art embedding models on devices has been restricted due to their limited public availability and large resource footprint. Our work addresses these issues by publicly releasing a collection of paralinguistic speech models that are small and near state-of-the-art performance. Our approach is based on knowledge distillation, and our models are distilled on public data only. We explore different architectures and thoroughly evaluate our models on the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. Our largest distilled model is less than 15% the size of the original model (314MB vs 2.2GB), achieves over 96% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks, and is trained on 6.5% the data. The smallest model is 1% in size (22MB) and achieves over 90% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks. Our models outperform the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 model on 6 of 7 tasks, and our smallest model outperforms the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks despite being 7% the size.'}, {'author': 'Rivera', 'year': 2023, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Practical Guidance', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of task performance. KD methods transfer information via soft logits, intermediate representations, attention or relational signals, synthesized or public data, and training protocols such as offline, online, multi-teacher, and self-distillation. Empirical results across vision, language, recommender, and generative tasks show that appropriately designed distillation can yield large inference and memory savings with modest accuracy loss; achieving reliable gains in practice requires attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and selection, and complementary compression techniques. Open problems include principled theory for when particular signals transfer well, robust distillation under data heterogeneity and privacy constraints, preserving rare or low-frequency phenomena, and automating teacher–student alignment for heterogeneous architectures.'}, {'author': 'Edwards', 'year': 2024, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practically driven toolbox for transferring performance from large teacher models to smaller student models across modalities and tasks. Methods span soft-label supervision, feature- and layer-wise imitation, adversarial and ensemble-based transfer, data- and privacy-aware protocols, and integration with complementary compression strategies (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but gains depend strongly on what is transferred, teacher–student alignment, domain shift, and data availability.'}, {'author': 'Bryant', 'year': 2025, 'title': 'Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, task-aware family of methods for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD uses a variety of transfer targets and training protocols to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under memory and latency constraints, and—when carefully applied—preserve much of teacher performance. Practical application treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline, combining distillation with architecture design, pruning, quantization, data strategies, and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.'}, {'author': 'Lewis', 'year': 2024, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Versatile, and Bounded', 'abstract': "Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core method for producing compact, efficient models from large deep networks across vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative tasks. KD delivers substantial inference and memory savings while often preserving much of the teacher's performance, enabling deployment in latency-, power-, and privacy-constrained settings. At the same time, KD transfers teacher imperfections (biases, distributional blind spots) and faces practical constraints (data mismatch, teacher–student capacity gaps, limited-data regimes). Effective use of KD therefore requires matching objectives, data strategies, and architectures to deployment goals and complementing distillation with pruning, quantization, or privacy-aware protocols when necessary."}, {'author': 'Hicks', 'year': 2022, 'title': 'Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt', 'abstract': "Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario."}, {'author': 'Elliott', 'year': 2020, 'title': 'Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance', 'abstract': 'Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible toolkit for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact students. Across vision, language, multimodal, generative, and recommender systems, KD methods have been developed to match outputs (soft targets), internal representations (features and attention), relational or contrastive signals, and task-specific rank or ordering information. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher and student design, data availability (including data-free strategies), and integration with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, and architecture search). Trade-offs include capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors or biases, degraded performance on low-frequency phenomena, and optimization challenges; many works propose curricula, student-friendly teacher training, or multi-teacher and online protocols to mitigate these issues. The field has matured into a central engineering primitive for deployment, while continuing to pursue principled transfer objectives, privacy-aware distillation, and robust domain- and architecture-aware pipelines.'}]

papers_seen.author: Carroll
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable collection of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or auxiliary models (“teachers”) into smaller, more deployable models (“students”). Over the last decade KD has diversified beyond simple soft-label matching to include feature- and attention-level imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data‑free protocols, and online or self-distillation schemes. Empirical work shows KD frequently recovers much of a teacher’s performance while enabling reductions in parameters, latency, and memory, but reliable deployment requires task‑aware design, careful handling of data and teacher imperfections, and integration with complementary compression methods.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Versatile Toolkit with Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broad set of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and sometimes more interpretable students. Across NLP and vision applications, KD enables deployment on resource-constrained hardware, supports privacy- and data-constrained settings, and can be adapted to preserve or transfer properties such as adversarial robustness, cross-modal behavior, and domain expertise. At the same time, KD interacts with factors such as teacher quality, data availability, label design, and training cost, and several specialized methods have been developed to address these practical trade-offs. This paper argues that KD is an indispensable, flexible approach for model compression and adaptation, and that best results arise from combining KD with complementary practices (e.g., pre-training, augmentation, curriculum selection, or generative replay) tailored to the deployment constraints and objectives.

papers_seen.author: Villarreal
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Component of Model‑Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an empirically powerful and practically flexible approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. KD should be treated as a central, configurable element of compression workflows: it routinely delivers large reductions in inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance, but it is not sufficient on its own. Reliable deployment requires task‑aware choices of distilled signals, teacher–student co‑design, data strategies (including data‑free and privacy‑aware options), and combination with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Galloway
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Versatile Framework for Model Compression: Evidence, Limits, and Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broadly applicable framework for compressing and adapting deep models across modalities, deployment constraints, and learning paradigms. Empirical work shows KD can produce compact models that approach teacher performance while enabling domain adaptation, federated and privacy-aware training, multimodal-to-mono-modal transfer, and efficient generative models. However, KD is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, propagation of teacher errors, sensitivity to teacher strength and data regime, and task-specific issues (e.g., generation vs. classification) require targeted algorithmic refinements. Advances such as feature-based distillation, adversarial and curriculum-based schemes, data augmentation during distillation, meta-learned teachers, and teacher-free formulations mitigate many failure modes and extend KD to low-data, heterogeneous-device, and few-shot settings. The combination of these innovations positions KD as a central tool for practical model compression and adaptation when used with methods that explicitly address its known limitations.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. When treated as a configurable, task-aware toolkit and combined with complementary compression methods, distillation enables deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and domain constraints. However, its effectiveness depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, and data strategy; it must be applied conditionally with safeguards against error and bias propagation.

papers_seen.author: Gutierrez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Context‑Aware First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile, and empirically supported family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD transfers predictive behavior and internal representations through soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational constraints, and many online or data-free protocols. While KD frequently enables large reductions in latency, memory, and compute with modest performance loss, its success is context dependent: it requires attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and task‑aware choices of distilled signals and complementary compression methods. When applied as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline — combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, careful data strategies, and safeguards against bias or distributional shift — KD is often the most practical and flexible first‑line approach for real-world model deployment.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Towards Model Agnostic Federated Learning Using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Is it possible to design an universal API for federated learning using which an ad-hoc group of data-holders (agents) collaborate with each other and perform federated learning? Such an API would necessarily need to be model-agnostic i.e. make no assumption about the model architecture being used by the agents, and also cannot rely on having representative public data at hand. Knowledge distillation (KD) is the obvious tool of choice to design such protocols. However, surprisingly, we show that most natural KD-based federated learning protocols have poor performance.   To investigate this, we propose a new theoretical framework, Federated Kernel ridge regression, which can capture both model heterogeneity as well as data heterogeneity. Our analysis shows that the degradation is largely due to a fundamental limitation of knowledge distillation under data heterogeneity. We further validate our framework by analyzing and designing new protocols based on KD. Their performance on real world experiments using neural networks, though still unsatisfactory, closely matches our theoretical predictions.

papers_seen.author: Potter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, Strengths, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a core set of techniques for transferring information from larger, high-capacity teacher models to smaller, efficient student models. Through objectives that match outputs, internal representations, or relational structure, KD enables reductions in latency, memory, and compute while often retaining much of teacher performance. The approach has been extended into many variants—feature- and layer-level alignment, attention- or projector-based mappings, multi-teacher and online schemes, data‑free and privacy-aware protocols, curriculum and adversarial sample strategies—and is applied across classification, retrieval, translation, evaluation metrics, and graph learning. Practical deployment requires addressing optimization and capacity mismatches, data and distributional constraints, and potential transfer of teacher artifacts; combining KD with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware distillation design produces the best results. Open directions center on principled selection of what to distill, robust distillation under data heterogeneity or privacy constraints, and automated, deployment-aware distillation pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Velasquez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large (teacher) models to smaller (student) models. KD methods vary by what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structure), how teachers and students are paired (single, ensemble, multi-teacher, or self-distillation), and by constraints on data, privacy, and deployment hardware. Across vision, language, speech, graphs, and reinforcement learning, KD produces compact models that often retain much of teacher performance while enabling lower latency, lower memory, and operation under communication- or privacy-constrained settings. However, gains depend on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and architectural alignment; practical pipelines therefore combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware design choices to close optimization and generalization gaps.

papers_seen.author: Mann
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Empirical Patterns, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. The literature has expanded KD beyond simple soft-target matching to include representation- and structure-level objectives, a variety of training schedules (offline, online, self-distillation, data-free), and many task- and architecture-aware adaptations. Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves most of teacher performance and sometimes improves robustness or calibration, but outcomes are sensitive to teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the data available for distillation, and the particular signals chosen for transfer. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture choices—and emphasizes task-aware design, data strategies, and safeguards against transferred biases or degraded low-frequency behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent work has shown that more effective dense retrieval models can be obtained by distilling ranking knowledge from an existing base re-ranking model. In this paper, we propose a generic curriculum learning based optimization framework called CL-DRD that controls the difficulty level of training data produced by the re-ranking (teacher) model. CL-DRD iteratively optimizes the dense retrieval (student) model by increasing the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data made available to it. In more detail, we initially provide the student model coarse-grained preference pairs between documents in the teacher's ranking and progressively move towards finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. In our experiments, we apply a simple implementation of the CL-DRD framework to enhance two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Experiments on three public passage retrieval datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: What Makes a "Good" Data Augmentation in Knowledge Distillation -- A Statistical Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a general neural network training approach that uses a teacher model to guide the student model. Existing works mainly study KD from the network output side (e.g., trying to design a better KD loss function), while few have attempted to understand it from the input side. Especially, its interplay with data augmentation (DA) has not been well understood. In this paper, we ask: Why do some DA schemes (e.g., CutMix) inherently perform much better than others in KD? What makes a "good" DA in KD? Our investigation from a statistical perspective suggests that a good DA scheme should reduce the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. A practical metric, the stddev of teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), is further presented and well justified empirically. Besides the theoretical understanding, we also introduce a new entropy-based data-mixing DA scheme, CutMixPick, to further enhance CutMix. Extensive empirical studies support our claims and demonstrate how we can harvest considerable performance gains simply by using a better DA scheme in knowledge distillation.

papers_seen.author: Hughes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically effective family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models to meet deployment constraints (latency, memory, compute, and privacy). KD spans logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, many-to-many layer mappings, online and multi‑teacher protocols, and data‑free or synthetic‑data variants. While KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss, its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, distillation signals, data availability, and safeguards against bias and privacy leakage. Thus KD should be treated as a configurable core of compression pipelines—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and task‑aware engineering—rather than a plug‑and‑play cure-all.

papers_seen.author: Fisher
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, flexible approach for producing compact models from larger teachers that preserves much of their performance across tasks and modalities. Its strengths arise from multiple transfer mechanisms (logits, intermediate features, attention, relational signals) and from compatibility with complementary compression tools. However, KD is not automatic: success requires careful choices about what to transfer, teacher quality, student capacity, data strategies, and integration with other compression methods. I argue that KD should be treated as a first-class, configurable component of modern model-deployment toolkits, with explicit practices to mitigate its failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Hodges
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Ubiquitous, but Demand-Aware
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely applicable approach for compressing high-capacity models into efficient students across modalities and tasks. Empirical results across vision, language, multimodal, graph, and generative settings show KD can recover much of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and device-heterogeneity constraints. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on how knowledge is represented and transferred (logits, features, attention, contrastive objectives), the alignment between teacher and student inputs, the data used for distillation, and attention to robustness, fairness, and privacy. Carefully chosen distillation algorithms and extensions (self-supervised distillation, meta-learned teachers, multi-teacher weighting, online and distributed schemes, and privacy-preserving perturbations) can mitigate common failure modes and broaden KD’s applicability in production and research settings.

papers_seen.author: Burke
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving or sometimes improving task performance. When treated as a configurable, task-aware component and combined with complementary compression techniques (e.g., pruning, quantization, layer mapping, or data synthesis), KD yields favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across modalities and supports deployment under latency, privacy, and data-constraint requirements. However, realizing KD's benefits reliably requires attention to teacher quality, student capacity, what signals are transferred, how layers are aligned, and which training data or augmentations are used.

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Approaches, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods transfer knowledge from larger, more expensive models to smaller, efficient ones. The approaches span soft-logit supervision, feature- and layer-level matching, contrastive and relational objectives, and adaptations for special settings such as low-precision inference, multimodal models, graph data, federated learning, and heterogeneous-device training. Empirical work shows KD can improve student accuracy, robustness, and latency while theoretical analyses connect KD to label smoothing and regularization effects. Best practice choices (which teacher signals to match, which samples or augmentations to use, and how to align heterogeneous inputs) materially affect outcomes. This synthesis summarizes known methods, insights about why KD helps, and practical considerations for deploying KD in real-world ML systems.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression (but Not a Standalone Solution)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically effective tool for producing compact models from larger teachers across vision and NLP. KD reliably reduces inference cost and supports deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but it also has concrete failure modes (capacity mismatch, propagated teacher artifacts, rare-token degradation, and data-availability limits). The best practical strategy treats KD as the default first-line compression mechanism that must be configured to the task and explicitly combined with complementary techniques and safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models to reduce latency, memory, and compute while retaining much of teacher performance. A diverse set of distillation targets and training protocols has been developed (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive signals; offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, and data‑free variants). Empirical work across vision, language, speech and multimodal tasks shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and is most effective when integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and when training/data procedures are adapted to task and deployment constraints. Remaining gaps include principled layer alignment across heterogeneous architectures, robust distillation under limited or private data, preservation of long‑tail/low‑frequency behaviors, and theoretical understanding of when particular teacher signals are necessary.

papers_seen.author: Rivera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Integrated Framework for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the functionality of larger teachers. KD works across modalities, supports deployment under resource and privacy constraints, and also acts as a regularizer; however, it has concrete failure modes that require complementary methods and careful teacher–student design. I argue that KD should be treated as a central, configurable component of any compression pipeline, used in combination with representation-aware objectives, curriculum and data strategies, and targeted safeguards for bias, low-frequency behavior, and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses high-capacity teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across modalities and tasks, a broad toolkit of distillation targets and protocols has been developed and combined with complementary compression methods to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Success is context dependent: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability, and careful task-aware design determine how much teacher performance is preserved and what tradeoffs arise.

papers_seen.author: Wheeler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression encompass a broad set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger or richer models to smaller, faster, or modality-restricted models. Across computer vision, natural language processing, reinforcement learning, graph learning, federated settings, and multi-modal systems, KD variants—ranging from feature- and layer-wise matching to self-distillation, data-free adversarial schemes, and task-aware filtering—have been applied to address capacity gaps, domain shifts, privacy constraints, and inference latency. Empirical and methodological work shows that careful alignment between teacher and student (in representation, task relevance, or sample selection), consideration of data heterogeneity, and incorporation of pre-training or auxiliary objectives improve student performance. Open challenges include robust distillation under heterogeneous architectures and non-iid data, mitigating bias transfer, and designing distillation objectives that prioritize downstream task relevance while remaining communication- and privacy-efficient.

papers_seen.author: Palmer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger or ensembled teachers to compact students. KD routinely enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and parameter count while preserving a large fraction of teacher performance when applied with task-aware choices about distilled signals, data, and architecture. However, KD is not a universal cure: its reliability depends on teacher–student alignment, data availability and selection, and explicit mitigations for transferred biases, privacy leakage, and rare-case degradation. The best outcomes treat KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that combines complementary methods and evaluation practices tailored to target tasks and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have become central strategies for deploying large deep models under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. A diverse set of methods—ranging from soft-label distillation, intermediate feature and attention matching, layer mapping, adversarial and data-free techniques, to task-adaptive architecture search and meta-learning of teachers—have been proposed to transfer performance from bulky teachers to compact students. These approaches are applied across domains including vision, language, multi-modal systems, recommender systems, and domain-specific NLP, and they trade off fidelity to the teacher, generalization, and computational efficiency. Empirical results show that properly designed distillation pipelines can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while yielding substantial speedups and memory reductions, and in some settings can even improve fairness, robustness, or downstream generalization. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous inputs and representations across teacher and student, coping with absent or private training data, and automatically selecting what and how to transfer for specific tasks and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: State of the Art, Practices, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly validated set of techniques for compressing large or ensemble models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or relational structure. KD variants and complementary compression methods enable deployment under constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and heterogeneous hardware across vision, language, speech, recommendation, and generative tasks. Success requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teachers and students, how to handle limited or private data, and how to integrate distillation with pretraining and other compression methods. Remaining challenges include teacher bias transfer, capacity mismatch, preserving low-frequency behaviors, and robust data-free or federated distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Core of Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD routinely yields substantial latency and memory reductions while retaining much teacher performance when it is applied as part of an integrated, task- and data-aware compression pipeline. However, KD is context-sensitive: its reliability depends on choices of distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategies (including synthetic or teacher-generated data), and explicit measures to avoid propagating teacher artifacts or biases.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Private Model Compression via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The soaring demand for intelligent mobile applications calls for deploying powerful deep neural networks (DNNs) on mobile devices. However, the outstanding performance of DNNs notoriously relies on increasingly complex models, which in turn is associated with an increase in computational expense far surpassing mobile devices' capacity. What is worse, app service providers need to collect and utilize a large volume of users' data, which contain sensitive information, to build the sophisticated DNN models. Directly deploying these models on public mobile devices presents prohibitive privacy risk. To benefit from the on-device deep learning without the capacity and privacy concerns, we design a private model compression framework RONA. Following the knowledge distillation paradigm, we jointly use hint learning, distillation learning, and self learning to train a compact and fast neural network. The knowledge distilled from the cumbersome model is adaptively bounded and carefully perturbed to enforce differential privacy. We further propose an elegant query sample selection method to reduce the number of queries and control the privacy loss. A series of empirical evaluations as well as the implementation on an Android mobile device show that RONA can not only compress cumbersome models efficiently but also provide a strong privacy guarantee. For example, on SVHN, when a meaningful $(9.83,10^{-6})$-differential privacy is guaranteed, the compact model trained by RONA can obtain 20$\times$ compression ratio and 19$\times$ speed-up with merely 0.97% accuracy loss.

papers_seen.author: Schultz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Findings from the Provided Literature
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring information from large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient student models so they can be deployed under constraints of latency, memory, compute, and privacy. The literature treats KD as a flexible, configurable component of compression pipelines rather than a single recipe: methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, channel- or relation-level signals), how transfer is organized (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, data-free/zero-shot), and how KD is combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, adversarial training). Empirical evidence shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but success depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the chosen distillation signals and objectives, and data availability or synthesis strategies. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable, task-aware tool integrated with other compression and robustness practices.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practically driven toolbox for transferring performance from large teacher models to smaller student models across modalities and tasks. Methods span soft-label supervision, feature- and layer-wise imitation, adversarial and ensemble-based transfer, data- and privacy-aware protocols, and integration with complementary compression strategies (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but gains depend strongly on what is transferred, teacher–student alignment, domain shift, and data availability.

papers_seen.author: Andrews
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, efficient students by transferring information from teachers via outputs, internal representations, or relational signals. KD is broadly applicable across modalities and settings and is most effective when combined with task-aware design choices and complementary compression methods. Despite strong empirical successes, important practical and theoretical challenges remain—teacher–student mismatch, data heterogeneity or scarcity, transferred biases, robustness under distribution shift, and privacy constraints—motivating targeted algorithmic and systems-level remedies and further study.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable approach for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact student models. The literature establishes a rich taxonomy of distillation signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational maps, contrastive objectives), training protocols (offline, online, self-distillation, data-free), and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Practical success depends on task- and data-aware choices, teacher and student design, and integration with other compression strategies; KD is powerful but not universally sufficient on its own. Ongoing directions emphasize task-adaptive objectives, data-efficient and privacy-preserving workflows, federated and heterogeneous-device scenarios, and theoretical understanding of when and why particular distilled signals help.

papers_seen.author: Murray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Conditional Component of Hybrid Model‑Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and empirically effective approach for producing compact, deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller students. While KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and supports deployment under compute, latency, and privacy constraints, its reliability depends on task-aware choices about distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data regimes, and complementary compression methods. I argue KD should be treated as a configurable core within hybrid compression pipelines, paired with complementary techniques and explicit safeguards to address robustness, fairness, and data- or privacy-limited settings.

papers_seen.author: Coffey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a flexible, empirically validated family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD methods span soft-label/logit transfer, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational or contrastive objectives, and specialized protocols for data-free, federated, cross‑modal, and adversarial settings. KD frequently yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade‑offs, but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, and the availability or synthesis of suitable data. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies—rather than as a standalone panacea.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods provide practical routes to deploy high-performing deep models under resource, privacy, and latency constraints. The literature has developed diverse approaches that transfer information via soft logits, intermediate features, attentional maps, channel-wise statistics, and online mutual learning; adaptations address task-specific compression, data-free or few-shot regimes, large-scale distributed training, and teacher-student co-optimization. Empirical and theoretical analyses highlight that distillation combines information transfer with regularization effects, and that selecting what, when, and how to transfer knowledge (e.g., logits vs. features, offline vs. online, task-aware filtering) is crucial to achieve favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across vision and language tasks.

papers_seen.author: Salas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of the Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used family of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce latency, memory, and compute while preserving much of task performance. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal domains, KD methods range from soft-target (logit) matching to richer objectives that mimic internal representations, attention, relational structure, or contrastive signals. KD is frequently combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and adapted to practical constraints via data-free, few-shot, online, or federated protocols. Success depends on careful, task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited data, privacy, distribution shift, and undesirable teacher behaviors. The literature emphasizes KD as a configurable component of broader compression pipelines rather than a turnkey algorithm.

papers_seen.author: Washington
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central but Insufficient — A Task‑Aware, Integrated Approach to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile mechanism for transferring competence from large teacher models to compact student models, enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory, and deployability while retaining much of teacher performance. However, KD alone does not guarantee robust, fair, or hardware‑optimal compression; its effectiveness depends on careful, task‑aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle limited or private data, and how to integrate complementary compression methods. Treating KD as the central element within an engineered pipeline — augmented by teacher selection, data strategies, and pruning/quantization or architecture adaptations — delivers the most reliable outcomes for real deployments.

For practical, robust compression, KD should be a central, configurable component of a task‑aware pipeline that incorporates complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), curriculum and sample‑selection strategies, and targeted remedies for distribution shift, low‑frequency phenomena, and privacy constraints.

Practical success depends on matching the distilled signal to student capacity and data regime, combining KD with other compression methods, and explicitly addressing known failure modes such as teacher bias, capacity mismatch, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: French
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or relational structure. papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Efficient Transformer-based Large Scale Language Representations using Hardware-friendly Block Structured Pruning
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained large-scale language models have increasingly demonstrated high accuracy on many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, the limited weight storage and computational speed on hardware platforms have impeded the popularity of pre-trained models, especially in the era of edge computing. In this work, we propose an efficient transformer-based large-scale language representation using hardware-friendly block structure pruning. We incorporate the reweighted group Lasso into block-structured pruning for optimization. Besides the significantly reduced weight storage and computation, the proposed approach achieves high compression rates. Experimental results on different models (BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT) on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark tasks show that we achieve up to 5.0x with zero or minor accuracy degradation on certain task(s). Our proposed method is also orthogonal to existing compact pre-trained language models such as DistilBERT using knowledge distillation, since a further 1.79x average compression rate can be achieved on top of DistilBERT with zero or minor accuracy degradation. It is suitable to deploy the final compressed model on resource-constrained edge devices.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a single compression trick into a flexible framework for producing compact, deployable models and for transferring behavior across domains, modalities, and privacy-constrained settings. When applied thoughtfully—choosing what signals to transfer, aligning teacher and student capacities, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods—KD enables significant reductions in model size and latency while preserving much of teacher performance. At the same time, distillation has clear failure modes (optimization gaps, distributional mismatch, and social harms) that require targeted mitigation and careful evaluation. I argue that KD should be treated as a central, application-driven toolkit for model compression and adaptation, not a one-size-fits-all recipe.
